metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defense, Schönemann Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This fine move has more significance than the mere development of a piece combined with a mating threat. The ulterior object is to create a permanent irremediable weakness in White’s kingside position by forcing one of the defending pawns to make a move.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defense, Schönemann Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The only possible defence. If instead 12 f4, then 12...exf3 13 Qxf3 Qxh2+ 14 Kf2 Bg4 and Black wins.
After the text move, Black starts an attack, but using his pieces rather than trying to break into the position by the pawn assault 12... h5 followed by ...h4.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defense, Schönemann Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black bases his attack on the theme of penetration. White has weakened the f3- and h3-squares by 12 g3, as these squares are no longer guarded by the g-pawn. These squares are now ‘holes’, as Steinitz first named them. Enemy pieces that settle themselves on these squares stand firm, as no pawns can ever drive them away.
The bishop attacks the queen, with the object of insinuating itself into f3 without loss of time.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defense, Schönemann Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: As good as there is. If White interposes the knight at e2 instead, then 13... Qh5, attacking the knight once more, forces 14 Re1, whereupon 14... Qh3 plants a piece in one hole. Black’s following move is 15... Bf3, occupying the other hole, and the stage is set for mate at g2.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defense, Schönemann Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The second step in the process of penetration.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defense, Schönemann Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Hoping for a line such as 14... Qe7 15 Bxd6 Qxd6 16 Qf4, when an exchange or two might ease his difficulties.
After White’s fourteenth move, Black has a forced mate in a few moves.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defense, Schönemann Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Deserts the bishop, but Black is interested only in getting the queen to h3, with a death grip on the light squares.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defense, Schönemann Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only possible chance to defend. The knight is to be brought to e3 to guard the g2-square, where mate impends.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defense, Schönemann Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Threatening instant mate.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defense, Schönemann Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Defending the critical square.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defense, Schönemann Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The new threat is mate at h2. Notice the clever use of the weakened light squares on the kingside as the black pieces infiltrate the enemy position.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defense, Schönemann Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Room for the king!

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defense, Schönemann Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: And mate comes next move.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Schliemann Defense, Schönemann Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This move accomplishes a great deal:
A pawn is fixed in the centre of the board.
The pawn exerts a grip on d5 and f5, and keeps Black’s pieces from settling on those squares.
White’s queen and bishop immediately have breathing space.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
With several objects in view:
One, to prevent White from dictating the opening. After the conventional reply 1... e5 White can play the Ruy Lopez, the Giuoco Piano, the Scotch, the Vienna Game or a dangerous gambit of some sort.
Another is that Black’s cramped position may tempt White into a disastrous premature attack.
A third is that the pawn at e6 supports an advance by 2... d5, an attack on the e-pawn which might wrest the initiative.
The French Defence is not to be underestimated. It conceals a great deal of dynamic energy behind a modest facade.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: If it’s worthwhile to establish one pawn in the centre, then keeping two pawns there should double the benefits.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black gives his queen more scope and challenges the centre.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Clearly an excellent response, as the knight develops to its proper square, protects the e-pawn, and bears down on d5.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black in turn brings his own knight to its strongest position with gain of time – a further attack on the e4-pawn.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Many players prefer to add to the pressure by 4 Bg5 (which develops a piece and renders one of the enemy’s impotent) rather than exchange pawns, which relaxes the tension.
Spielmann, who likes wide-open positions, clears away a couple of pawns to give his pieces more room for their activities.
Which move is better? Which should you play? The answer is: play the move that you like, the one that best suits your style and temperament. If you are a careful, cautious player who knows the full value of a pawn – that each one is a potential queen, and that the loss of a pawn may be the loss of the game – stick to 4 Bg5 and the openings of positional chess, the Ruy Lopez, the Queen’s Pawn openings, the Réti and the English. On the other hand, if you prefer daring, adventurous chess, and a pawn is simply a barrier to the sweeping onrush of an attack by your pieces, play openings which allow scope for your imagination, the Evans, Danish, King’s and other gambits.
The best openings to play are the ones you are most at home in.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Better than taking with the knight. Black keeps a pawn in the centre and frees his c8-bishop.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White pins the knight and threatens to break up Black’s game by 6 Bxf6 gxf6 (6... Qxf6 loses the d5-pawn), when Black is left with a weak doubled pawn.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The simplest way of unpinning the knight. Moving the bishop only one square may not seem much of a move, but it complies with the first law of rapid development: Get your pieces off the back rank!

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This bishop’s stand is aggressive, especially against kingside castling.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This knight’s debut is even more menacing, as it threatens to take the d-pawn.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
After the customary development 7 Nf3, Black pins the knight by 7... Bg4 and again threatens the d-pawn. White could save the pawn, for instance by 8 Be2, but would lose the initiative.
After the text-move, if Black pins the knight by 7... Bg4, 8 f3 repels the bishop and causes it to lose time retreating.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Intending to get rid of a dangerous enemy piece and also to assure himself of a little advantage in keeping both his bishops.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Now we see another reason for developing the knight to e2. White wants to anchor a piece at f5, a dominating position for a knight or a bishop. A piece need do no more than just stand there and look menacing to rattle the opponent.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Mission accomplished. Black has a slight technical superiority in retaining two long-range bishops against White’s knight and bishop, but...

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: ...at the cost of a loss of time. Black has made three moves with the knight to exchange it for a bishop that moved only once. More than that, his knight came off the board completely, while the bishop left a piece in its place. The result is that White has four active pieces in play against two of Black’s. White is also prepared to castle on either side and mobilize both rooks quickly. Whatever advantage exists is therefore White’s.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This pawn move prevents White from placing his knight at f5, but it creates an organic weakness in Black’s position, one that is irremediable. The squares f6 and h6, no longer guarded by the pawn, are weak and remain so permanently.
Notice that the pawn was induced but not forced to move forward. The mere threat of an inroad by the knight was enough to influence Black to make a natural preventive move. It is the sort of move nine out of ten players make automatically in similar situations, which is why it is important to know how to exploit its defects, for no move is weak unless proper advantage is taken of its flaws.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
No violence, please, until the reserves have been brought up. Blackburne used to say, “Never start an attack until your queen’s rook is developed.”
White secures the safety of his king and gets one rook out of hiding.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Strengthens Black’s pawn-centre and opens another avenue for his queen.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White seizes the only open file (since rooks belong on open files or on files likely to be opened) and pins the bishop.
It is worth noting that a pinned piece not only is unable to move but is also powerless to capture. It does not protect any other pieces, since it is completely paralysed. Hence it follows that not only is the bishop immobilized and in danger of its life (as it may be attacked again and again) but the knight that depends on it for protection is no longer secure. Briefly, Black is now threatened with loss of a piece by 12 Bxf6.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: “When we know about the inspiring ideas, how simple the sacrifices appear!” says Znosko-Borovsky.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must recapture, leaving the knight pinned and a fine target for further attack.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Putting pressure on the pinned piece, and threatening to take the knight.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king comes to the rescue of the knight. Against the alternative defence 13... Bf5 Spielmann had this pretty continuation: 14 Nxf5 gxf5 15 Qg3(threatening g mate on the move by 16 Bxf6#) 15... Kg7 (or 15... Kh8 16 Qh4 Kg7 17 Qh6+ Kg8 18 Bxf6 and White wins) 16 Bxf6++ Kxf6 17 Qh4+ Ke6 18 Re1+ Kd7 19 Qxe7+ and all Black’s pieces come off.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White must keep hammering at the pinned knight, no matter how many brilliant moves he has to find! Again, White’s immediate threat is simple: 15 Bxf6+, winning instantaneously.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must take this knight or lose his own.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Three pieces now attack the helpless knight. “Chess is not for the kind-hearted,” says the French proverb.
White now threatens 16 Bxf6+ followed by 17 Bxe7.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
On 15... Qxe4 White has the pleasant choice of winning the queen by 16 Bxf6+ (removing the protector of the queen), followed by 17 Qxe4, or forcing mate by 16 Qxf6+ Kg8 17 Bh6 followed by 18 Qg7#.
In the last line of play, notice how White screws his pieces firmly into the two holes in Black’s position, f6 and h6, the squares no longer guarded by the g-pawn after its advance.
With his last move, Black saves the queen. He is still ahead in material but has a lost game, as White’s pieces will insinuate themselves along the dark squares to get at the king.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Exchange Variation, Svenonius Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
One reason for the popularity of queen’s pawn openings is that from the very first move they present problems for the defender. T no method by which Black can seize the initiative or even equalize in a hurry.
Despite its inherently positional nature, the queen’s pawn appeals tremendously to attacking players and has always been a favourite weapon of such aggressive spirits as Alekhine, Keres, Pillsbury, Bogoljubow, Spielmann and Colle.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Brings a piece into play where it has an influence on the centre. The knight move prevents White from continuing with 2 e4.
A master moves his knight to f6 as instinctively as he breathes.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The knight develops toward the centre, where he has the greatest freedom of action and the widest scope for his activities.
The knight possesses the peculiar property of being able to attack any other piece (except another knight) without being under attack in return. This attribute makes it a fascinating piece to manoeuvre about the board. Combinations involving play with the knights often have a ballet-like quality to them.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black can avoid the general attack of the Colle by playing 2... d5, ready to reply to 3 e3 with 3... Bf5. Then 4 Bd3 Bxd3 exchanges bishops and Black rids himself of White’s most dangerous attacking piece (in this form of the opening).
With his actual move, Black releases his f8-bishop and does not commit himself to any specific line of defence.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Indicating his design: obviously White is preparing the typical Colle formation of bishop at d3 and knight at d2, to control the key e4-square, a jumping-off point for the pieces in this attack.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black plants a pawn firmly in the centre but this move, in combination with 2... e6, does block in the c8-bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White begins the concentration of pressure on e4, essential in the Colle. Generally speaking, it is a good plan to mobilize the pieces on the kingside first, to enable early castling on that side.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This move is almost indispensable in queen ’ s pawn openings. It is important not to play ... Nc6 first, as Black’s c-pawn must not be obstructed.
Black’s move strikes at the centre and establishes a state of tension in that area.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White reinforces the d-pawn. In the event of 5...cxd4, White can recapture with the e-pawn and open the diagonal for the c1-bishop.
It may seem that White’s last move denies the b1-knight his best square, but in this form of attack the knight belongs at d2.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This is probably superior to placing the knight at c6. At d7, the knights are in touch with each other, so that if the f6-knight is exchanged the other can get to f6, an ideal square for attack or defence. At d7, the knight keeps clear of the c-file. The more open the file is, the more useful will it be for the queen or rook that occupies it. Finally, should White play 6 dxc5, the knight can recapture and come strongly into the game.
In queen’s pawn openings, Black’s queen’s knight often does a better job at d7 than at c6.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Intensifying the pressure on e4. To the uninitiated, White’s development has an awkward look. The pieces seem to be in each other’s way, but as will be seen they can spring into action smoothly and easily.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: More energetic than 6... Be7, when the bishop is limited to defensive duties.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White secures the safety of his king before starting any decisive action. It is dangerous to open up the position and leave the king in the centre where it is exposed to a possible counterattack.
White’s castling is aggressive in character as the king’s rook plays an important role in the coming attack.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black’s castling is a defensive measure. But why give the king’s permanent address when White has revealed that he is preparing an assault on the kingside? It would be better strategy to keep the opponent in the dark – delay castling for a while and continue developing the pieces (which surely can do no harm). Black might bring his queen to c7, with a view to an early ...e5, and then fianchetto his c8-bishop (...b6, followed by ... Bb7).

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Still more pressure on e4! The rook gets a grip on the e-file; it is closed now but will be opened after White plays e4 and pawns are exchanged.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: An ideal location for the queen. From c7 the queen bears down on the centre, especially e5, and exerts great pressure on the c-file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The key move in the Colle! With this move White intends to blast the position wide open and release all the stored-up energy of his pieces in a searing attack.
The immediate threat is 10 e5, a simple, brutal attack on two pieces.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: As compensation for being on the defensive, Black controls the open c-file – temporarily.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Better than taking with the knight, which lets Black place pieces on e5 and c5.
White meanwhile renews the threat of winning a piece by 11 e5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black parries the threat and saddles White with an isolated d-pawn. Such a pawn is especially vulnerable to attack as it cannot be protected by another pawn, the nearest one being a couple of files away.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Certainly not 11 Bxe4 because 11... Nxe4 would be the response, and White loses the services of his valuable light-squared bishop. “As Rousseau could not compose without his cat beside him, so I without my king’s bishop cannot play chess,” says Tarrasch. “In its absence the game to me is lifeless and cold. The vitalizing factor is missing, and I can devise no plan of attack.”

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Intending to mobilize his c8-bishop. Somewhat more to the point was 11... Bf4 restraining one of White’s menacing bishops.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop joins the attack, and vacates the c1-square. The a1-rook will swing there, drive the queen off and assume complete control of a beautiful open file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Apparently Black was afraid to play 12... Bb7 as the continuation 13 Nxf6+ Nxf6 14 Bxf6 gxf6 breaks up his kingside pawn position.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Superior to the natural 13 Bxe4, when Black might reply 13... Bb7 forcing 14 Bd3 (to avoid exchanging bishops). Then he could continue 14... Bxf3 15 Qxf3 Bxh2+ consoling himself with a pawn for his troubles.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: There is hardly anything better than this, which offers the bishop a long diagonal. If, for example, Black plays 13... Nf6, then 14 Rh4 is hard to meet. Then the threat of winning a pawn by 15 Bxf6 gxf6 16 Bxh7+ could not be parried by 14... h6 as 15 Bxf6 gxf6 16 Rxh6 still wins a pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A fine ‘in-between’ move! The rook is developed effectively on the open file, while the queen is banished to the first rank. There she interferes with the a8-rook, preventing its development for a long time – forever, as it turns out!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: There is nothing else as 14... Bxe4 15 Rxc7 Bxf3 16 Qxf3 Bxc7 17 Qc6 wins a piece for White.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The point! White’s threat of 16 Bxh7+ forces one of the pawns in front of the king to move forward. White gets an advantage, no matter which pawn advances, as:
Every pawn move loosens the defending structure.
Every undefended square (occasioned by such an advance) creates a weakness in the position.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
If Black tries defending the h-pawn by 15... Nf6, then 16 Bxf6 gxf6 17 Bxh7+ wins the pawn just the same. Or if Black advances the h-pawn by 15... h6, then 16 Bxh6 gxh6 17 Rxh6 is an obvious sacrificial combination which shatters the cordon of pawns and exposes the king to a mating attack.
After the text-move. White has accomplished what he set out to do: he has forced the advance of the g-pawn. But how does he exploit the resulting weakness? Is there an attack against the pawn? Apparently there isn’t, as in order to strike at it with the h-pawn, he must move the rook out of the way, and then play h4 and h5, a process which takes time and achieves little.
What other line is there? Sacrifice a piece for the g-pawn? Obviously this is useless, as White still does not break through.
But the pawn did advance, and there is a weakness somewhere. We know this fact to be true, and in this fact there must be the clue to the winning combination.
The pawn’s advance weakened the squares h6 and f6, as they are no longer guarded by the pawn. This means that White must try to get control of these squares, either seize and occupy them with his pieces, or use them as a means of penetrating into the enemy camp.
But wait! Doesn’t Black’s knight still guard the f6-square? Indeed it does, and this knowledge provides us with the information we need. The knight is the guardian of the dark squares, and the knight must be destroyed!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Attacks the knight, which strangely enough has no place to escape to!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
What other way is there to protect the knight?
If 16... Bc8, then 17 Bc6 wins the exchange.
If 16 ... Bxf3 17 Qxf3 Qe8, then 18 Qb7 wins a piece.
After the actual move, the knight is pinned and a good target for further attack.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: In chess you may hit a man when he’s down.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Taking the props out from under the knight! The technique is simple: if you cannot increase the pressure on a piece, see if you can dispose of one of its defenders.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Certainly not 18... Rxc8, when 19 Bxd7 wins two pieces for a rook, and then corners the queen!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White has two pieces for the rook - and the attack!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Not 19 ... Qb7 or 19... Qb8, as 20 Bc6 wins the exchange. The alternative was 19 . . . Qa6, but Black hopes for some counterplay on the c-file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The first step toward exploiting the weak dark squares brings with it a threat of mate by 21 Nf6+ Kh8 (21... Kg7 is the same) 22 Rxh7#.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight comes in on one of the critical dark squares to strike the first blow.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: If 21 ... Kh8, then 22 Rxh5+ forces a quick mate.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Sacrificing the knight to sweep away the pawns shielding the enemy king.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must take the knight, because White mates after 22... Kg8 (or 22 ... Kh7) 23 Nf6+ Kg7 24 Rh7#.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The queen’s first move threatens two immediate mates on the h-file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The only move to stop mate - temporarily.
Appropriately enough, White administers the coup de grâce on the second critical dark square.
Mate follows in two moves.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black resigns.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This first move occupies the centre with a pawn and frees four squares for the queen and five for the f 1-bishop. One of the reasons many players prefer 1 e4 to any other opening move is that it gets the kingside pieces rolling quickly, enabling early castling on that side.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
In the old days this was almost compulsory. It indicated that you were willing to stand toe-to-toe and slug it out. Only a coward would avoid 1... e5 and a possible gambit by White.
Objectively considered, the text-move is perhaps Black’s strongest response. It challenges possession of the centre and prevents White from monopolizing it by continuing 2 d4.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
What happens if White persists and plays 2 d4? The reply 2...exd4 leads to 3 Qxd4 Nc6 4 Qe3 Nf6, when Black has two pieces in play to one of White’s. This amounts to taking the initiative away from White early in the game.
The text-move is far more effective than random development of the knight, for instance at h3, where it is out of touch with affairs in the centre, or at e2, where it blocks all traffic.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The logical way to meet the attack on the pawn; a minor piece develops toward the centre and defends the pawn.
The general plan of mobilization is to establish a pawn in the centre, develop the minor pieces (the knights before bishops, whenever feasible), then castle to get the rooks to the centre files, and finally bring the queen out – but not too far from home. Premature development of the queen is dangerous, as it is subject to annoying attacks by pawns and minor pieces.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The most natural move on the board: White strikes at the defender of the pawn he attacks. It is true that he cannot win the pawn at once, as after 4 Bxc6 dxc6 5 Nxe5 Qd4 Black regains the pawn, but the pressure on Black is constant, and the threat is always in the air.
The Ruy Lopez is probably the strongest of all kingside openings. White has more to say in the centre, since he will be able to play d4 without much trouble, while Black will find it difficult to achieve ...d5.
White’s pieces have more room to move around in, while Black’s game is considerably cramped in many variations.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This can become like the story The House that Jack Built: the pawn attacks the bishop that attacks the knight that defends the pawn that the knight attacks.
Black’s purpose is to dislodge the bishop from its favourable position. The loss of time involved in moving a pawn is compensated for by the fact that the threatened bishop must also lose a move in retreating.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is in the spirit of the opening as it maintains pressure on the knight. The alternative withdrawal to c4 is inferior, as the same position could have arisen after the move 3 Bc4, except that here Black has the additional move ...a6, which can only be to his benefit.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black develops a piece, attacks a pawn and prepares early kingside castling. More could hardly be expected of one move.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White brings his king to safety and swings the rook over toward the centre files.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A favourite continuation with many players is 5 ... Nxe4, not with the idea of winning a pawn, as White regains it easily, but in order to obtain a free, open game. The danger in this line is that it leaves Black’s position in the centre somewhat insecure.
The text leads to a more blocked position, difficult to break through, but requires patience on Black’s part. The bishop’s development at e7 is satisfactory even though it has moved only one square away from home. The important thing is that it has left the back rank and facilitated castling.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White brings his rook toward the centre. In lieu of an open file, the rook prepares to take command of a file liable to be opened. In guarding his own e-pawn, White renews the threat of 7 Bxc6 dxc6 8 Nxe5 winning a pawn.
The rook’s move is preferable to developing the b1-knight to c3. White may want to provide a retreat for his bishop by c3, guarding it against an exchange.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White meets the threat by forcing the bishop back.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Obviously the only move.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black protects the e-pawn, releases the c8-bishop and prepares 8 . . . Na5 to remove the troublesome enemy bishop.
At first glance it seems illogical to give one bishop freedom while hemming in the other, but since the dark-squared bishop does a good job at e7, it remains for the light-squared bishop to go out into the world.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
With two objects:
To provide refuge for the bishop against an attempt to remove it by 8 ... Na5 .
To support an advance of the d-pawn, establishing a strong pawn-centre.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Not so much to strike at the bishop as to make way for 9... c5 to dispute control of the central squares. In this line of the Lopez, Black’s best counter-chances lie in action on the queenside.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Naturally, White wants to keep both bishops. He loses a tempo, but it is offset by Black’s posting of a knight at the side of the board.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black intensifies his pressure on the central square d4 and provides an egress (as the old books used to say) for the queen.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
One of the chief objectives in king’s pawn openings is to advance the d-pawn to the centre as soon as circumstances permit, just as in queen’s pawn openings it is desirable to get the e-pawn to e4 when there is an opportunity to do so.
White again threatens to win the e-pawn by the double attack on it.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black gives his pawn further support and develops his queen at the same time. It would not do to exchange by 10...exd4 11 cxd4 cxd4 12 Nxd4 as it surrenders the centre and leaves Black with an isolated centre pawn. “An isolated pawn,” says Tartakower, “casts gloom over the entire chessboard.” White would benefit too in that his knight, standing firmly in the centre of the board, could not be dislodged by unfriendly pawns.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
To prevent the pin .... Bg4, which might embarrass the knight and the piece it shields, the queen. Both pieces are needed for the protection of the d-pawn and the maintenance of the pawn formation in the centre. An exchange of the white knight by .... Bxf3, and the recapture by the queen, removes at one stroke two supports of the d-pawn.
Is White violating principle in moving one of the pawns near his king? Maybe, but one must know when to slight conventions as well as observe them. In this particular situation it is important to prevent an attack on the knight, its subsequent exchange and the break-up of White’s pawns in the centre. The move of the h-pawn is weakening, but a lesser evil than would result from permitting the pin. But wait a moment! Is it a weakening move if Black is unable to benefit by it? Is it detrimental to the position if Black cannot exploit it by a kingside attack?
The answer is no! A move is weak only if the opponent can turn its imperfections to his advantage. The entire position is strong or weak only in relation to the position of the opponent. In this case, the move of the h-pawn is expedient as it conforms to the requirements of the specific position.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The knight returns and adds weight to the pressure on the d-pawn.
Black threatens a series of exchanges by 12...exd4 13 cxd4 cxd4, resulting in the gain of a pawn, as the further sequence 14 Nxd4? Nxd4 15 Qxd4 Qxc2 would cost White a piece. Black hopes to tempt White into playing 12 d5 to meet this threat. This looks good, as it would evict the c6-knight from a good post, but it has the drawback (for White) of releasing the tension in the centre, as well as making d5 unavailable for the use of his pieces.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White is in no hurry. He brings aid to the d-pawn by developing another piece.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Removing the king to safer quarters and pressing the rook into active service.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This knight has been developed where he has little mobility and seems to have no future to speak of, but it is the first step that counts. Little as this is, its consequence is worth emphasizing:
The knight’s move clears the first rank and enables the major pieces (the queen and the rooks) to get in touch with each other.
Get your pieces off the back rank and into active play!

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black does likewise: his bishop vacates the back row to let the rooks come to the centre files.
The rooks are powerful pieces and must not be shut in.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: In the early stages of the game, the rooks may not do much but they must be ready for action when it comes. This they best do by placing themselves at the head of open files. If none are available, then they should work on partly open files. If none of those exist, the rooks should still be brought toward the centre, as those files are most likely to be opened. But in any case, get the rooks out of the corners!

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Planning to advance the f-pawn. This pawn will dispute the centre with White’s e-pawn while opening the f-file for the rook.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight retreats to gain momentum for a leap to g3 and then f5, a beautiful outpost.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Not only to keep the knight out but also to support 16... f5, a thrust at the centre.
The advance of the g-pawn weakens the squares f6 and h6, as they are no longer guarded by the pawn. This may strike the average player as an interesting but perhaps insignificant point, but recognizing a weakness and knowing how to take advantage of it marks the master player. Good players do not win games by waiting for you to make monumental mistakes. They don’t expect you to leave pieces en prise.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White immediately anchors a piece on one of the vulnerable kingside squares.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only move to prevent loss of the exchange by 17 Bxf8.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight comes back into the game by a slightly different route than was planned earlier. Not only does it add to the pressure on d5 but it also threatens to settle down powerfully on that square.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black could not stop the knight coming in by 17 ... Be6, as 18 d5 in reply wins a piece.
He also abandons the contemplated break by 17... f5, as it opens the position, and open lines favour the player whose development is superior and who is better equipped to use these lines in an attack.
With his actual move, Black tries to keep a tightly knit defensive position, one that is difficult to break through.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A very fine move whose object is more profound than the obvious one of fixing a piece on a strong central square.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The queen must flee from the knight’s attack.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is the point! The knight gives up his good position for a worthy cause. It is important, in order to capitalize on the weakness of the dark square f6, to remove the guardian of this square, the dark-squared bishop on e7. With this bishop out of the way the weakness is accentuated and White can then consider some means of invading, and then fastening a piece, on the critical square.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is forced, as 19 ... Nxe7 20 dxe5 dxe5 21 Nxe5 costs a pawn.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The purpose of this exchange is to open a nice long file for the queen.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must recapture or lose a pawn.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Beautiful exploitation of the open d-file! The attack on the c-pawn gains a tempo toward the queen’s entry at f6.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must lose a move in saving this pawn.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With this move, which incidentally threatens instant mate, White fastens another piece in the holes in Black’s position created by the move ...g6. White’s advantage is decisive and the winning procedure should be what the books call ‘a matter of technique’. The process of realizing his advantage is an interesting one.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black stops the mate and attempts to drive the queen away.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: It would be a mistake to play 23 Qg5 as Black, instead of moving his threatened rook on f8, would first play 23... f6, banishing the queen completely from his premises.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The knight blocks the bishop’s attack on the rook and is prepared to counter 24 Qf6 by 24 ... Nh5, repeating the device of harassing the enemy queen.
How does White continue, to force a win?

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
By rearranging his pieces and bringing up the reserves!
This First move in the new formation gains time by the threat of 25 Bc5 winning the exchange.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Once more into the breach! Black cannot save the game by repeating moves, since after 25 ... Ng7 26 Bc5 Re6 (or 26 ... Nh5 27 Qh4, and White wins the exchange) 27 Qh4 Rfe8 28 Ng5 the threat of mate will win the rook at e6.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must hang on to the valuable e-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Once again White has his ideal position, with pieces firmly planted in the holes near Black’s king. It will be hard for Black to chase them off as he does not have the earlier resource of . . . Nh5.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The rook must flee the bishop’s attack. Interposing the knight instead is of course a blunder as mate follows instantaneously.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Before proceeding to the final attack, White gets a stronger grip on the position by seizing the open d-file. The next step (since Black must wait helplessly) is 28 Rd5, attacking the e-pawn a third time and threatening to double rooks on the file. This ought to be enough to beat down resistance if no quicker win is available.
Note that White has not embarked on dubious long-range combinations. His plan, in most cases aimed at increasing his positional superiority, is made for a few moves only. Don’t believe all those stories you hear of chess masters analysing intricate combinations with dozens of variations for thirty moves ahead. They don’t do this because they don’t have to! It is far easier and more to the point to look only a few moves ahead and try to maintain at least an equal game at every stage. Winning by accumulating small advantages is more consistent with a common-sense approach than to seek to overwhelm the opponent with bewildering combinations and venturesome sacrificial attacks. Strengthening one’s own position gradually while undermining that of the opponent is more important than indulging in fruitless speculative fancies.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black’s idea is to reduce the pressure by offering an exchange of queens. White will then either have to acquiesce to the exchange, or withdraw his queen.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A very fine move! The knight, which seemed well posted at f3, is re-routed to augment the pressure on the dark squares.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Continuing the plan of evicting White’s queen from his camp.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White supports his queen and is ready, in the event of an exchange of queens, to maintain a tight grip on the dark squares. If Black plays 29 ... Qxf6, then 30 Nxf6+ Kh8 31 Rxd7 wins a piece for White.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This does not help, but there is no way to save the game: if 29 ... Re7, then 30 Be3 (threatening 31 Nh6+ Kf8 32 Qh8#) 30 ... Re8 31 Nh6+ Kf8 32 Qxf7#.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The simplest. If no mate is in sight, the modern master dispenses with the fireworks. Dawdling is for dilettantes, so he simplifies and cuts down any chance of resistance. After 30 ... Rxe7 31 Nf6+ Kh8 32 Rxd7 White wins a piece, giving Black no opportunity to complicate the ending.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Closed
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This opening move makes an outlet for two pieces, the queen and light-squared bishop. It does more than that.
It frees a square for the king and gives an extra one to the g1-knight. It is true that the knight is best developed at f3, but there are times when it is expedient to bring it to e2 – perhaps to reach f5 by way of g3. It is just as well to add to the knight’s freedom of movement, if no time is lost thereby. As to the king, there’s no harm in letting him have a bit more breathing space too. Many a king has been smothered by a lack of consideration, or by carelessness.
Consider this case history, from a minor tournament: McGrouther-McCann, Dundee 1893: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 d4 cxd4 4 Nxd4 e5 5 Nf5 Nge7 6 Nd6# (1-0).
And if this seems farfetched, here is another specimen, again in a minor tournament: Arnold-Böhm, Munich 1932: 1 e4 c6 2 d4 d5 3 Nc3 dxe4 4 Nxe4 Nd7 5 Qe2 Ngf6 6 Nd6# (1-0) .

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Though less aggressive than 1... e5, this move does release two pieces and has the advantage of restricting White’s choice of attack. White no longer has the whole range of Open Games at his disposal, and he is less able to steer the game into highly tactical channels by adopting an opening such as the King’s Gambit.
The French Defence conceals a great deal of potential dynamic energy and is a fine weapon against an over-enthusiastic attacking player. Black’s position is not easily assaulted despite its cramped appearance.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: As strong as it is natural. Of this pawn formation, Staunton, in the nineteenth century, said, “It is generally advantageous for your pawns to occupy the middle of the board, because when there they greatly retard the movements of the opposing forces. The e-pawn and the d-pawn at their fourth squares are well posted, but it is not easy to maintain them in that position, and if you are driven to advance one of them, the power of both is much diminished.”

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black attacks the e-pawn while giving his queen more mobility.
It is important to dispute control of the centre.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White has two reasons for developing the knight at d2:
He wants to avoid the knight being pinned, as might occur after 3 Nc3.
He is prepared, in the event of an attack on his d-pawn by ...c5, to reply c3, supporting the centre. Should pawns be exchanged on d4, he recaptures with the c-pawn and keeps a pawn in the centre.
It is true that his c1-bishop is blocked, but this condition is only temporary. Pieces can get out of each other ’ s way.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
If followed up correctly, there is nothing wrong with this move. The idea is that by attacking the e4-pawn, Black aims to force this pawn forward to e5. As Staunton explained above, once White’s two central pawns do not stand abreast, his whole central structure is weakened.
An alternative and equally good plan was to fight for control of the centre by 3... c5, incidentally permitting his queen the use of another diagonal and access to the queenside.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Why does White disregard Staunton’s advice about keeping two pawns on the fourth rank? He knows that the pawn may be weaker at e5, but he weighs strengths and weaknesses. At e5 the pawn drives the knight away from its most useful post and sends it off to another square where it interferes with the free movements of Black’s other pieces.
Clearly, the value of this or any other move is arrived at by balancing the benefits it confers against any disadvantages that might accrue.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Just about the only move left. On 4 . . . Ne4, White plays 5 Nxe4 dxe4 and then has the pleasant choice between 6 Bc4 and 6 Be3. In both cases White controls more space and has free development for his pieces. Black, on the other hand, has to worry about his pawn on e4, which is disconnected from the rest of his forces and extremely vulnerable to attack.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White gets his kingside pieces rolling to facilitate early castling on that side.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Very good, as Black must not delay in trying to free his constricted position. The pawn move strikes at the centre and opens another path for Black’s queen.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Ready to reply to 6...cxd4 with 7 cxd4, and preserve the pawn-chain, which so cramps the enemy.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight develops with tempo, as the d-pawn is now twice attacked.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: One of those rare times when the knight belongs here instead of at f3. It is true that f3 should be occupied by a knight, and White will arrange to have one there. His plan is to swing the knight from d2 to f3, meanwhile freeing his c 1-bishop.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black puts more pressure on the white d-pawn, threatening to win it by 8...cxd4 9 cxd4 Nxd4 10 Nxd4 Qxd4.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A clever knight shift protects the pawn and clears the decks for the dark-squared bishop’s appearance.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Another plausible move, but far too passive. Black’s position is cramped by the chain of enemy pawns on d4 and e5, and he should not allow this situation to persist. He must try to break White’s grip on the centre to obtain more space for his pieces. The correct continuation was 8...cxd4 9 cxd4 f6, virtually forcing 10 exf6 Nxf6. Then the problem with the d7-knight blocking in the c8-bishop has been resolved, and the disappearance of the e5-pawn means that Black has gained the d6-square for the development of his dark-squared bishop. If Black does not take the necessary liberating action, then he is likely to be gradually squeezed to death. Such a fate befell even so great a player as Capablanca in his game with Alekhine at AVRO 1938. As a consequence of his inferior opening play, Capablanca was tied up so badly that he could not stir and that he resigned with nearly all his pieces still on the board.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king must be spirited off to a safer spot before any violent action is undertaken.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black is still playing mechanical chess, unconscious of possible danger. With this move he misses the last chance of striking at the pawn chain by 9... f6.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Definitely putting an end to any possibility of disturbing the line-up of pawns, as 10... f6 is refuted by 11 Nxe6, while 10...cxd4 11 cxd4 Nxd4 12 Nxd4 Qxd4 13 Bxh7+, uncovering an attack on the queen, is unthinkable.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black recognizes at last that his pieces will remain impotent until he rids the board of White’s annoying e-pawn. He therefore protects his own e-pawn so that he can enforce 11... f6 and break up White’s pawn formation.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Creating an obvious threat to the black h-pawn. The profound purpose of the move is to compel one of the pawns near the king to move forward.
The advance of any pawn around the king loosens the defensive structure and results in a permanent weakening which can be exploited, while the pawn that made the forward step itself often becomes a target for direct attack.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This relaxes the bind on Black, but it opens up lines for an attack. Open lines favour the player whose development is superior and whose pieces enjoy greater mobility.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Not only to get the knight back into the game but also to defend his h-pawn, which again was threatened.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Once more attacking the pawn, this time including a threat of 14 Bxh7+ Kh8 (14 ... Nxh7 15 Qxh7#) 15 Ng6#.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Forced, as 13... h6 saves the pawn but allows the mate.
With the advance of the g-pawn, a target comes into view at which White can direct his attack. He can visualize a decisive blow, one that will wreck Black’s entire defensive structure!

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This sacrifice must be accepted, as otherwise Black will be a pawn down with nothing to show for it but a shattered position. If he tries 14... h6, then 15 Bh7+ Kg7 16 Qg6+ Kh8 17 Qxh6, and the threat of mate by the knight as well as the danger of discovered check is too much to withstand.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With this dramatic entrance on the scene, the queen, attended by her two knights, will quickly force submission.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only move.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Clearing the g6-square for the knight.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Interposing the knight instead allows mate on the move.
The threats of mate by 18 Qh8# or 18 Nxe7# cannot both be parried.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: 1-0 White wins by checkmate.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Closed Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
In chess, unlike tennis, you cannot win by serving an ace. There is no trick move in the opening that will catch even a fair-to-middling player off-balance.
What you can do is apply order and method in your conduct of this phase, so as to increase your chances of getting a favourable position. All you need do is follow a few simple rules for sound development:
Begin with 1 e4 or 1 d4, either of which moves releases two pieces.
Anchor at least one pawn in the centre and give it solid support. Pawns in the centre keep enemy pieces from settling themselves on the best squares.
Wherever feasible, bring out your knights before the bishops. Broadly speaking, the knights do their best work at f3 and c3 (f 6 and c 6 when Black), where their power is tremendous for defence as well as offence.
Of two developing moves, select the more aggressive one. Develop with a threat if you can.
Move each piece only once in the opening. Place it at once on a square where it has some bearing on the centre and where it has the greatest scope for attack.
Move at most two pawns in the early stages of the game. Play with the pieces.
Develop the pieces with a view to controlling the centre, either by occupying it or bearing down on it from a distance, as fianchettoed bishops do.
Develop the queen, but close to home to avoid her being harassed by pawns and minor pieces.
Do not chase after pawns at the expense of development.
Secure the safety of the king by early castling, preferably on the kingside.
Capablanca summed all this up when he said, “The main thing is to develop the pieces quickly: get them into play as fast as you can.”
Now back to Flohr and Pitschak:
White’s first move fixes a pawn in the centre and liberates two pieces.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black brings his king’s knight out to its most favourable post and hinders White from continuing with 2 e4.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Napier recalls that in the first of several lessons he took from Steinitz, the World Champion said, “No doubt you move your knight out on each side before the bishop? And do you know why?” Napier says he was stuck for an intelligent answer. Steinitz went on to explain: “One good reason is that you know where the knight belongs before you know that much of your bishop; certainty is a far better friend than doubt.”

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black postpones the straightforward reply 2... d5, which lets him in for the regular lines of the Queen’s Gambit. Meanwhile he opens a line for the f 8 -bishop.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A typical knight manoeuvre in the Colle Attack: the knight puts pressure on the critical e4-square without blocking the c-file.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black strikes a blow at the d-pawn in an attempt to secure control of the centre. This flank thrust is almost compulsory in queen’s pawn openings because Black must try to disturb White’s central formation.
The immediate threat is 4...cxd4, so that the recapture by 5 Nxd4 leaves no white pawn remaining in the centre.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White shores up the d-pawn and provides an outlet for the f1-bishop.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black too props up his advanced pawn and prepares to fianchetto the c8-bishop.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Customary practice in this system of attack: the bishop adds his strength to the pressure exerted on e4 in preparation for an advance by the e-pawn, which will open up lines of attack for the pieces in the background. The bishop also aims at Black’s h-pawn, a fine target after the enemy king castles on that side.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This solves one of Black’s chief problems in queen’s pawn openings – an effective disposition of the light-squared bishop. By means of this fianchetto arrangement, the bishop commands the longest diagonal on the board and participates in the fight for domination of e4, the strategic square in the Colle System.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: As part of the process of development, White shields his king from danger and brings his rook closer to the centre files.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Despite its modest appearance, there is a great deal of latent energy in the placement of this bishop at e7. It is close enough to home to help defend the king, yet easily manoeuvrable to a more aggressive post if occasion requires.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
More in the spirit of the Colle formation is the quiet 7 c3 to supply a support for the d4-pawn. The e-pawn is then free to advance, and if Black at any time plays ...cxd4, White recaptures with the c-pawn and maintains a strong pawn in the centre.
The idea of the text-move apparently is to prevent Black’s pieces from using d5 as a pivot for their movements about the board.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black goes quietly about the business of mustering out all the troops. At one stroke his rook appears on the scene while the king is whisked away.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Clearly in order to develop the bishop at b2. This fianchettoing of the bishop is not conventional procedure in the Colle, but Flohr may have wanted to test some ideas of his own.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black seizes the opportunity to dispute possession of the centre. He also puts an end to White’s contemplated advance of the e-pawn, as he bears down on the critical e4-square with knight, pawn and bishop, while White has only two pieces trained on it.
It is true that the b7-bishop’s diagonal is blocked, but this condition is only temporary.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Considerably better was the simple development of the dark-squared bishop at b 2 , which he prepared with his previous move.
The purpose of 9 Qc2 is to secure control of e4 and to prevent Black from establishing an outpost on that square by 9... Ne4. The trouble with the move is that it permits Black to seize the initiative and thereafter direct the course of events.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A powerful move which combines development, aggressive intent and prophylaxis!
Development, in that the knight is placed at once on its most suitable square.
Aggression, in the knight’s threat to advance to b4, attacking queen and bishop and forcing an exchange which rids the board of White’s dangerous light-squared bishop.
Prophylaxis, in the prevention of 10 e4, the continuation after which would be 10 ... Nb4 11 Qc3 xd3 12 Qxd3 dxe4, and Black wins apiece.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black exchanges to clarify the position in the centre and to open the c-file for the convenience of his a8-rook.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The alternative capture 11 exd4 was unpleasant as the reply 11...dxc4 forces 12 Qxc4 (otherwise White’s d-pawn is lost), when 12... Rc8 exercises uncomfortable pressure on White’s centre. Another possibility instead of the text-move is 11 Nxd4 Nxd4 12 exd4 dxc4 13 Qxc4 (to save the d-pawn) 13 ... Rc8 14 Qa4 Bc6 15 Qxa7 (or 15 Qc4 Bxg2 and Black wins easily) 15 ... Ra8 and Black wins the queen.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black nets a pawn with this and (as if it were not enough) takes over the attack.
The queen is in no danger, as White’s pieces are not sufficiently well developed to cause her any inconvenience.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White opens the position to get some counterplay; he hopes to utilize the e-file for his rook and the e4-square as a pivot for his pieces.
Instead the superficially attractive 12 e4 does not accomplish much, as after 12... Qh5 the vital e4-square is occupied by a pawn, making it unavailable for the manoeuvring of pieces, while Black benefits in having an extra passed pawn on the d-file.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This attack on the queen gains time as White must lose a move with his queen.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Obviously 13 Nxd4 would not do, as Black’s queen pounces down with instantaneous mate, while 13 Qb2 Nxf3+ 14 Nxf3 Qxd3 costs a piece. On 13 Qc3, Black continues 13 ... Rfd8 followed by 14... Rac8, and again the queen must flee.
White’s actual move is probably the least of the evils.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Intensifying the pressure along the d-file and particularly on the bishop, whose life is threatened by 14 ... Nxf3+ 15 Nxf3 Qxd3 16 Qxd3 Rxd3.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White protects his bishop as well as the vulnerable g-pawn.
Against 14 Bc2 Black can choose from these themes:
1) Simplification (being a pawn ahead), by 14... Nxc2.
2) Stepping up the pressure by 14... Rac8, banishing the c2-bishop to the first rank.
3) Combination, by 14 ... Ne2+ 15 Kh1 Ba6 (threatening to win the exchange by 16... Nc3) 16 Re1 Ng4 17 Ne4 Qxe4! 18 Bxe4 Nxf2#.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
There is no direct threat in this queen move, but Black threatens to threaten! He intends to storm White’s citadel of pawns with his queen supported by a minor piece, for instance by 15... Bd6 or 15... Ng4. This would compel one of the pawns to leave its base and create weaknesses that Black could exploit. The advanced pawn itself might be susceptible to attack, or avenues might be opened leading to the king.
This chipping away at the foundation is an interesting process for rendering an apparently strongly fortified position vulnerable to assault.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White has no dependable defence (especially against nebulous threats) so continues to develop his pieces. The more he has in play, the better his chances of surviving the coming storm.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
With a simple but unmistakable threat: mate on the move!
How does White defend?
1) 16 Nef3 Nxf3+ 17 Nxf3 Bxf3 18 gxf3 Qxh2#.
2) 16 f4 Bc5 (threatening the deadly 17... Ne2++ 18 Kh1 Ng3#) 17 Kh1 Ng4 18 h3 Qxh3+ and mate next move.
3) 16 h3 Qe5 (again aiming for mate at h2) 17 g3 Qd5 (now trying for 18... Qh1#) 18 f3 Qg5, and White’s game falls to pieces.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: By a process of elimination, the only defence, if one still exists.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s g-pawn has been compelled to step forward; now the threat of 17... Qxh2# forces the h-pawn’s advance.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White has no other move than this, which keeps the queen out – or does it?

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This is brilliant! Not because of the fact that the queen is offered, but because it brings to an appropriate climax the systematic exploitation of pawn weaknesses cleverly brought into being.
Black introduces two threats of mate in one, at h1 and h2.
After 18 gxh4 the reply 18... Bh2# would come quick as a flash.

metadata.Opening: Indian Defense: Knights Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Despite the fact that only one piece is freed by this move, against the two that are released by 1 e4 or 1 d4, the English is one of the strongest opening weapons in White’s arsenal. It appeals to those who like originality right from the start, as it allows manoeuvring of the pieces without coming to grips too early with the enemy. In many forms of this opening, White does not even try to occupy the centre. He lets Black mass pieces and pawns there, and then attacks them from the sides. He might fianchetto his bishops, for example, and strike at the centre from a distance, in order to undermine it.
Should White decide to temper his originality with caution, he can transpose from the English to some form of queen’s pawn opening and still retain a fine game.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black develops in the good old-fashioned way: he plants a pawn in the centre and frees two pieces for action.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White brings a piece out in preference to advancing a centre pawn.
In fact, on 2 d4 exd4 3 Qxd4 Nc6 the queen must retreat and lose a move. Or if 2 e4, White remains with a backward d-pawn, while the f1-bishop cannot get to c4.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black watches the order of his moves. The knight move is not merely routine development of a piece. Its purpose is to offset the pressure of White’s knight and pawn on the d5-square.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Clearly with the intention of making room for the bishop at g2, where it will operate on a long diagonal and also contribute to the pressure on d5.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black frees his game by opening new paths for the queenside pieces. Simultaneously, he puts the question to White’s c-pawn.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev
