annotation: White is happy to exchange a flank pawn for a centre pawn. At the same time, his c-file, now clear of pawns, offers good prospects for his queen’s rook when it gets to c1.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Such recaptures are practically compulsory. A delay might give White time to protect and hold on to the extra pawn.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White develops a piece with gain of tempo – an attack on the d5-knight.
In the old days, Black would probably have met this by 5... Be6, protecting the knight while developing another piece. Today’s players regard with suspicion even the most natural moves, in their search for truth (and new ways to win).

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop can wait! The advantage of this move is that Black is able to retain control of the d4-square, and so prevent White from opening up the centre by advancing his d-pawn to d4. After 5... Be6, on the other hand, play might continue 6 Nf3 Nc6 7 0-0 Be7 8 d4, when Black is in trouble, since the position is becoming open while his king is still in the centre.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Again one of White’s pieces develops with a threat – this time against the e-pawn.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black defends in the simplest, most natural, way by posting the b8-knight on its most effective station.
Despite the fact that Black has fewer pieces in play than White, his game is not inferior. He does have a pawn in the centre, and his bishops, undeveloped as yet, have great potential, as their cruising range is more extensive than White’s.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White does not commit himself, but spirits away the king and mobilizes one of his rooks.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: As in the previous game, the bishop’s unobtrusive position at e7 is deceptive: it is prepared to keep out invaders and is also on the alert to switch to the attack.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White makes room for the c1-bishop to take a hand in the game.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Removes the king from the danger area and gets the rook up on deck.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With the bishop on this square, White may be able to get in 10 d4 and rid himself of Black’s cramping centre pawn.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
An excellent deployment, as the bishop has a powerful restraining effect on White’s kingside, as well as on the contemplated advance of his d-pawn.
If White does try 10 d4, the response 10... Nc4 is hard to meet. If White replies 11 Nxe5, then after 11... N6xe5 12 dxe5 Nxe3 13 fxe3 he is left with a rickety column of pawns on the e-file. Or if White plays 11 Qc1 to save his b-pawn and to recapture at e3 with the queen, then 11... Nxe3 12 Qxe3 exd4 13 Qe4 Bxf3, followed by 14...dxc3, wins a piece for Black.
White’s best line is probably 10 Na4, in order to swing the knight to c5, a square which White must try to control in this type of English Opening. Otherwise he might continue developing by 10 Rc1 and only then consider the knight manoeuvre.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A move which is impelled by a desire to make the annoying bishop declare his intentions – either take the knight or vacate the premises! Unfortunately, moves such as this, dictated more by instinct than reason, have an injurious effect on the castled position, as the structure is loosened. Once the pawns near the king make a move, they themselves become more susceptible to attack, in spite of the cluster of pieces ranged around them for protection.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop retreats one square but maintains the pressure. Despite the bishop’s restricted mobility, its continued influence is more troublesome to White’s position (and his frame of mind) than would be its return to e6, where it enjoys more freedom but does nothing to disturb the opponent.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Evidently in order to control the c-file and perhaps work up an attack on the queenside.
A good alternative is 11 Qb3 followed, when feasible, by Rad1 and d4, to open the d-file for White’s rooks and get some counterplay in the centre. Action in the centre is the best remedy against a kingside attack.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
All the pieces must do their bit! The queen moves only one step forward and dominates an important diagonal!
Development of the queen serves another purpose in that the first rank is cleared for the rooks. They can now switch over toward the centre and get control of the most important files.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White’s idea is to create a diversion by taking command of c5 with his knight and keeping Black occupied with threats on the queenside.
Against routine defensive moves, for instance 12 Kh2, Black gets an attack rolling by 12... f5 and 13... f4, and the pawn will demolish White’s kingside pawn formation.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Presenting White with an unhappy choice of recaptures: if he takes with the pawn, his d-pawn becomes isolated and weak; if he takes with the bishop, he loses a pawn immediately.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White gives up the h-pawn, trusting that he will regain a pawn quickly by his next exchange of pieces.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: After this capture, Black’s attacking prospects are very bright. Without bothering to analyse the petty details, he can visualize winning lines of play beginning with 14... f5 followed either by 15... f4, to destroy White’s g-pawn (the key to the defensive structure), or by 15... Rf6, and then swinging the rook over to g6 or h6.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Forced, but an agreeable obligation. Black is quite pleased to see the last of this long-range bishop.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Material is now equal, but the white king is in danger, with the enemy queen breathing on his neck.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A tremendous move! One threat from this beautifully centralized knight is 16... Nxe3 17 fxe3 Qxg3+ 18 Kh1 Qh3+ 19 Kg1 Bg5, and White’s game is in ruins, while another threat is 16... Nf6, followed by 17... Ng4 and 18... Qh2#.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Not at once 16... Nf6 as 17 f3 keeps the knight out (note how essential it is to have the g-pawn protected).
With his last move Black prepares to play 17... f4. If 18 gxf4 then 18... Rxf4 19 Bxf4 Nxf4, and Black mates at g2. If White does not take the pawn but plays 18 Bc5, Black wins cleverly by 18... f3 (threatening 19... Qg2#) 19 exf3 Nf4 (again aiming at the mate) 20 gxf4 Rf5, and White can only stop 21... Rh5, followed by mate, by giving up his queen with 21 Qxe5.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
If White tries to rid himself of Black’s troublesome knight by 17 Nc3 Black pursues the attack by 17... Nf6 18 f3 Nh5 (concentrating on the vital g-pawn) 19 Bf2 Bh4 (still hammering at the pawn) 20 gxh4 Nf4 and forces mate at g2.
The text-move gives White a faint chance of holding out after 17... Bxc5 18 Nxc5 Nf6 19 f3, or if 17... Nf6 then 18 Rxf6.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Not only to strike at the g-pawn but also to clear a path for the rook’s passage to f5 and h5 to assist the queen in a mating operation.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
If instead 18 g4 to keep the rook out, Black has three or four easy wins on tap:
1) 18... f3 19 exf3 Nf4, followed by mate at g2.
2) 18... Qxg4+ 19 Kh2 and then:
2a) 19... Rf5, and the rook mates.
2b) 19... f3 20 Rg1 Qh4#.
The move played exchanges to reduce the number of pieces besetting his king. He hopes for the simple recapture by 18... Nxe7, when the knight, no longer centralized, is less of a menace.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With the simple, brutal threat of 19... Qh2#.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only reply.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Threatening 20... Qg2#.
There is no defence: 20 Rf2 Qxg3+ 21 Kh1 Rxf2 wins easily, or 20 Rxf8+ Rxf8 21 Qf2 Rxf2 22 Kxf2 Qg2+ 23 Kxe3 Qxc6 and the rest is elementary.
In this game Flohr gained revenge for his loss to Pitschak in the previous game by adopting the technique with which he was defeated. He weakened the pawns around the castled king and then ripped open the defences with a devastating attack.

metadata.Opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Four Knights Variation, Fianchetto Line, with Nb6
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This is one of the best ways to begin what is a race and a struggle: a race to get the pieces out rapidly and onto squares where they can operate most efficiently; a struggle to gain control of the centre.
At one stroke the e-pawn takes up an important square in the centre and attacks two others, while the queen and bishop control eight more squares.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This quietly aggressive move prepares to dispute White’s centre by 2... d5.
This defence has the merit of avoiding the many strong openings White can play after the customary 1... e5 reply.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Of a similar move, Philidor in his Chess Analysed (1791) says, “This Pawn is played two Moves for two very important Reafons: the firft is, to hinder your Adverfary’s King’s Bifhop to play upon your King’s Bifhop’s Pawn; and the fecond, to put the Strength of your Pawns in the Middle of the Exchequer, which is of great Confequence to attain the making of a Queen.”
We may ftill follow the advice if not the fpelling.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: An attack on the e-pawn which immediately challenges the centre.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Of the various courses open to White (advancing the e-pawn to e5, exchanging pawns, sacrificing his centre pawn or protecting it) he takes that which enables him to develop a piece and maintain the pressure.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Temporarily allowing White more freedom of action, but Black hopes to play ...c5 later and destroy the troublesome d-pawn.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The recapture leaves White with a slight edge in his centralized knight and pawn position.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Preparing a support for the g8-knight’s development at f6. If White then exchanges knights, Black can recapture with the d7-knight.
If he played instead 4... Nf6 then comes 5 Nxf6+ and Black must either break up his kingside pawns by 5...gxf6 or capture with the queen and risk its being bothered by the minor pieces. A sample of what could happen (after 4... Nf6 5 Nxf6+ Qxf6) is this little trap: 6 Nf3 Bd7 (to seize the long diagonal) 7 Bd3 Bc6 8 Bg5 Bxf3 9 Qd2! Qxd4 10 Bb5+ and White wins the enemy queen.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The best possible way to put the king’s knight to work – by developing it at f3 where it has enormous influence on the centre, and where it stands peerless in defence of the castled king.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A noncommittal developing move (it brings a piece off the back rank and helps the king castle quickly) but not so good as the conventional 5... Ngf6 .
If Black tries instead the fianchetto development of his c8-bishop (tempting in view of White’s exposed knight), there is a pretty trap he can stumble into: 5... b6 6 Bb5 Bb7 7 Ne5! Bxe4 (or 7... Bc8 8 Bg5 Nf6 9 Nc6, winning the queen) 8 Bxd7+ Ke7 9 Bc6! and Black must lose some material.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is probably sharper than 6 Bc4 but either move places the bishop in a good spot and clears the first rank for kingside castling.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black too prepares to get his king into safety by developing (at long last) his g8-knight.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White develops a piece and supports his central knight strongly with queen and bishop.
This is more restraining on Black’s cramped position than 7 Nxf6+ Bxf6, when Black can initiate an attack on White’s centre with ...c5.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king seeks security in the corner. There was no easy freeing manoeuvre in 7... Nxe4 8 Bxe4 Nf6 since 9 Bxb7 Bxb7 10 Qb5+ followed by 11 Qxb7 wins a pawn for White.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White’s castling is less to escape danger than to let the h1-rook take an active part in the game.
White’s position is so promising as to offer him a good attacking line in 8 Bg5 Nxe4 9 Qxe4 g6 (certainly not 9... Nf6 to prevent mate, as 10 Bxf6 wins on the spot) 10 h4, when White can castle on the queenside and storm the enemy bastions with his kingside pawns.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black exchanges to get some elbow-room.
9 Q Xe4!
Takes command of the board with a threat of mate! Offhand it looks risky to make this capture and leave the queen exposed to harassment by the minor pieces, but Black is in no position (in either sense of the word) to make trouble. He has all he can do to stay alive!

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Naturally, Black does not wish to advance one of the kingside pawns, for instance 9... g6, unless compelled to, but what’s wrong with the move he plays, 9... Nf6? Does it not bring the knight to its best square, guard against mate, beat off the queen, and free his own queenside?
Indeed it does all these things, and under the circumstances it is probably Black’s best move. It is strange that a move made under duress often does not have the same positive effect as a move made of one’s own volition.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: After this, Black’s knight, which to be sure stands on a good square, must remain on that square to guard against mate.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The c8-bishop, barred by Black’s very first move from coming out to the kingside, seeks other means to take part in the battle. Development at b7 looks attractive, as from there it commands the long diagonal.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Excellent strategy! White attacks the most important defensive piece, the knight that guards against mate. The specific threat is 12 Bxf6 Bxf6 13 Qxh7#.
A simple threat and easy to meet – all Black has to do is play 11... g6 or 11... h6.
What then is White aiming at?
The hidden purpose is to force Black to move one of the kingside pawns, to avoid being mated. A move by either of these pawns creates a looseness in the defensive structure that can never be repaired. It weakens the position organically as it makes a breach that can never be closed. The pawn that advances can never go back to its former position in the line of defensive pawns.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: On the alternative 11... h6 White wins by 12 Bxf6 Bxf6 13 Qe4, when the threat of mate wins the rook on a8, an innocent bystander.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black has no effective counterattack. The best he can do is to keep on developing pieces on the most favourable squares to make a hard fight of it.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Threatening, after the preparatory 14 Rad1, to take the e6-pawn so that the forced recapture by 15...fxe6 deprives Black’s g-pawn of one of its props.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This unexpected zwischenzug (in-between move) threatens immediate victory by 15 Rxe7 Qxe7 16 Bxf6 Qd6 17 Ng5 h5 18 Qxh5! gxh5 19 Bh7#!

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black offers a pawn to deflect one of the pieces bearing down so heavily on his f6-knight and e7-bishop.
There was no relief in 14... Kg7 to support the knight, as White responds with the brutal 15 Bh6+ winning the exchange.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
But not 15 Bxh6, which permits 15... Ne4 driving off White’s queen.
White now plans 16 Bxg6 fxg6 17 Qxg6+ Kh8 18 Nd4 (threatening to win by 19 Ne6, 19 Nf5 or 19 Re3 followed by 20 Rh3+) 18... Qe8 19 Qh6+ Kg8 20 Nf5 Rf7 21 Bxf6 winning easily.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White has a neat win against the defence by 15... Ne4. He plays 16 Bxe7 Qxe7 17 cxd5 (threatening to capture the pinned e4-knight next) 17.... Bxd5 18 Bxe4 Bxe4 19 Rxe4! Qxe4 20 Ng5, when Black must lose his queen or be mated.
The text-move is of course an attempt to chase the queen away.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White supports the bishop, attacks the knight and threatens to win by 17 Bxe7. What more can be achieved by one move?

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Returning the knight to f6 leads to catastrophe, viz.: 16... Nf6 17 Rxe7 Qxe7 18 Bxf6 and White attacks Black’s queen while threatening 19 Qh8#.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Once again the theme song – mate at h7.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
And Black must dance to the tune, by bringing the knight back to f6.
Here too Black posts the knight on a good square, but not of his own free will.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This restricts Black more than would manoeuvring the rook over to h3 by way of e3. For example, after 18 Re3 Re8 19 Rh3 Kf8 the king escapes immediate disaster.
After White’s actual move, if Black tries 18... Re8 he falls into 19 Bxg6 Rxe1+ 20 Rxe1 fxg6 21 Qxg6+ Kh8 22 Nf7#.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Threatening to capture the knight, and then mate with the queen.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Had Black played 19...fxe6, there would have followed 20 Qxg6+ Kh8 21 Qh6+ Kg8 22 Bh7+ Kh8 23 Bf5+ Kg8 24 Bxe6+ Rf7 25 Bxf7#.
It is interesting to note how the startling 19 Re6 move not only threatens to take the knight but also exploits the fact that the f-pawn dare not capture the rook and abandon the defence of the g-pawn.
Black’s last move is intended to clear the f8-square for the king, if White should take the knight and then check at h7 with his queen.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Breaking through the pawn barrier! White’s threat is 21 Bxf7#.
There is no defence:
1) 20...fxe6 21 Bf7#.
2) 20...fxg6 21 Qxg6+ Kh8 22 Nf7#.
3) 20... Qd7 21 Bh7+ Nxh7 (or 21... Kh8 22 Qxf6#) 22 Qxh7+ Kf8 23 Qh8#.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is an excellent start toward developing the pieces, as lines are immediately opened for the queen and a bishop. The e-pawn itself helps in the battle for the centre by occupying a key square and attacking two others, d5 and f5.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: In spite of its modest appearance, this move is just as good as the straightforward 1... e5. Black’s idea is to follow up with 2... d5, attacking White’s centre. He is then prepared to meet 3 exd5 by recapturing with the e-pawn, thus maintaining a pawn in the centre.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Naturally! White puts another pawn in the centre, now making e5 and c5 forbidden territory for Black’s pieces. Meanwhile, his own queen and dark-squared bishop have more freedom of movement.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Putting the question to the e-pawn!
White has a choice of various replies:
1) 3 exd5, in order to simplify.
2) 3 e5, to cramp Black with the pawn chain.
3) 3 Nc3 (also 3 Nd2 or, less effectively, 3 Bd3), to protect the pawn and develop a piece at the same time.
The first method was favoured by Morphy, who liked open positions that gave his pieces wide scope for attack. Nowadays it is rarely adopted, as after the exchange of pawns the positions are equal and symmetrical and an attack is difficult to whip up, unless you are a Morphy.
The cramping move 3 e5 has a great many advocates, but the argument against this system is that White’s pawn chain is rigid and susceptible to undermining tactics. Black initiates a strong counterattack on the base of the pawn-chain by 3... c5, followed by ... Nc6 and ... Qb6, when White finds himself defending a centre that has lost its flexibility.
There remains the third way, which is simple and consistent with common sense in chess – to support the e-pawn and bring a piece out on the scene.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Typical Tarrasch: he selects the method which furthers his development and maintains tension in the centre. This move brings a knight out, protects the e-pawn and increases the pressure on d5.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Tarrasch disapproves of this exchange of pawns, as Black surrenders the centre without obtaining any compensation. If results are a measure of the merit of an opinion, Tarrasch proved his point in this match. Mieses played 3...dxe4 seven times with Black, with the consequence that two games were drawn and five were won by Tarrasch.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Now White has a beautifully centralized knight, pressure on e5 and c5, and a superior pawn position (a pawn at d4 to one at e6) which assures him greater freedom of action.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Intending to support the g8-knight when it reaches f6. If Black plays 4... Nf6 at once, White can exchange knights by 5 Nxf6+. Black’s recapture either brings his queen too early into the game, or with 5...gxf6 allows his kingside pawn structure to be broken up.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This is where the king’s knight is most useful, so why not place it there at once?
Even the greatest masters do not play startling, bizarre or ‘brilliant’ moves in the opening in an effort to be different, or to impress others with their ability to find extraordinary moves in commonplace positions. They are content to develop their pieces quickly, placing them on squares where they will operate to greatest effect, and then wait for Nature to take its course. When the time is ripe for combinative play, the odds are it will turn in favour of the player whose development is superior.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A sound developing move. Not only does the g8-knight move to the square most suitable for its powers, but it challenges the sovereignty of White’s knight and disputes its hold on the centre.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Rather than retreat, White supports the knight by developing another piece. If Black exchanges on e4, White remains with a piece in the centre.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The bishop is well placed at e7, and the decks are cleared for early kingside castling.
6... Nxe4 7 Bxe4 Nf6 8 Bd3 is an interesting alternative, when the time lost by the bishop’s retreat compensates Black for the tempo he lost when he played 3...dxe4.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king hides behind a pawn barricade while the rook moves in toward the half-open e-file.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black exchanges to free his crowded position and let the queenside pieces get some air.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The recapture gives White a monopoly on the important squares and poses Black the problem of attaining equality.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is always a fine square for the knight, and in this case the knight gets there with gain of time by attacking the unprotected bishop.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This mobile bishop is too valuable for White to allow its exchange. Any such transaction benefits Black as a reduction in the number of pieces on the board eases the pressure on him.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Understandably, Black wants his light-squared bishop on the job and intends developing it at b7. There is danger, though, in attempting this before the king has castled. Not only is there the risk of a check on the a4-e8 diagonal, which might compel the king to move and forfeit his right to castle, but there is also the possibility of White planting a knight on c6, a square weakened by the advance of Black’s b-pawn.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight occupies a wonderful outpost and will put a restraining hand on Black’s ambition to expand.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black realizes that 10... Bb7 is refuted by 11 Bb5+, to which he must respond either with 11... Kf8 losing the castling privilege, or with 11... c6 giving up a pawn.
Naturally, it would be silly to snatch a pawn by 10... Qxd4 and fall into 11 Bb5+, losing the queen by a discovered attack.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Immediately pouncing on the weakened square, with a view to removing Black’s dark-squared bishop. But why give up the knight, which I said a moment ago was occupying a wonderful outpost, for a bishop that seems to have little potential?
There are at least three good reasons:
The exchange deprives Black of one of his bishops, and the mere possession of both bishops is a formidable attacking weapon, no matter how placid the position.
The reduction in material increases the dynamic power of White’s pair of bishops, which have more space to work in. The emptier the board, the better they can sweep the area, one operating on light and the other on dark diagonals.
The third reason is rather subtle:
Black’s kingside position is stoutly defended by the knight, and the knight in turn by the bishop and queen. In order to get at the knight, which must eventually be destroyed for a kingside attack to succeed, White first removes one of its firm supports, the bishop. The substitution of Black’s queen for the bishop will make a pin on the knight a potent one – one which can not easily be shaken off.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: As good as any other move the queen can make.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A very important zwischenzug (in-between move). It is stronger than the immediate 12 Nxe7+ and causes Black to modify his plans. Let us analyse both moves:
If White plays 12 Nxe7+, then after 12... Qxe7 13 Qf3 White attacks the rook. The rook evades the queen by escaping to b8, and Black’s next move, 14... Bb7, drives the queen off the long diagonal, leaving Black’s bishop in control of it.
After the actual move 12 Qf3, Black is threatened with 13 Nxe7+ Qxe7 14 Qxa8 – loss of a rook. This time the rook cannot run from the queen, as the flight square b8 is covered by White’s knight, and the response 12... Bb7 (to interpose the bishop, meanwhile developing it on the long diagonal) fails after 13 Nxe7+ Qxe7 14 Qxb7, and White wins a piece.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The upshot of all this is that in order to save the rook’s life the bishop must be content to move to d7, where it has little scope.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Strategically, this represents a triumph for White. Not only does he remain with the advantage of the two bishops against Black’s knight and bishop, but he has also compelled Black’s remaining bishop to take up an unfavourable post, while White retains control of the long light-squared diagonal.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black recaptures with the impression that his position is solid enough, though defensive in character.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White puts paralysing pressure on the knight with this powerful pin. Before going any further, let’s review the bidding:
By doing nothing more remarkable than making simple developing moves, White has an advantage in his pair of bishops, a better all-around position, more pieces in play, and an enduring initiative.
More pieces in play? Yes, his queen and both bishops are actively posted, while Black’s knight is unable to move, his queen must hover about the knight (or lose a pawn after Bxf6) and his bishop has little mobility, shut off as it is from the kingside by Black’s own e-pawn. The pawn position in the centre also favours White, in that his d-pawn on the fourth rank has more to say about affairs than the enemy pawn at e6.
White now plans to create a breach in the line-up of pawns screening Black’s king, by next playing the surprising but logical 15 Qe4. Black could not reply 15... Nxe4 to this, as after 16 Bxe7 (attacking two pieces) 16... Re8 17 Bxe4 he has no time to take the e7-bishop as his a8-rook is under attack. The idea underlying 15 Qe4 is not to induce Black to snatch the queen, but by the threat of 16 Bxf6 Qxf6 17 Qxh7# to compel him to play 15... g6. The effect of this pawn move would be to loosen the defensive structure shielding the king, remove a prop from under the pinned knight, and offer White points of entry on the weakened dark squares h6 and f6, which are no longer guarded by the g-pawn. One possibility, for example, is 15 Qe4 g6 16 Qh4 (attacking the knight) 16... Kg7 17 Bh6+, and White wins the exchange.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black shifts the rook from the line of fire, so that 15 Qe4 Nxe4 16 Bxe7 Rfe8 retains material equality.
Constructively, Black intends to follow up with 15... c5, coming to grips with White’s centre pawn and opening the c-file for his rook.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A useful developing, restraining and preparatory move:
It brings the rook out to a half-open file.
It prevents any attempt by Black to free himself by prying open the e-file.
It makes provision for utilizing the e1-rook in a kingside attack, somewhat like this: 16 Qh3 (again threatening to win by 17 Bxf6) 16... h6 17 Bxh6 gxh6 18 Qxh6, and the rook comes in decisively by way of e5 and g5 to inflict mate.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The winning move - although it appears that White has been playing a long string of winning moves.
The pressure is now redoubled on the h-pawn, which White threatens to win either by 17 Bxf6 followed by 18 Qxh7+ or simply by taking it at once with the bishop, as Black’s pinned knight dare not recapture, and his king may not take the bishop.
How does Black defend himself against White’s threats?
If 16... h6, then 17 Bxh6 gxh6 18 Qxh6 Qf8 (otherwise 19 Re5 will lead to mate) 19 Qxf6, when White, two pawns up, wins easily.
If 16... g6 (saving the h-pawn but depriving the knight of any real support), White wins by 17 Qh4 Kg7 18 Re4!, followed by 19 Rf4, and the rook too hits out at the helpless knight.
If 16... e5 (uncovering an attack on the queen), then 17 Bxf6 Bxh3 (or 17... Qxf6 18 Qxd7, and White wins a piece) 18 Bxe7 and White is a piece ahead.
Finally, after 16... c5 17 Bxh7+ Kf8 18 Be4 (threatening a devastating check at h8) 18... Kg8, Black is a pawn down and still on the defensive.
All these variations are pleasant – especially if you are on the winning side!

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White removes the only defender in the neighbourhood of the black king, and...

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: ...uproots the g-pawn, exposing the king.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Holding the king fast! The idea is to keep him from escaping by way of f8 while facing him with deadly threats. The modus operandi after the text-move is 19 Bxh7+! Kh8 20 Bg6+ Kg8 21 Qh7+ Kf8 22 Qxf7#.
If you can play this sort of move (18 Qh6), you are a cut above the average player. Most young players (in a chess sense) have a tendency to try checking the king to death only to find after something like 18 Qxh7+ Kf8 19 Qh8+ Ke7 that the king has escaped and the attack is exhausted. What is worse is that White’s queen and d-pawn are threatened, and that saving both by 20 Qh4 lets Black respond with 20... Rh8 and suddenly White is thrown on the defensive!

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Intercepting the bishop’s line of attack.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Obviously threatening check at g3, which would force Black to give up his queen in order to avoid instant mate.
Notice how the occupation of the partly open e-file by the rook enables the convenient use of e3 as a transfer point, allowing the rook to switch over to the open files on the kingside.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Guarding the g7-square, so that after 20 Rg3+ Kh8, White has no check there with his queen.
If instead 19... f6, to try escaping with the king, then 20 Rg3+ Kf7 21 Qg7# is mate. Or if 19... Kh8, then 20 Rh3 forces 20... Kg8, when 21 Rg3+ is fatal.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A beautiful coup de repos!
Black is helpless: his queen dare not leave the diagonal leading to g7, and 20... Qg7 21 Rg3 pins the queen, while 20... Qh8 succumbs to 21 Rg3+, and the poor king’s only flight square is occupied by his queen!
This game was awarded a brilliancy prize.

metadata.Opening: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Blackburne Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With his first move, White gets a foothold in the centre and enables the development of his kingside pieces.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black must also establish a pawn in the centre, while preventing 2 d4 from being freely played.
What if White does continue 2 d4? After 2...exd4 3 Qxd4 Nc6 4 Qe3 Nf6 5 Nc3 Bb4 Black has three pieces in play with easy development. It is true that White has a pawn in the centre, but it will need constant care, and his queen meanwhile has lost valuable time. In short, after 1... e5 White may respond 2 d4 but not to advantage.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight is posted without delay on its most effective square in the opening. The move is ideal, as the knight develops with a threat. This limits the opponent’s choice of replies, since he must do something to meet the threat before going about his business.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The best way to protect the pawn. The knight’s development is natural, and no time is lost meeting the threat.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The strongest move on the board here, this characterizes the Ruy Lopez, the most powerful of kingside openings. As Reuben Fine puts it, “One reason why the Ruy Lopez is so strong is that the most natural sequence of moves leads to an ideal position for White.”

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black brings his g8-knight out toward the centre with an attack on the e4-pawn.
Lasker favoured the knight’s development at this point, but modern theory inclines to interpolating 3... a6 first, to make the bishop declare its intentions, and in any case to dislodge it from its fine position.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Very much to the point: the king is whisked away into safety while the h1-rook is activated.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Should Black capture this pawn? Lasker’s view was: “When you are conscious not to have violated the rules laid down, you should accept the sacrifice of an important central pawn. If you do not, as a rule, the pawn which you have rejected will become very troublesome to you.”

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is stronger than 5 Re1. Black’s e-pawn is doubly attacked, while lines are opened up for White’s queen and dark-squared bishop.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Puts the question to the bishop, which apparently must capture the knight or retreat.
An alternative course was 5... Be7, developing another piece instead of moving the same one twice. Black must not waste time holding on to the extra pawn but should continue bringing pieces into play.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Initiating an attack which is troublesome to meet. White temporarily offers a piece, but he can be sure of regaining it quickly. This is superior to the less dynamic 6 Ba4, which gives Black time to reply 6... e4 with good counterplay.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight’s excursion has cost Black valuable time, as the knight has made four moves to capture a bishop that has only moved once.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White attacks the knight at once to recover the piece he lost.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A fifth move by the same knight! White will surely have a strong attack in return for the pawn he intends to sacrifice.
Black should have played 7... Nbd4 8 Nxd4 Nxd4 9 Qxd4 d5, a better way of returning the piece as it frees his bishops.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Not a happy recapture, as the d-pawn is blocked, but certainly better than taking with the pawn, when Black’s position is even more awkward.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
En avant! The obvious threat of mate camouflages the real purpose of this move.
White’s last two moves are those of a beginner – or perhaps of a great master! The knight has moved twice to assist the queen in an attack, which the books say is premature, since White’s development is not complete. Why does Alekhine violate elementary opening principles?
The reason he does so is that routine development (“You get your pieces out quietly and I’ll do the same with mine”) would give Black time to reorganize his position. Black has committed some indiscretions (such as moving one knight five times in the opening!), and the way to punish these lapses is to keep him occupied – face him with problems at every point and give him no time to recover. If it requires unconventional moves to force weaknesses in his position, then play these unorthodox moves! Moves are good or bad by one standard only – their effect on the position at hand.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
What other choice was there?
If Black castles in order to avoid 11 Qxf7#, he falls into 11 Qxh7#, or if he exchanges by 10... Bxg5 then 11 Bxg5 forces 11... Ne7, when the pin 12 Re1 wins a piece – as a start!

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White anchors the queen on this square, which is no longer guarded by Black’s g-pawn, as the first step in controlling the dark squares.
White now threatens to penetrate further into the heart of the position by 12 Qg7, attacking the rook. This would force 12... Rf8 in reply, when 13 Nxh7 wins the exchange, a rook for a knight.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Not only must further invasion be prevented, but the queen must be driven back.
Black has little choice, as castling is against the law, while 11... Bxg5 loses to 12 Bxg5 f6 13 Qg7 Rf8 14 Re1+ Ne7 15 Bh6 Rf7 16 Qg8+ Rf8 17 Qxf8#.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Forcing Black to tie himself up in knots.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Certainly not 12.... Be7, when 13 Qg7 Rf8 14 Nxh7 (threatening 15 Qxf8#) 14... d5 15 Nf6# is mate.
At this point, in spite of White’s disregard of conventional methods of development, he has three pieces in active play, while Black has none! Black does have one piece off the first rank, but it is held fast by a pin and unable to move.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: One way to get at the king is to make him come out into the open.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Moving the king forfeits the privilege of castling, but unfortunately it’s Black’s only move.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Now threatening 16... Bxf6. The alternative attack by 15... Ng8 pins the knight and strikes at it with two pieces, but is refuted by 16 Qc4+ Kxf6 (or 16... Kg7 17 Ne8+ and Black must give up his queen) 17 Qh4+ and White wins the queen.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Protecting the knight, which had no flight square.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation

Threatening the knight again by hitting out at one of its defenders.
If 16... Ng8 instead, White has a pretty combination in 17 Nxg8 Qxg8 18 Re7+ Kf8 19 Bh6 followed by 20 Qf6+, forcing mate. Or he may prefer to win by 17 Qc4+ d5 18 Nxd5 Qxg5 19 Nxc7+ Kf6 20 Ne8#.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The hallmark of an Alekhine combination is the kick at the end of a series of apparently innocuous moves.
White’s threat is obvious: mate on the move.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: On 18... Kxe7, the only other way of preventing mate at f7, White replies 19 Nd5++, and wins the queen next move.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Direct attack on the king and discovered attack on the queen.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The point of the combination: in return for his rook and bishop, White gets the queen – and a lasting initiative!

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must take the bishop.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White could win more simply by 21 Qg8 Kf6 22 Qxh7 Kf7 23 Nc3 d6 24 Re1, followed by 25 Re7+, but the text-move is good enough. The queen remains active while Black’s queenside is immobilized.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king flees from the line of fire. Black hopes to free himself by 24... Rh8 and 25.... Bd8, driving the queen off, followed by the advance of his d-pawn to release his queenside pieces.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White seizes the open file. Controlling it gives the rook a clear road and access to the enemy camp.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black intends either to evict the queen by 25... Bd8 or to dispute ownership of the e-file by 25... Re8.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Nailing down the d-pawn and paralysing Black’s forces on the queenside.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
What else is there? 25... Re8 26 Rxe8 Kxe8 27 Qxf6 wins a piece, or if 25... b6, then 26 Qd5+ catches the a8-rook.
Black’s idea is to follow up with 26... Ra6, dislodging the queen and getting his queenside pieces rolling.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Excellent! White brings another piece up to join in the attack. Notice how the master player selects the move he would like to make, sees that it can’t be made (here the knight is left en prise ) and then makes the move!

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black does not grab the knight with 26.... Bxc3, as White mates by 27 Re7+ Kf8 (or 27... Kg8 28 Qd5+ and mate next move) 28 Rxd7+ Kg8 29 Qd5+ Kf8 30 Qf7#.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s queen must retreat from the rook’s attack, but she gains time by checking.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Or 27... Kf8 28 Nb5 (threatening 29 Nd6) 28... Re6 29 Rxe6 dxe6 30 Qc5+ Kg7 31 Qc7+ and a bishop falls with check.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Ready to switch over to d6 in order to support the queen in a mate threat at f7.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Otherwise the knight goes to d6 and cuts the rook off from participating in the defence.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight goes there anyway, settling down on this fine outpost where it will either take a hand in a decisive combination or simply stay there and choke Black to death.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Naturally, 29... Rxe2 is unthinkable, as 30 Qf7# would come in a flash.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White protects the rook and declares his intention of winning by 31 Nxc8 Rxc8 32 Qxd7+, followed by taking a rook or two.
There is no fight left.

metadata.Opening: Ruy Lopez: Open Berlin Defense, l'Hermet Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
One of the merits of beginning a game with 1 d4 is that the pawn standing in the centre is protected. It is safe from attack, whereas in openings starting with 1 e4, the e-pawn is more vulnerable.
In queen’s pawn openings, with the queen firmly backing up the centre pawn, White dictates the tempo. He has the initiative and keeps it for a long time against any defence, any line of play that Black may select. Right from the start, White is given the opportunity to build up his position, with little danger of being bothered by a counterattack, while Black struggles to achieve equality. If Black plays timidly – if he fails to dispute the centre by ...c5 at some stage – his queenside pieces, especially the c8-bishop, will be badly cramped and unable to develop decent activity. If he develops carelessly – moving the same piece several times in the opening or bringing his bishops out before the knights – punishment will come swiftly.
The purpose of chess being to win, not to entertain the gallery with pretty pictures on the chessboard, it is no wonder that many players prefer the ‘dull, safe Queen’s Gambit’ to the romantic but risky adventures of the kingside gambits.
I venture to say (and this opinion has forty years of research behind it) that the queen’s pawn openings have contributed as many masterpieces and as many genuine brilliancies as did any of the kingside openings.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This is the best way for Black to stabilize the pressure in the centre.
Each side now has a pawn firmly stationed in the middle of the board, occupying one square and attacking two others; each side has released two pieces for action.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The object of this move is to destroy Black’s pawn-centre. First, White offers a pawn to induce Black to surrender the centre. If that does not work, White threatens to dissolve it by 3 cxd5 Qxd5 4 Nc3 Qa5 5 e4, and White controls most of the centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black’s idea with this capture is to avoid the constricted positions that are normally his lot in the Queen’s Gambit Declined, but in doing so he has given up a beautifully centralized pawn for a less central one.
Accepting the gambit is perfectly sound, but the resulting play requires great care on Black’s part. Above all, he must not hold on to the extra pawn for too long.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A good move, but more to the point is 3 Nf3 to prevent the counterthrust 3... e5.
White plays to release his light-square bishop and recover the pawn at once.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
By this, Black hopes to solve the problem of the shut-in c8-bishop, one of the evils the defence is heir to. However, the solution is not quite so simple! The bishop’s absence from the queenside weakens that section of the board and leaves the b-pawn vulnerable. Another drawback in Black’s move is that it violates one of the precepts for sound development:
Bring out your knights before the bishops!
Instead of the text-move, Black’s best bet is in counterattack, viz.: 3... e5 4 Bxc4 (or 4 dxe5 Qxd1+ 5 Kxd1 Be6) 4...exd4 5 exd4 Bb4+.
Attempting to hold on to the extra pawn might lead Black into one of the traps prepared for the greedy: 3... b5 4 a4 c6 5 axb5 cxb5 6 Qf3, and White wins a piece.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The recovery of the pawn equalizes the material, but White’s position is slightly superior.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A pawn move that contributes to the development of a piece, in this case the f8-bishop, is always in order.
Developing one of the knights first is somewhat risky. For instance, 4... Nf6 5 Qb3 threatens to win a pawn by 6 Qxb7 or 6 Bxf7+, or if 4... Nc6 5 Qb3 Na5, then 6 Bxf7+ Kd7 7 Qd5+ Kc8 8 Qxf5+ Kb8 9 Qxa5, and White wins two pieces.
Even at this early stage White is directing events.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Why does White move his queen instead of getting his knights out?
His purpose is to punish Black for faulty development. Black’s play has not been normal procedure, and the way to take advantage of his sins is not with routine moves.
White’s move, developing a piece with a threat (6 Qxb7) keeps Black on the run. It does not give him time to consolidate his position.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This looks attractive, since Black protects his b-pawn, and at the same time threatens to play 6... Bxg2, winning a rook.
Black’s move, however, is abnormal and a serious infraction of the opening principle which states:
Move each piece only once in the opening; place it at once on the square where it exerts most power and where it has the greatest freedom of movement.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This move is justified on more than one count. Not only does it parry a threat in an economical way, but it also forces Black to lose a move in the retreat of his bishop. Incidentally, the pawn at f3 will firmly support a later advance of the e3-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Now we see the results of the bishop’s ill-timed expedition. It stands at c6, depriving the b8-knight of its natural square of development in the opening. Worse yet, it obstructs the c-pawn. If this pawn cannot get to c5 to dispute control of the centre and to open the c-file for Black’s pieces, there is a danger that Black will be smothered.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
“But the knight belongs on f3!” you must be protesting. So it does, but if it cannot develop at f3, get it into the game somehow! Move it, if only to get it off the back rank! Of course, the same comment applies to the other three knights, too.
White is ready to castle and get the h1-rook working.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: At last, a normal, reasonable developing move to which no exception can be taken! In nearly every variation of every opening, the king’s knight does its job most effectively at f6 (or f3 for White).

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The only square open to the bishop. If instead 8... Bd6, the reply 9 e5 wins a piece for White.
The back rank is cleared and Black is ready to castle – if White lets him!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Bringing another piece into play with gain of tempo. The threat is 10 d5 exd5 11 exd5 Bd7 12 Qxb7, and White wins a piece.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must guard the b-pawn and put aside any thought of castling for a while.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: In order to drive the bishop back to the second rank.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This exchange of pawns is inferior to simply retreating the bishop. The opening up of lines favours the side that is better developed, and in this case White will benefit.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This recapture opens the e-file for the use of White’s major pieces and compels Black’s bishop on c6 to retreat.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Anything else loses material.
Before making his next move, White must decide whether to continue bringing pieces into play or to try exploiting his present lead in development. Thus, he pauses to take stock before committing himself to a definite course of action.
He has a pawn stationed at d5, which at first glance is doing an excellent job. It prevents Black’s b8-knight from developing at c6, keeps the d7-bishop from coming to e6, and restrains the f6-knight. The pawn does this single-handed, but at a price! In standing at d5 it occupies a square that should be reserved for pieces. Pieces have more mobility than pawns and can attack more readily. Pieces can utilize d5 as a jumping-off square, a point of departure to any part of the board. In fact, the wretched pawn does a disservice in obstructing the diagonal of the bishop and the supporting queen and takes up room on a file which should be open! Better that the d5-square be vacant than that a pawn block traffic there! (And in this last sentence, as we shall see, is the key to White’s problem).
What about Black’s prospects?
With the exception of the f6-knight, his pieces are confined to the first two ranks. His position is a bit crowded, but if he gets a chance to castle and reorganize his forces, it will be hard to subdue him.
White must not allow him time to do this. White must not dawdle!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This energetic thrust opens the diagonal leading to Black’s tender spot, the f7-pawn, clears the d-file for later exploitation by a rook, and vacates the strategically important d5-square for the use of a piece. Meanwhile, the attack on Black’s bishop leaves him no time to breathe!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Better than 12...cxd6 hemming the bishop in.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This will smoke the king out! Once the king moves and loses the privilege of castling, he stands on insecure ground to the end of his days (which may not be far off).

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This pin paralyses Black’s most useful piece. Meanwhile – and this sums up the miserable state of his game – Black’s mighty queen is smothered by his own pieces!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black’s idea is to develop a piece and give the queen and a8-rook freedom to move – if only to the next square! It is hard to suggest a better move, as every move is inadequate in a losing position. Black might have ventured on a more active defence, such as 14... Be8 followed by 15... Rf8, 15... Qd7 or 15... Qf5. He must try to beat back White’s attacking pieces or get rid of them by exchanges.
The formula in such cases is:
In a cramped position try to relieve the pressure by forcing exchanges of pieces.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White puts more strain on the pinned knight. The threat (and there always is a threat when a pinned piece is attacked more than once) is 16 Nxf6 gxf6 17 Bxf6+, and White wins a rook.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Protecting the knight once again, and at the same time unpinning it. This is a better defence than 15... Be5, which helps guard the knight but does nothing to relieve the pin. In such situations, the extra defender itself may be on shaky ground and apt to be disturbed. For instance, after 15... Be5 16 f4 Bd4 17 Nxd4 (removing one of the knight’s protectors) 17... Nxd4 18 Qc3 Black is embarrassed for a plausible continuation.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White does well to remove this rock of defence.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black takes with the pawn, as he wants to keep both his bishops.
With his king so well sheltered by pieces, it looks difficult to penetrate Black’s barricades.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Much more energetic than castling on the other side. White’s king is somewhat exposed, but as compensation his a1-rook has an instant and powerful grip on the open d-file, putting particular pressure on the unfortunate bishop, which now is pinned. The manoeuvre of castling on the queenside gains a tempo for the attack, while White’s king is in little danger, since Black’s development is so backward.
White threatens 18 Be6 or 18 Qe6, either of which adds pressure to the pin.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Not only to help the bishop but also to play 18... Nxf7, removing one of his tormentors.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Threatening sudden death by 19 Ne6#.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
An unhappy situation for Black’s queen, but the king needs a flight square.
What else was there? If 18... Bf8 to free the e7-square for the king, then 19 Qe6 (threatening 20 Qe8#) 19... Be7 20 Qxe5! fxe5 21 Ne6# mates neatly.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With the queen’s entrance into the enemy camp, the attack gains momentum. White plans a win by 20 Nxf6 (striking once more at the hapless bishop and threatening 21 Rxd7+ and quick mate) 20... Bxf6 21 Qxf6+ Kc8 22 Qxh8+ and mate next move.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Hoping to scare off the bishop, when his f-pawn would be protected by the rook. The alternative 19... Qc8 runs into 20 Qxe5 and the previous win.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Isn’t it remarkable how threats are summoned up as if by magic against a piece that is pinned?

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Interfering with the rook’s action on the open file and thereby threatening to take the queen.
Other defences promise no favourable results:
1) 20... Rxf7 21 Rxd7+ and mate in two.
2) 20... Bxf6 21 Qxf6+ Kc8 22 Qxe5 Rxf7 23 Qh8+.
3) 20... Qc8 21 Qxe5 Rxf7 22 Ne6#.
With the text, Black unpins his d7-bishop, guards the e5-knight, attacks the queen and threatens the f7-bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This one hurts a bit. The knight captures one piece and attacks three others.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black recaptures and disposes of a troublesome piece.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The doubling of heavy pieces on the open e-file, with the consequent threat of 23 Qe8+ Rxe8 24 Rxe8#, is enough to break anyone’s spirit.
The c-pawn cannot move to give the king room because of the reply 23 Rxd6, and if 22... Nc5, then 23 Qe7+ Kc8 24 Qxf8+ Qxf8 25 Re8# is the finishing touch.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Accepted: Old Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White opens with one of the strongest possible first moves:
The d-pawn occupies an important square in the centre and attacks two valuable points, e5 and c5.
Control of these squares keeps the opponent from making use of them for his pieces.
The queen and dark-squared bishop can now leave the first rank.
The king is safe from some of the surprise attacks that occur in king’s pawn openings. These come about when Black develops his f8-bishop at c5 and sacrifices it for White’s f2-pawn to force the king out into the open and subject him to assault by the other pieces.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black equalizes the pressure in the centre, prevents White from continuing with 2 e4, and also releases two of his own pieces for action.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This is a threat and an offer! The threat, a positional one, is 3 cxd5, when after the recapture 3... Qxd5, 4 Nc3 drives the queen off and leaves White dominating the centre.
The offer of a pawn has as its purpose the removal of Black’s d-pawn from its fine position in the centre. This offer, unlike the one in the King’s Gambit, involves no risk. White regains the pawn easily and retains an advantage. It is in effect an exchange of a flank pawn for Black’s centre pawn. The point of playing 2 c4 so soon is that it disputes the centre at once, without endangering the safety of the king.
There is also another purpose – a strategic one. An exchange of pawns must come, sooner or later, resulting in the opening of the c-file. Ownership of this file is of paramount importance in the Queen ’ s Gambit. White generally tries to get full possession of it by posting his queen at c2, and developing his queen’s rook at c1.
Control of this file and of the c5-square on this file is equivalent to control of the game. Of such peculiar significance is this c5-square that it is almost enough simply to plant a piece securely there to get a paralysing grip on Black’s game.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black defends the centre pawn by supporting it with another pawn.
He does not care to capture by 2...dxc4 as that means surrendering the centre to gain a pawn which he cannot hold on to. White, in reply to this, would play 3 Nf3 (to prevent 3... e5), follow up with 4 e3, and then get the pawn back by 5 Bxc4, with a central superiority.
Defending the d-pawn by 2... Nf6 is weak. White would play in response 3 cxd5, and Black would have to recapture with a piece. On 3... Qxd5, 4 Nc3 banishes the queen from the centre and costs Black time, while 3... Nxd5 lets White seize the centre with 4 e4 and evict the knight in the process.
After the actual move, Black is set to meet 3 cxd5 by 3...exd5, keeping his hold on the centre by maintaining a pawn there.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is a commendable developing move, as it settles a minor piece on its most suitable square without loss of time. The knight bears down on the e4-square and adds its pressure to that of the c-pawn in the attack on d5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev
