annotation: This knight carries out his part of Black’s opening strategy by simply leaving the back rank. Naturally, his development is toward the centre, where he counteracts the influence of White’s knight on two of the important squares there.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A highly efficient move as it combines rapid development of a piece with a threat. This latter consists of 5 cxd5 exd5 6 Bxf6 gxf6 (or 6... Qxf6 7 Nxd5, and White wins a pawn) and Black’s kingside pawn position is shattered.
The opening thus far had been given sporadic earlier trials by various players, but Pillsbury was the first to appreciate its enormous winning possibilities. He pictured the bishop move (most masters brought the bishop quietly into the game at f4) as a sort of Ruy Lopez on the other side of the board! With this particular sequence of moves, which he perfected and popularized, he achieved some remarkable victories, notably in his debut at the Hastings 1895 tournament.
In this game, we see him applying the great power of the Queen’s Gambit to crush an opponent who is not familiar with its fine points and who puts up less than flawless defence. He beats Mason ‘like a child’, as Marshall used to express it.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: If nothing else, the development of the bishop anywhere furthers Black’s progress, as the decks are cleared for kingside castling. At e7, the bishop is happily placed for defence, and, if the need arises, can be transferred quickly to a more aggressive position. Incidentally, the knight is unpinned and White’s threat nullified.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: In queen’s pawn openings the king’s knight’s job is the control and sometimes the occupation of the outpost e5. In fact, entrenching the knight at this square and supporting it solidly with the d-pawn and the f-pawn is the motif of what later came to be known as the Pillsbury Attack, a tremendously effective assault on the kingside.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
At first glance, this seems to be a simple and natural way to develop the c8-bishop, as it is hemmed in on the other side by the e-pawn. It took many years, and a great many losses by Black, to discover that an early fianchetto of the bishop was not an easy solution to the problem of the bishop’s development.
After a great deal of trial and error, a reasonable defence was hit upon, which consisted of playing ...dxc4 at an early stage, followed after suitable preparation by an attack on White’s d-pawn by ...c5 or ...e5. The first of these moves (...c5) is intended to dispute control of the centre, open the c-file for the use of Black’s pieces and in general free his cramped position. The attack by ...e5 is meant to take away the control of e5 from White’s d-pawn, and to open a diagonal for Black’s c8-bishop.
In short, Black first puts up a fight for the centre before he thinks of developing the bishop.
It is of almost vital importance that Black play ...c5 sooner or later. This move strikes at White’s d-pawn, establishes tension in the centre, opens the c-file for his own major pieces and frees the crowded position on the queenside. Failure to make this move permits White to seize control of the c-file and the c5-square. Should White manage to post a piece on that square, it will exert terrific pressure on Black’s entire position, and this one factor alone may be enough to cause Black’s downfall.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White strengthens his centre and clears a path for his f1-bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black completes the fianchetto development of the c8-bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The rook hurries over to the important c-file. This is only partly open now, but an exchange of pawns will clear the file and accentuate the rook’s power along its whole length.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black usually waits until White moves his f1-bishop before making this capture, as then the bishop loses a move in recapturing. Apparently Black is anxious to give his b7-bishop more scope on the long central diagonal.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White recaptures the pawn and gets another piece into play.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This disposition of the knight is characteristic in queen’s pawn openings. The knight must not go to c6, blocking the c-pawn. The pawn must be free to advance and challenge the centre.
At d7, the knight is situated ideally: it supports an advance by ...c5 or ...e5, attacking the centre, it participates in the fight for possession of these squares, and it cooperates with the knight on f6.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king disappears from the scene while the rook is made available for duty.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The advantage of castling is that the king is safer in the corner, where he is sheltered by three pawns and a stalwart knight, than in the centre of the board, while the rook is brought toward the centre files in the most convenient way possible.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The two most effective squares that White’s queen can occupy in this opening are e2 and c2. At c2, the queen supplements the rook’s action in exploiting the c-file, while in another direction guards the strategically important e4-square from invasion by Black’s f6-knight. At e2, the queen prevents Black from breaking up the kingside pawn position by 10... Bxf3, supports an advance of the e-pawn which would monopolize the centre, and clears the way for the f1-rook to reach d1.
Developing the queen to e2 offers another advantage: attack on the queenside. By playing 11 Ba6, White can force an exchange of bishops and then bring pressure to bear on Black’s light squares, weakened by the removal of the bishop controlling those squares.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black’s purpose in this is to free his cramped position by bringing about an exchange or two.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White is willing to simplify by clearing away some pieces, as he can then return to his theme of exerting painful pressure on the c-file.
The alternative, retreat by 11 Bf4, offers Black a choice of too many good continuations. He could play 11... Nxf4 (leaving himself with the two bishops) 12 exf4 Nf6 followed by 13... Nd5, keeping a piece permanently on a square where no enemy pawns could dislodge it, or Black might attack the centre at once with 11... c5. Finally, he could swing the d7-knight over to f6 with a respectable game.
White’s actual move has the merit of restricting Black’s choice of reply.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is preferable to capturing by 11... Nxe7 as Black gets his queen into play and unites his rooks. Naturally, he cannot go in for 11... Nxc3 12 Bxd8 Nxe2+ 13 Bxe2 Rfxd8 14 Rxc7 (triumph of the rook on the open file) as it loses a pawn and the game.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This time the knight exchange suits White, who now can dictate the course of events.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Forced, as 12... Bxd5 13 Bxd5 exd5 14 Rxc7 costs a pawn.
In forcing Black to take with the pawn, White has compelled the closing of the long diagonal, so that Black’s bishop is now terribly limited in scope.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Presto! The file is suddenly open, and the c-file action begins with the rook’s attack on the c7-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black guards the pawn and prepares to dislodge White’s bishop by 14... c6.
It is already too late to advance the pawn to c5 as after 13... c5 (seemingly a safe move as the pawn is triply defended and only twice attacked) 14 Bxd7 Qxd7 (note how White disposes of two of the defenders with one stroke) 15 dxc5 bxc5 16 Rxc5 White wins a pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White makes room for the other rook at cl, to add to the pressure. The device of doubling rooks on an open file more than doubles their strength on that file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black tries to evict the annoying bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is much stronger than 15 Ba4, when Black gets some troublesome counterplay by 15... b5 16 Bb3 a5 (threatening to win the bishop by 17... a4) 17 a3 Nb6, and the knight settles itself firmly at c4.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Blissfully unconscious of the impending danger, Black goes about his business, which in this case consists of bringing the knight over to attack, and perhaps to occupy e4. Ordinarily, this is commendable procedure, but all strategy must be conditioned by the circumstances, the position at hand. All moves must be made with respect to the threats of the opponent, not to arbitrary judgements which declare that certain moves are always ‘good’ or ‘bad’. All moves must be measured by their worth in the particular position being played.
White has declared his intention of piling up as much pressure as possible on the c-file and on the c6-pawn. Black must meet that threat by bringing all his resources to bear for defence of the file, or institute a counterattack vigorous enough to divert White’s forces from the assault.
Black must do something to resolve his immediate difficulties, and he must do it at once, before his opponent gets a death grip on the open file.
With his last move, Black misses a golden opportunity – his last chance to play 15... c5, establish a state of tension in the centre, and give his pieces more room to move around in.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This fixes Black’s c-pawn by preventing it from moving; if 16... c5, then 17 dxc5 bxc5 18 Rxc5 and White wins a pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Rushing to the defence of the c-pawn and renewing (now that Black realizes his peril) the possibility of pushing the pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Very fine strategy! White wants to remove Black’s bishop, since minor pieces are excellent defenders of pawns that are attacked by the heavy pieces. White’s rooks could never seriously threaten the c-pawn while the bishop protected it.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Was there anything else Black could have done? If 17... Rc7, White wins by 18 Bxb7 Rxb7 19 Rxc6 or if 17... Qc7 , then 18 b4 further restrains the pawn, after which White intensifies the pressure by 19 Ne5, simplifies by exchanging bishops and then takes the pawn off.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The queen comes closer, attacking not only the a-pawn directly, but also the c-pawn indirectly by the threat 19 Qb7 Rc7 20 Rxc6 Rxb7 21 Rxd6, and White wins.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s strategy is simple: he piles up more pressure on the c-pawn. It is now attacked by three pieces and defended by two.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The planned 19... Rfc8 lets White win nicely by 20 Nxc6 Rxc6 21 Qxc8+! Rxc8 22 Rxc8+ Qf8 23 Rxf8+ Kxf8 24 Rc7 a5 25 Rb7 and the rest is child’s play.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: From now on, White simply removes anything that isn’t nailed down.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black is not wild about exchanging pieces when he is a pawn down, but what can he do? If he disputes the c-file by 20... Rfc8 then 21 Qxc8+ wins, as in the earlier note, while on 20... Re7 (the c7-rook’s only flight square) 21 Rc6 Qd8 (or 21... Qb4 22 Nd3 Qd2 23 R6c2 Qa5 24 Qxa5 bxa5, and the forced exchange of queens leaves Black’s position in ruins) 22 a3 White’s threat of winning the queen by 23 Rc8 Qd6 24 R1c6 is hard to meet.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The rook recaptures, disdainful of the pinned pawn which is helpless to remove it, and remains in control of the valuable open file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This looks attractive as the knight attacks two pieces. If White replies 22 Nxd7, then 22... Qxd7 leaves a queen and rook ending which is not easy to win. White would eventually have to advance his pawn majority on the kingside and expose his king to a possible drawing perpetual check.
If the rook retreats, Black continues 22... Nxe5 23 dxe5 Qxe5, again with drawing chances.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Neatly side-stepping the knight exchange, the rook gains time by attacking the queen.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black is forced into making this ‘combination’ as the retreat by 22... Qe7 is disastrous after 23 Rc7 (pinning the knight) 23... Rd8 24 Qb5 (triple attack!), and White wins a piece.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Simplify! That’s the magic word to remember in endings where you have an advantage in material.
With you are a pawn ahead, reduce the material (and your opponent's chances) by exchanging pieces, if it does not weaken your position.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Forced, of course.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A master move! You or I might grab the d-pawn in order to be two pawns ahead. This could win, but why complicate matters? Why let Black seize the c-file with 24... Rc8 and start a counterattack?
Note that Pillsbury retains his attack on the d-pawn with the text-move, adds to it a threat against the a-pawn and prevents Black from playing 24... Rc8, when the knight check at e7 would annihilate him!
It is subtle moves in apparently simple positions and not queen sacrifices that mark the master player.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Sooner or later, the king will need some air. The king is also anxious to lend a hand in the ending by moving toward the centre, by way of g7.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Another pawn falls, while two more are threatened by the rook.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Unable to get to c8, the rook makes frantic efforts to enter the fight.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight withdraws, still in position to punish 26... Rc8 by 27 Ne7+ winning the rook.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black moves the king out of range of the knight check and closer to the centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
There is no hurry about taking the d-pawn. White guards his a-pawn from any discovered attack on it by the rook hidden away at a8, and also prevents Black’s knight from later emerging at b4.
Note that White avoids 27 Rxd5 Rc8 28 Rd6 (the knight cannot move due to the mate threat) 28... Nb4, when Black wins the helpless knight.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Finally posting his rook on the coveted file, but can Black make use of it?

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White’s king also needs an escape square. Black was threatening to win a piece by 28... Nb8, twice attacking the knight which could not run away.
The break-up of the pawn position around the castled king is of no consequence in the ending. It is in the opening and middlegame that these moves endanger the health of the king, as then he may be assaulted by every piece on the board.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black protects his d-pawn, but at the cost of blocking the rook. There was little choice because White was threatening 29 Ne7 (attacking the black rook and a couple of pawns) 29... Rc1+ 30 Kg2 Rb1 31 Rxb6, and the two connected passed pawns assure White an easy win.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Once again chasing the rook from the open c-file. White threatens the rook, attacks the b-pawn and doubly attacks the d-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must hang on to the b-pawn as long as possible, as with its loss White’s pawns on the queenside are free to go on to queen.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The pressure must not be relaxed! Pillsbury prefers this to the rook ending resulting from 30 Nxd5 Nxd5 31 Rxd5, though that would also win.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight must leave, as the effort to protect it by 30... Rb7 fails after 31 Nxd5 winning a piece.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The d-pawn falls at last, giving White a passed pawn on the d-file and a rook on the seventh rank (in addition to the pawns he picked up).

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Rather than be gradually crushed to death, Black gives up another pawn to get some sort of counterplay on the open file. If his rook can get behind White’s pawns, it might gather up a couple of them.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White can play safe and keep the rook out by 32 Nc3 but capturing the b-pawn leaves him with three passed pawns – an offer hard to resist!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Occupation of the seventh rank is the logical consequence of play on an open file by a rook. This could mean trouble for White except that he has powerful antidotes in all those pawns ready to rush up the board to become queens!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The pawn lightly evades the rook’s attack.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s pawns are not readily hindered from advancing, but perhaps White’s deserted king might be sensitive to an attack by knight and rook.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White goes calmly about his business of pushing the passed pawns and getting a queen.
It was tempting to drive the knight off with 34 f4 but this move, believe it or not, enables Black to draw the game! After 34 f4 Nf3+ 35 Kf1 (definitely not 35 Kh1 Rxh2#) 35... Rd2! 36 Nc4 Nxh2+ 37 Kg1 Nf3+ 38 Kf1 Nh2+ 39 Ke1 Nf3+ Black draws by perpetual check.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black tries another means of entry.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Again, Pillsbury resists the impulse to get in a dig at the knight. If 35 f3, then 35... Ng5 again threatens 36... Nxf3+ and a draw by perpetual check.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Can Black conjure up a mating attack?

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White demonstrates the futility of his opponent’s gestures by paying no attention to them! The passed pawn has only two more squares to cover and cannot be stopped in its march.
Black decides that it would be too much to hope for this bit of luck: 36... Nh3+ 37 Kh1? Ng5 38 a7? Nf3 39 a8 Q Rxh2#! Of course, White would play 37 Kf1, when he wins easily.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
In the opening, it is advantageous to occupy the centre with a pawn and to develop the pieces with a view to controlling the centre.
White begins by placing a pawn where it takes complete possession of one important square and attacks two others. Control of the two squares e5 and c5 makes it impossible for Black to place pieces there. White can hope to use e5 and c5 as outposts for his pieces, which will have the support of the d-pawn.
The advance of the d-pawn serves an additional purpose in opening lines for White’s queen and c1-bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is the simplest way for Black to get an equal grip on the centre and to prevent White acquiring more territory with 2 e4.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White offers a pawn to divert Black’s d-pawn from the centre. In effect, it is an offer to exchange a flank pawn for a centre pawn, as White can regain the pawn without any trouble.
Concealed in White’s proposal is a threat of destroying Black’s pawn-centre by 3 cxd5 Qxd5 4 Nc3 (gaining a tempo, as White develops a piece while Black must move the same one again) 4... Qa5 5 e4, and White’s control of the centre is imposing.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black defends the centre by supporting the d-pawn with another pawn. If White plays 3 cxd5, Black can recapture with a pawn and maintain a pawn in the centre.
Black does not capture White’s c4-pawn as that means surrendering the centre and his grip on e4.
The shutting in of his c8-bishop (after 2... e6) and the consequent difficulty in developing that piece effectively is one of the reasons for the popularity of the Queen’s Gambit – for White.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A good move, as the knight attacks the two central squares e4 and d5, adding its influence to the pawn’s pressure on the latter.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black’s knight develops toward the centre, where its mobility is greatest and where it can counter the pressure exerted by White’s knight.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A pin which threatens 5 cxd5 exd5 6 Bxf6, when Black must either submit to being left with a badly doubled pawn by 6...gxf6 or lose a pawn after 6... Qxf6 7 Nxd5.
The threat is actually of minor importance. White’s real aim in pinning the knight is not to institute a threat that can so easily be parried. What White is interested in is the most effective placement of his pieces, and the development of the bishop at g5 is extremely strong. The restraint it places on Black’s knight and the cramping effect it has on Black’s whole game is not easily shaken off.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
In queen’s pawn openings, Black’s queen’s knight does its best job at d7, not c6. At d7 it supports the other knight and helps prepare the advance of the c-pawn to c5. The b8-knight must not move to c6, where it obstructs the c-pawn. The c-pawn must be free to advance and attack White’s centre.
Black incidentally sets a trap with the text-move, which is designed to catch the greedy player.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Why not win a pawn by 5 cxd5 exd5 6 Nxd5 instead? There would then follow 6... Nxd5! (the knight breaks the pin by brute force) 7 Bxd8 Bb4+ 8 Qd2 Bxd2+ 9 Kxd2 Kxd8 and Black has gained a piece.
White could not fall into the trap if he followed the principle which covers these cases:
Do not chase after pawns at the expense of your development.
White’s last move supports the central d4-pawn and creates an outlet for the f1-bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black strengthens his d-pawn and opens a diagonal for his queen’s use. He plans a counterattack beginning with 6.. Qa5 and 7... Bb4 .

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This puts a stop to any such manoeuvre, as Black’s bishop can never get to b4 to pin the knight.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black develops a piece, unpins the knight and clears the back rank for castling.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: An ideal development for the queen in this opening. At c2, the queen exerts pressure on the c-file (which will be strongly evident after centre pawns are exchanged) and controls the e4-square. The latter circumstance is the reason for the queen coming into play at this point, instead of the expected mobilization of the kingside pieces. It is vital to guard the e4-square so that Black cannot free himself easily by playing 7... Ne4 and exchanging some pieces.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black moves his king to safer quarters. He cannot free his crowded position by the Lasker manoeuvre 7... Ne4 as White responds 8 Bxe7 Qxe7 9 Nxe4 dxe4 10 Qxe4 and wins a pawn. Notice that White’s pawn at a3 prevents Black from regaining the pawn by 10... Qb4+, showing that White’s sixth move was not a waste of time.
Instead of the passive kingside castling, Black should have tried for counterplay by 7...dxc4 8 Bxc4 e5!, which disputes control of the centre and helps clear a diagonal for his c8-bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White brings his king’s knight to its best post and attacks the e5-square again, putting an end to any contemplated break by ...e5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Preparation for the manoeuvre 9...dxc4 10 Bxc4 b5 11 Bd3 Bb7, followed by an eventual ...c5. This would serve to develop the c8-bishop, free his queenside and start action against White’s pawn-centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
If Black is going in for an attack on the wing, White is prepared to meet it with the recommended antidote – play in the centre!
The position of the rook at d1 acts as a deterrent to central pawn exchanges by Black, as any clearances on the d-file increase the pressure of the rook on that file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black brings his rook to the e-file, as the centre is usually the theatre of action.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With the entrance of this bishop, White’s development is nearly complete. Notice that he plays no combinations of any sort, either to win material or to start an attack on the king, until most of his pieces are brought off the back rank and into play. It is only after these pieces are posted where they are most effective – where they control the centre, enjoy their greatest mobility, and take possession of a good part of the important territory – that White looks around for a combination, a stroke that will decide the game quickly.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black has delayed taking this pawn until White’s f1-bishop made a move, so that the bishop will now lose a move in recapturing.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The recapture is forced.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black makes the bishop lose time in retreating and vacates the b7-square, ready for the development of the c8-bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
From this square, the bishop manages to be remarkably useful:
It reaches out in two directions to attack, it helps guard e4 from invasion, it threatens Black’s kingside and, by attacking h7, prevents Black from freeing himself by means of 12... c5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
If 12... c5, then 13 dxc5 Bxc5 (certainly not 13... Nxc5 14 Bxh7+ and White wins the queen by discovered attack) 14 Bxh7+ and White wins a pawn, as the pinned knight is helpless to take the bishop.
With the text-move, Black moves the h-pawn out of the attack of White’s queen and bishop. Now he hopes to free his queenside and establish a state of tension in the centre by 13... c5. Incidentally, he would like White’s g5-bishop to declare its intentions.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A very fine concept! White does not waste time holding on to the two bishops but plays to prevent any counterplay by ...c5. If he can keep the c-pawn from advancing, Black’s game will be fearfully cramped, and he may never solve the problem of getting his light-squared bishop settled on a decent square.
The immediate object of 13 Bxf6 is to divert one of Black’s recapturing pieces, the knight or the bishop, from its surveillance of the c5-square and the support of a pawn moving to that square.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is probably better than taking with the bishop, as Black’s queen and c8-bishop now have more freedom.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king (who must be secure from danger at all costs) goes into hiding, while the rook (that must take part in the fighting) comes closer to the scene of action.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
With rook and queen on the same file, it would be foolhardy to venture on 14... c5. White simply takes the pawn, 15 dxc5, and punishes the recapture 15... Bxc5 with 16 Bh7+ winning the queen.
Black’s idea, besides that of developing the light-squared bishop, is to bring his rook to c8 and then push the c-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White clears the c-file so that he now has three pieces (queen, knight and d4-pawn) concentrating their power on c5, with the aim of making an advance of Black’s c-pawn to that square impossible.
Notice too how White has resisted the temptation to play e4, filling up the centre with pawns. Instead he keeps the e4-square free and utilizes it as a springboard for his pieces.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Otherwise, White might swing the knight over to c5 and completely smother Black’s queenside.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Still keeping Black under restraint: he may not play 16... c5 as his b7-bishop would be snapped up.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must drive the bishop off at once, even at the cost of weakening the pawn position on his kingside. A delay gives White time to play 17 Ne5 (intensifying the pressure on the c-pawn and incidentally providing the f3-square for a bishop retreat) followed if need be by 18 Rc1.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The third visit of the bishop to this square.
White must not be hasty and play 17 Bxc6 as the reply 17... Rc8 pins the bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Once again preparing the liberating pawn-push.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The position demands that White devote all his efforts to sustaining the blockade of Black’s c-pawn. White must acquire undisputed control of the c5-square, so that the pawn may never advance. He must not relax for a moment, as domination of the key c5-square virtually assures him of a positional win.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black persists in his plan to push the pawn. If he does not get this move in, his b7-bishop will never have any air.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White nails the pawn down! White has a won game, strategically. What remains is to apply the proper tactical touches to compel the opponent to yield. The time is ripe for the combinations to appear!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Ready to parry 20 Qb3 (threatening 21 Qxe6+ or 21 Bxf5) with 20... Qd5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A powerful blow! White attacks the unfortunate c-pawn (which must stay where it is) a third time. Against passive resistance, White plans 21 f4 (to give his knight additional support and to stabilize the centre), followed by 22 Be2 and 23 Bf3, after which the c-pawn must perish.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Again threatening 22 Qxe6+ or 22 Bxf5.
White probably gave no more than a glance to 21 bxa5, to which Black can reply 21... Qxa5, 21... Bxa3 or 21... c5, any of which gives him far too much freedom – from White’s point of view!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The defence that Black had relied on is ruled out: if 21... Qd5, then 22 Qxd5 and White wins a pawn after 22...exd5 23 Bxf5 or 22...cxd5 23 Bxb5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The first bit of actual violence brings in a pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With an attack on the bishop and a double attack on the knight, Black hopes to get his pawn back.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The idea of this withdrawal to the back rank is to support the queen in an attack along a diagonal, either by moving the queen to c2 or by shifting the bishop to a2 behind the queen.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black does not care to part with the services of an active piece, but he must do so in order to recover the pawn he lost.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Forced.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Material is even, and Black seems to have survived the worst.
It is true that White can win a pawn by 25 bxa5, but he would be left with doubled and isolated pawns on the a-file, and it is doubtful that he could get any advantage from the extra pawn. There must be a better reward for fine positional play than this dubious bounty!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White spurns the pawn, in favour of piling on more pressure. The rook now holds Black’s queenside in a paralysing grip. The strength of White’s move is evident in the fact that the rook can never be dislodged!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: An intermediary move, whose purpose is not only to save the pawn, but also to gauge White’s plans by his next queen move.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A remarkable retreat! One would expect 26 Qc2 so that the queen, backed up by the bishop, might penetrate Black’s kingside position. However, Black refutes this cleverly by 26... Qf6 and now:
1) 27 Qh7+ is met by 27... Kf7, when White has no means of furthering the attack.
2) 27 e4 (intending to banish the queen by 28 e5 and then pierce the position) 27... e5 and Black repels any invasion.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Now this grouping has more effect! White threatens 28 Qh7+ Kf8 29 Bg6 Red8 30 Qh8+ Ke7 31 Qxg7#.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: If 27... e5 to guard the g6-square with the queen, then 28 Qh7+ Kf7 (on 28... Kf8, 29 Bg6 wins easily) 29 f4 (threatening 30 fxe5+) 29... e4 30 Ba2+ Kf6 31 Qf5+ Ke7 32 Qf7+ and White wins the bishop, as a start.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Control of the light squares leading to Black’s king renders this a decisive invasion; the cramping of Black’s queenside and the smothering of his bishop make it difficult for Black to hold out.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: On 28... Kf7 White can either win the exchange by a bishop check or pursue the attack by 29 f4, when the continuation might be 29... Rh8 30 Qg6+ Kf8 31 f5 e5 (or 31... Qe7 32 f6) 32 f6 and White wins.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Further confines the king while attacking the rook. The threat is 30 Qh8+ Ke7 31 Qxg7# .
Black can only delay the execution at great cost in material.
White’s play is a fine example of the value of preventive strategy. In paralysing Black’s queenside, he demonstrates the extraordinary fact that weaknesses on one wing can lead to complete collapse on the other! Once Black is held in restraint, his efforts to make some sort of stand seem little more than feeble flutterings.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation, Anti-Cambridge Springs Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Beginning the game with this pawn move releases two pieces at one stroke. This is as much as White can achieve in one move in the way of getting the pieces off the back rank and into play. The pawn itself plays an important part in the struggle for domination of the centre and the control of key squares.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Probably Black’s best reply. With it, he offsets White’s pressure on the centre.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This is an attack, as well as an offer of a pawn. It is an attack in that White threatens by 3 cxd5 Qxd5 4 Nc3 Qa5 5 e4 to establish two pawns abreast in the centre. It is an offer, since Black can gain a pawn (temporarily, it is true) by 2...dxc4.
Either way you look at it, White’s purpose is to destroy Black’s pawn-centre, either by removing Black’s d-pawn from d5, or enticing it away from there.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black is ready to meet 3 cxd5 with 3...cxd5, recapturing with a pawn in order to maintain a pawn in the centre.
Black’s second move has the merit of not shutting in the c8-bishop, as the alternative 2... e6 does. On the debit side though, if Black does develop his bishop freely, he must be prepared to beat off troublesome attacks on his d-pawn and his b-pawn, occasioned by the absence of the bishop. Another and more important consideration is that while the c-pawn standing at c6 represents a fine support for the d-pawn, it is not fulfilling its main purpose in life, which is to challenge White’s control of the centre. It must be available to advance to c5 in order to attack White’s d-pawn and to open the c-file for the use of Black’s heavy pieces.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Why doesn’t White play 3 c5 and stifle his opponent completely on the queenside? These are some of the reasons he does not do so:
1) It is good strategy to maintain tension in the centre – to keep the pawn position fluid, not static.
2) In advancing to c5, White gives up his attack on the enemy centre, and the option of exchanging pawns when it is worthwhile to do so. Such an exchange might be the means of demolishing Black’s whole centre!
3) The c5-square should be an outpost for a piece, not a pawn. A piece posted there exerts a tremendous effect on Black’s whole queenside.
4) Placing a pawn at c5 closes the c-file and makes it useless for the operations of the queen or the rooks.
5) In the opening, pieces, not pawns, should be moved.
All the foregoing explains why a chess master ‘instinctively’ finds the right moves. It is not that he can analyse twenty moves ahead, or that he bothers to examine the effects of every possible move. Sometimes he does not even look one move ahead! He saves time by dismissing from consideration any move which his instinct (or more accurately his experience and judgement) warns is contrary to principle and cannot possibly lead to favourable results. By discarding moves which offend his feeling for what is proper, by avoiding artificial expedients which are distasteful to his positional judgement, he plays stronger, sounder chess at ten seconds a move than does the average amateur in his serious tournament games.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This quiet move strengthens his centre and frees the f8-bishop.
Black’s intentions are still unclear. He might capture the c4-pawn next move and then try to hold on to it by ...b5, or he might go in for the Stonewall formation, by playing 4... f5 followed by 5... Nf6 and possibly 6... Ne4.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White plays safe by protecting the c4-pawn. He releases one bishop at the expense of another, but one cannot have everything.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight takes up a good post, extending powerful influence on d5 and e4, two of the four strategically important squares in the centre.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The bishop occupies a diagonal where it can operate with great effect, while the kingside is cleared for speedy castling.
Broadly speaking, it is good policy to develop the kingside pieces first, so that the king can find safer quarters. Most players are familiar enough with this procedure and its benefits to carry it out faithfully, some even to the extent of completely forgetting about releasing the queenside pieces!

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Excellent, as the knight supports an eventual thrust at White’s centre by ...c5 or ...e5. Being in touch with the other knight also has its uses, as it can replace the f6-knight.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The chief object of this move is to back up an advance of the e-pawn as in the Colle System. A second purpose of the knight’s development at d2 instead of c3 is to recapture with the knight if Black plays 6...dxc4, and then anchor one of the knights at e5, strongly supported by the other.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A good defensive move – perhaps too much so! The bishop is well placed at e7, and progress is made toward castling, but no attempt is made to prevent White from expanding and acquiring more territory. Black must get in the counter-thrust ...c5 or be slowly crowded back and confined to a small area.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king flees to a safer part of the board, while the h1-rook takes a more active position.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Another quiet developing move, which might better have been replaced by the aggressive 7... c5. Black cannot temporize but must fight for equal rights. Chess is no game for cowards!

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This resembles the Colle device for breaking up the position in the centre and opening lines of attack for the pieces crouched in the background.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black cannot allow the pawn to go to e5. There it would drive away his f6-knight and put it completely out of action.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: More energetic than recapturing with the bishop. The knight gets out of the way of the c1-bishop and puts the question to the enemy knight.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must exchange to relieve his constricted position.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The exchange of pieces suits White too. The more material disappears from the board, the more scope there is for the activities of his pieces, especially the wide-ranging bishops.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The attack on the bishop gains a tempo for Black while giving his queenside pieces a bit more room.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The bishop retreats, but to a fine vantage point. It is poised for a kingside attack but can quickly shift to the queenside if necessary.
White’s position is distinctly superior. He enjoys these advantages:
His bishops have a great range of attack.
He dominates the centre with his pawns.
He controls the strategically important e5-square.
His major pieces can operate with great effect on the centre files.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: To develop the bishop at b7, since it is shut in by the e-pawn on the other diagonal.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White develops another piece and intensifies the pressure on e5. Control of this square will make it difficult, if not impossible, for Black to free his position by advancing the e-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With the development of this bishop, Black seems to be finding a way out of his troubles. He is now set to play ...c5 next move, operate on the long diagonal with his light-squared bishop and establish a proper state of tension in the centre. Will he have time for this, or has he missed the right moment to hit out with ...c5?

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A magnificent outpost for the knight! From this central station, the knight radiates power in eight directions, accentuating Black’s difficulties in gaining freedom for his pieces.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This looks plausible, since Black mobilizes the rook while attacking a pawn.
It is too late, alas, to play the liberating 13... c5; White’s reply 14 Ba4+ would force Black’s king to move (interposing the knight or bishop instead costs a piece) and forfeit the right to castle.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White defends without loss of time. The rook guards the pawn and develops simultaneously, going to the file it would have chosen in any event.
Rooks belong on open files, or on files likely to be opened.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The advance 14... c5 is still premature, being met by 15 Ba4+ and Black must either move the king and lose the castling privilege, or play 15... Nd7 losing the exchange after 16 Bxd7+ Rxd7 17 Nxd7.
Before White makes his next move, let us sum up his advantages:
His pawn position in the centre, restraining the free movements of the enemy pieces, is definitely superior to Black’s.
His queen attacks nine squares while Black’s is limited to five.
His bishops control thirteen squares, whereas Black’s are limited to seven.
His knight enjoys wonderful mobility, while Black’s knight can only retreat.
Clearly, White has established a definite positional superiority. His pieces have greater mobility, as simple arithmetic shows, and their power to attack is definitely greater than that of Black’s army. White has earned the right to look for a decisive combination that will exploit to the full his positional advantages.
It is interesting to see what form of attack will succeed in breaking through Black’s strongly entrenched position.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop develops with a threat against the queen. White intends to play 16 Ng6 next move, discovering an attack on the queen by the bishop. After the queen moves away, White will capture the f8-rook, winning the exchange.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The alternative 15... Qc8, moving the queen out of the bishop’s range, does not look appetizing. With the text, Black prevents the knight from moving and uncovering an attack.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This begins a series of vigorous blows which do not let up until Black surrenders. White’s idea is twofold: he will dislodge the bishop and permanently seal up Black’s queenside position.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is forced, as on 16... Bxe5 White can win by 17 Bxe5 Qc8 18 Bxf6 gxf6 19 Qg4+ Kh8 20 Bxh7 Kxh7 21 Rd3 followed by 22 Rh3#.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Another pawn springs up to stab at the bishop.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Or 17... Bxc5 18 Ng6 and White wins the exchange.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This recapture attacks the queen and keeps Black on the run.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: If 18... Qc8 White wins by 19 Bxf6 gxf6 20 Qg4+ Kh8 21 Qh4 (threatening mate) 21... f5 22 Qf6+ Kg8 23 h4 (intending to push the pawn to h6 and then to mate at g7) 24... Rd7 (to follow with 24... Qd8 driving White’s queen off) 24 Rxd7 Qxd7 25 Rd1 Qc7 26 h5, when the two threats of 27 h6 and 27 Rd3 (followed by 28 Rg3+) are decisive.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White does away with the knight, the best defender of a castled position, as a prelude to breaking into the stronghold of the king.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: After this, Black’s position on the kingside is torn apart, where it should be barricaded. On the queenside, where his pieces need room for their movements, his position is nailed up – and by an unprotected pawn at that!

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is more accurate than 20 Qe4. It leaves Black with only one reply.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king must go to the corner.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Now threatening mate on the move.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black’s only defence.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Penetrating into the heart of the enemy’s position. The attack on the black bishop is a device whose purpose is to occupy the opponent, even if only for a moment, with the problem of saving the bishop. This will give White the time he needs to carry out his real threat, an attack on both the black rooks.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: If Black plays 22... Rb8 to protect the bishop, White wins this way: 23 Qf6+ Kg8 24 Rd3 f4 25 Rh3 (threatening 26 Bxh7#) 25... Rfd8 26 Rxh7 and mate follows.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A knockout blow! The queen is forced off the diagonal leading to the rook at d8 – which needs her protection!
What can Black do?
1) 23... Qxb4 24 Rxd8 Rxd8 25 Qxd8+ wins.
2) 23... Rfe8 is met by 24 Qf6+ followed by 25 bxa5.
3) 23... Rxd1+ 24 Rxd1 leaves two strong threats on tap: 25 Qxf8# and 25 bxa5, which cannot both be parried at the same time.

metadata.Opening: Slav Defense: Modern Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A hundred and forty years ago, players began their games almost automatically with 1 e4, and if they could offer a gambit, they did so.
Today, when everyone wants to win with the minimum of risk, 1 d4 has become equally popular. The queen’s pawn openings lead to positions which are safe and sound. They offer security, and as additional inducement let White have a slight advantage right from the start.
With his first move, White occupies and exerts pressure in the centre with a pawn which is protected and simultaneously frees his queen and dark-squared bishop.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The classical reply, this equalizes the pressure in the centre. It also prevents White from playing 2 e4 and monopolizing most of the best squares.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
With several objects in mind:
To induce Black to surrender the centre, by offering him a pawn.
To exchange pawns (if Black does not) and open the c-file for his rooks.
To institute an attack on Black’s d-pawn, and the d5-square.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black supports the d-pawn with another pawn. He is prepared, if White plays 3 cxd5, to recapture with a pawn and maintain a pawn in the centre.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A good development for the knight, now that it does not block the c-pawn and the opening of the c-file. It is a bit sharper than 3 Nf3 since it steps up the pressure on d5, an important square in this opening.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This move had the unqualified endorsement of Tarrasch. He held that Black had no better means of developing his pieces freely and easily, even if pawn exchanges in the centre leave him with an isolated pawn.
One advantage of 3... c5 is that it disputes possession of the centre at once by the attack on the d4-pawn. Another is that it enables Black to post his queen’s knight at c6, instead of at d7 where it interferes for a long time with the career of the c8-bishop.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The best way to keep the initiative! This exchange aims to saddle Black with an isolated d-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The safest recapture. Black can offer a pawn by 4...cxd4 5 Qxd4 Nc6 6 Qd1 exd5 7 Qxd5 Be6 but this gambit is dubious.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s knights now have all four of the strategically important central squares (e4, e5, d4 and d5) under surveillance.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: It makes little difference whether Black plays this or 5... Nc6 first.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Probably the best of the many good moves White has at his disposal. He can also play the placid 6 e3 or 6 Bf4, either of which gives him a safe, substantial position, or he can attack at once by the aggressive 6 Bg5, with which Alekhine beat Kussman brilliantly in a 1924 simultaneous exhibition.
With the quiet text-move, Rubinstein intends to fianchetto his light-squared bishop and increase the pressure on d5.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black attains one of the objectives that motivated him to select the Tarrasch Defence. His queen’s knight enjoys some influence in the centre, while the light-squared bishop (usually restrained by a knight at d7) is free and unrestrained.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop commands the long diagonal and will devote special attention to Black’s d-pawn. For the moment, the knight obstructs its path, but a knight can readily leap aside.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black exchanges to give his pieces more scope (note the increased mobility of his dark-squared bishop) but this is not without its dangers. Open lines favour the player whose development is superior, and in this case it is White.
Somewhat better is the quiet move 7... Be7, developing a piece or, if Black feels pugnacious, the sharp 7... Bg4 putting more pressure on the d4-pawn by striking at one of its defenders.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The recapture leaves Black with an isolated pawn in the centre of the board. Such a pawn must depend on pieces to defend it from attack, as there are no pawns on either side that can come to its support. Another consideration is that an enemy piece can be posted firmly on the square directly in front of the isolated pawn, in this case d4, without any fear of being driven off by a pawn.
All this is very discouraging, but in return for these shortcomings, the possessor of the isolated pawn is rewarded with open files and diagonals – room for the activities of his pieces. The pawn itself, in spite of its forlorn appearance, often becomes the spearhead that pierces and breaks up a fortified position.
The theorists themselves are not in complete agreement on the merits or demerits of an isolated pawn. Many years ago, Philidor said in his Chess Analysed: or Instructions by Which a Perfect Knowledge of This Noble Game May in a Short Time Be Acquired: “A pawn, when separated from his fellows, will seldom or never make a fortune.” For the defence, we have Tarrasch, who said, “He who fears possession of an isolated d-pawn should give up chess.”
There are arguments for both sides:
Black has in his favour: increased mobility for his pieces, possible outposts for his pieces at e4 and c4 (supported by the d-pawn) and open files for his major pieces (the e- and c-files).
White has advantages in the fact that he can station a piece permanently at d4 and can keep Black busy warding off threats to the d-pawn. Not that the pawn can easily be captured, since the number of pieces attacking it can always be equalled by the number of pieces defending it, but by virtue of the fact that the pawn needs constant care, White can switch the attack to another section of the board. Black must not only be prepared to fight back there but also keep in close touch with the weak pawn.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Urging his opponent to exchange knights or defend by 9 e3, blocking the path of his dark-squared bishop.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A suggestion White is delighted to fall in with! He relieves Black of the isolated pawn, but in return fixes him with other weaknesses. From now on White will forget about the d5-square and turn his attention to dominating d4 and c5 completely. By anchoring pieces on those squares he can prevent Black from advancing his d-pawn or his c-pawn. The effect of blockading these pawns will be to shut in all of Black’s pieces behind the pawns.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The alternative capture 9... Qxc6 loses the d-pawn at once.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Before pursuing the attack, White conveys his king to safer quarters. The king’s rook meanwhile becomes available for action on the centre files.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Unfortunately, Black may not advance either of the pawns marked for doom: if 10... c5, then 11 Nxd5 wins a pawn, or if 10... d4, then 11 Na4 forces the queen to desert one of the threatened pawns.
There were better chances of resistance with 10.... Be6, protecting the d-pawn once more so as to get in the freeing ...c5 as quickly as possible. Black cannot rely on passive measures or he will be crushed to death.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White is not interested in scaring the queen. The knight does not move to attack but to get a grip on the c5-square so that a white piece may settle itself securely there.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The queen stays in the neighbourhood to help ward off the invaders.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
You would expect this bishop to go to f4, where its range is long and where it does not obstruct the e-pawn’s movements; or you might consider g5 where it cramps Black’s game. These are good and natural moves, but they do not fit in with the strategic concept governing this position. Once there is a definite, logical plan to follow, we must play moves that conform to that plan, so that the improvement of our own position or the undermining of the opponent’s is conducted systematically and not as a result of accidental circumstances. Development, at this point, must not be carried out for its own sake.
It may seem strange that control of one square can cause a position to collapse, but it is true. It is one of the fine points in the Queen’s Gambit that such domination (resulting from Black’s neglect to dispute the centre and also free his queenside by ...c5) enables White to confine his opponent’s pieces to a small area and drive them back step by step, while he (White) either starts escorting a pawn to the queening square or turns to the other side of the board and beleaguers the enemy king.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Not having read the previous note, Black is content to make ‘good’ developing moves.
He should concentrate his energies on advancing the c-pawn one square before it is permanently fixed at c6. Pushing the pawn at once is premature, as after 12... c5 13 Bxd5 Nxd5 14 Qxd5 Qxa4 15 Qxa8 White has won the exchange, but Black could put up more fight with 12... Be6 (protecting the d-pawn and preparing to move the c-pawn) followed by 13... Nd7 and 14... Rc8, all of which is designed to help the c-pawn to advance one square.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White seizes the half-open file, brings more pressure to bear on c5, and prepares to post a piece there.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A double attack on the e2-pawn, which may be embarrassing to meet. How does White answer it?
If 14 Re1, the rook’s development is wretched.
If 14 Nc3, then Q 14...xb2 wins a pawn.
If 14 Rc2, Black snaps up the knight.
If 14 f3, White loosens the pawn position around his king and hems in his own bishop.
In spite of all these arguments in favour of Black’s move, Tarrasch used to dismiss such demonstrations with: “Beginning of an attack...

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
...and end of attack!”
The hemming in of the g2-bishop is only temporary, and as for the weakness of the king-side pawns, it is of no consequence if Black cannot exploit it.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop finds the right square, but it is too late – much too late!

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Now that the strategically important d4- and c5-squares are under his control, White stations a piece where it will immobilize Black’s pawns and restrict the movement of his pieces.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must either protect his bishop or submit to an exchange of pieces. The latter option does not appeal to him, as after 15... Bxc5+, the reply 16 Rxc5 replaces one blockader with another and gains a tempo by the attack on the queen.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A very fine move! After White plays e3, the rook can switch over to c2 to help exploit the c-file. It also vacates f1, so that the bishop can occupy a more useful diagonal.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black attacks the bishop a third time, with the hope of forcing it to retreat.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop does not withdraw, as that lets Black get in the thrust 17... c5, breaking the bind on his position. Nor does White support the bishop by 17 b4, the kind of move many players would make instantly. The consequence would be 17... Bxc5, forcing the pawn to recapture, since 18 Rxc5 costs the exchange, and 18 Nxc5 allows 18... Qxb4. However, after 18 bxc5 the pawn stationed at c5 is not only immobile and useless but itself closes the c-file to White’s pieces. This would negate the whole strategy of the position, which is to occupy the weak squares in the opponent’s position with pieces, not pawns. Pieces can be freely moved about, so that lines are kept open for the attack, and one blockader can make room for a different one, if occasion demands it.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must recapture.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Excellent! The centralization of the queen is tremendously effective. Not only does the queen exert its influence on every part of the board, but it also both prohibits Black from getting in the freeing ...c5 move and prepares the posting of the knight at c5. Notice how, from its new position, the queen still guards the knight and keeps an eye on the b-pawn. The knight is free to move, while the e2-pawn, abandoned by the queen, is now under the rook’s care.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This rook retreats to help defend the c-file against White’s attack, since a move by the a8-rook costs a pawn.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A subtle means of activating the bishop. The alternative 19 f4 is not nearly as good, as it gives Black’s pieces much more room in which to manoeuvre, his bishop and knight then having access to the e4-square.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Reviving the possibility of playing 20... c5. Black must have realized by this time that if he does not get this move in, he might just as well sit back and wait for the axe to fall.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Such a little move, but it accomplishes a great deal! It gains a tempo or two as it uncovers an attack on the queen (forcing Black to lose a move by its retreat), opens up a diagonal for the bishop, and clears a pathway on the second rank, so that the rook can switch from f2 to c2 and increase the pressure along the c-file.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Discretion is the better part of valour, as Beaumont and Fletcher said, anticipating Shakespeare.
The desperate thrust 20... c5 is refuted by 21 Rxc5, when Black dare not take the rook as his queen is still under attack.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Blockade! The knight settles down on c5 and barricades Black’s position.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black removes the knight, not only to get rid of an active blockader but also on the theory that exchanges help relieve a cramped position.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Not so agile as its predecessor, the new blockader enjoys the privilege of immunity to harassment by pawns or the enemy bishop, which is confined to squares of opposite colour to the one the rook occupies.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black cannot counterattack; all he can do is sit tight and await events.
But how does White profit by his opponent’s lack of mobility? How does he overcome passive resistance?

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
First by doubling rooks on the open file, which more than doubles the strength of the rooks.
At present, the rooks seem to be biting on granite, but there are ways and means! Have faith!

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black sticks to noncommittal moves, until his opponent declares himself by a threatening gesture.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This is the point! While the rooks keep a grip on the enemy, the pawn will spearhead an attack on the position.
White’s immediate threat is 25 b5, striking a third time at the immobilized c-pawn.
