metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must not allow the pawn to advance.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Shifting the attack so as to keep Black occupied guarding all the weak points (the new target is a6). Transferring the rook does not relinquish the pressure on the c-pawn, which must remain where it is.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Protecting the valuable b-pawn (which is destined to bring the enemy to his knees) before proceeding with the attack.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black saves the a-pawn, which was under double attack, but loses a different pawn. However, there was no way for Black to safeguard all the vulnerable points. Had he tried 26... Bc8, White would have won a pawn by 27 Qxb6 Rxb6 28 Rxd5, exploiting the pinned c-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This bit of plunder is the first material evidence of the merit of White’s positional strategy. It is no more than justice that the c-pawn, the cause of Black’s troubles, should be the first to fall.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Better than retreating to b7 or exchanging queens: if 27... Qb7, then 28 Raxa6 wins another pawn and leaves White with two connected passed pawns ready to race up the board. Or if 27... Qxd4 28 exd4, then White will gather up the triply attacked a-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The recapture keeps Black on his toes. His rook is attacked and so is the a-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Rescues the pawn, as 29 Rxa6 Rxa7 30 Rxc6 Rxa3 nets Black a pawn in return.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Again taking possession of the c-file and the key square, this time with the queen.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black avoids the exchange of queens, since after 29... Qxc5 30 Rxc5 Kf8 31 Ra5 Black can save the a-pawn only by abandoning the d-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Not only to fortify the kingside but to move the king closer to the centre for the endgame, in the event that the queens are exchanged.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This demonstration does not intimidate White or divert him from his purpose of effecting a decision on the queenside.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White shelters the king from any annoying checks that might ensue once the position is opened up.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black’s pieces are tied down to the defence of the two isolated pawns, so he makes a waiting move with a pawn.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White responds vigorously by attacking the a-pawn with a third piece. The queen’s further infiltration into Black’s territory also clears the c5-square so that the rook can use that as a springboard to get to the seventh rank.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black cannot guard all his pawns (if 32.... Bc8, then 33 Qxd5), so he deserts the a-pawn to try to get at White’s king via the open c-file.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Not through the Iron Duke! It is more important to retain control of the c-file and to keep Black’s pieces off it than to pick up stray pawns.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The queen hasn’t a wide choice of squares to flee from the rook’s attack.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This immobilizes Black’s kingside pawns and also guards against any surprise attack on that wing.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black tries to open a file for his queen by main force.
What else is there? After 34... Kg7 35 Rc7 Qb8 36 Bxa6 Kg8 (or 36... Rxa6 37 Rxf7+ winning the queen) 37 Bb7! Ra7 38 Rc8+ Bxc8 39 Qxb8 White wins easily.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This reduces the queen’s flight squares to the minimum – just one square!
White is now in full control of all the strategically important areas – the c-file, the all-important c5-square, the d-file, the sixth rank and the seventh rank.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only hiding place! The queen is driven further and further back.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A new source of trouble! White has a passed pawn moving up the board.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must give his rook more room.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Threatening to continue with 38 b7 Ra7 39 Rc8+ Bxc8 40 Qxb8, winning everything in sight.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The rook accomplishes nothing here, but there is no real defence.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Renewing the threat of winning the queen by 39 Rc8+.
There is no holding out any longer:
1) 38... Kg7 39 Rxf7+ wins the queen at once by discovered attack.
2) 38... Qe8 39 Qb6 wins the rook in an odd way.
3) 38... Qa7 39 Qd8+ Kg7 40 b8 Q leaves White with an extra queen.
The whole game is a remarkable example of the systematic exploitation of a positional advantage. The manner in which the c5-square is used as a springboard for White’s pieces – the bishop, knight, rook and then the queen occupying it in turn – contributes a bit of sleight of hand to an artistic achievement of the highest sort.

metadata.Opening: Tarrasch Defense: Prague Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This is one of the best moves on the board – and so is 1 e4!
Either move establishes a pawn in the centre, while permitting two pieces to come into play.
Which move should you adopt? The choice is a matter of taste. Broadly speaking, 1 e4 leads more often to wide-open attacking games, while 1 d4 tends toward a struggle for positional advantage. Blackburne says, “The first piece of advice I would offer to the young student who wishes to improve his chess is that in the formation of his style he should try to follow his own aptitude and temperament. One player derives pleasure in working a game out accurately like a sum in mathematics; another cares for nothing but ingenious combinations and brilliant attacks. It is by far the best for each to develop his own qualities.”

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: An excellent reply, as it prevents White from continuing with 2 e4, when the two pawns abreast dominate the centre. Black, too, frees his queen and a bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Instead of this, White often plays 2 c4, offering a pawn. This is a gambit only by the grace of definition, since White recovers the pawn easily while maintaining a strong position.
The knight move has the virtue of developing a piece to its most useful post while retaining the option of transposing into the Queen’s Gambit.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Perfectly safe, but somewhat modest. I would prefer 2... Nf6, which does not commit Black to defensive play and does not interfere with the c8-bishop’s development.
The text-move is the best way to support the d-pawn after White has attacked it by c4, but White has not yet made this threatening gesture!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This thrust at the pawn-centre is practically compulsory for Black in queen’s pawn openings.
Black must fight for an equal share of the centre.
Black must dispute possession of the important squares.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Supporting White’s centre and making ready for Bd3, since it prepares the retreat square c2 in case Black should attack this bishop by ...c4.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Natural and strong. This is the best possible disposition of the king’s knight. It is developed toward the centre, so as to take part in the events there. It is in the centre that most of the fighting takes place, and whatever happens there affects the rest of the chessboard. Superiority in the centre is essential for a positional advantage, and control of the centre is indispensable to the successful conduct of a kingside attack.
All development should therefore be conducted with a view to the effect on the centre.
A plausible move, instead of the text, is the advance 4... c4 to prevent White from placing his bishop at d3. It is the kind of move many players find irresistible, but it must be avoided. It is an error in strategy, as it relaxes the pressure on White’s d-pawn and the centre.
It is important to keep the pawn position in the centre fluid.
It is important to maintain pressure on White’s d-pawn in the centre.
It is important to retain the option of exchanging pawns in the centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: An ideal development for the bishop: it controls the b1-h7 diagonal leading to Black’s king (after he castles) and bears down on the key e4-square, where the break will come.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight comes into play toward the centre, as prescribed. Black has an eye to freeing his game by an early ...e5. A good alternative is 5... Nbd7 in order to recapture with the knight, instead of with the bishop, if White should play 6 dxc5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Offhand this looks unnatural, as the knight seems awkwardly placed and blocks the path of the c1-bishop. In reality the knight performs its two assigned tasks: it gets into the game , even if it is only at the modest d2-square, and it also lends support to the coming action at the critical point e4. The c1-bishop is inconvenienced, but only temporarily.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is preferable to the aggressive development at d6. The bishop is needed closer to home for defence of the king.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This remarkable coup, by means of which the king is spirited away to safety while the rook magically appears on the scene, is probably the most significant contribution to civilization since the invention of the wheel.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black also hurries to safeguard his king and put the king’s rook to work.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A perfect spot for the queen in nearly every form of queen’s pawn opening. The queen supports the contemplated advance of the e-pawn and will add a great deal of weight to the consequent attack.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Rooks must seize open files! What if there are none? Then bring your rooks toward the centre! They will then be at the head of files most likely to be opened. That is why the king’s rook is usually developed at e8 or d8, while the queen’s rook goes to d8 or c8.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must recapture or be a pawn down.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The key move in the Colle Attack! It is the forcible break which releases all the fury of the pent-up pieces.
How should Black reply? If he exchanges by 10...dxe4, then after 11 Nxe4 Nxe4 12 Qxe4, he is threatened with the devastating 13 Qxh7+. No longer does he have a knight at f6 (the best defender of a castled position) so he would have to weaken himself by moving one of the pawns in front of the king.
If he avoids exchanging pawns and plays 10... d4 instead, then comes 11 Nb3 Bb6 (the bishop must stay in touch with the d-pawn) 12 e5 Nd5, and White should win “accurately like a sum in mathematics”, as Blackburne puts it, by 13 cxd4. The attempt to win through “ingenious combination and brilliant attack” by 13 Bxh7+ Kxh7 14 Ng5+ succeeds after 14... Kg6 15 Qe4+ f5 16 exf6+ Kxf6 17 Qf3+ Ke7 (if 17... Ke5, then 18 Nf7#) 18 Qf7+ Kd6 19 Ne4+ Ke5 20 Qh5+ g5 (20... Kxe4 21 Nd2+ Kd3 22 Qg6+ Ke2 23 Qg4+ Kd3 24 Qe4#) 21 Bxg5, leading to mate in a few moves. However, 14... Kg8 15 Qh5 Nxe5 is a dash of cold water, after which White would be hard-pressed to justify his sacrifice.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black avoids both pitfalls and plays to prevent 11 e5, which would dislodge the knight. Meanwhile, the rook has more elbow-room, and the c8-bishop can now take part in the action.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Work in progress! White continues the process of opening lines for the attack. The e4-square is now available as a jumping-off spot for his pieces.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black did not care to capture with his queen, as after 11... Qxd5 12 Bc4 these lines are possible:
1) 12... Qd6 13 Ng5 (threatening 14 Bxf7+, winning the exchange) 13... Re7 14 Nde4 Nxe4 15 Nxe4, and White wins the bishop.
2) 12... Qd7 13 Ng5 Re7 14 Nde4 Nxe4 15 Qxe4 (threatening the h-pawn) 15... g6 16 Qh4 h5 17 Ne4, and Black must give up his bishop to avert loss of his queen by a knight fork.
3) 12... Qd8 13 Nb3 Bb6, and White will have a happy time weighing the effects of various attacks beginning with 14 Bg5, 14 Rd1 or 14 Ng5 .

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Gaining a tempo by the attack on the exposed bishop. Note too that White’s c1-bishop now has lots of room.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A move with deceptive aspects. It is true that the queen has made a developing move and that the bishop is now protected, but other factors appear in the reckoning. Black’s kingside lacks pieces for defence, and his knight at d5 is loose (unguarded by another piece or a pawn).
Is there a combination? Is there a check or capture – a move that does some damage? Yes, indeed there is!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Such opportunities must be seized at once, before the opponent has a chance to catch his breath.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Refusing to capture is even worse: the bishop can run away with his booty or stay put while the attack continues with 14 Qc4, and the queen pounces on the stranded pieces in the centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The point! By means of a double attack White regains his piece, with an extra pawn as interest on his investment.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: There is nothing to be gained by interposing a pawn by 14... f5 or 14... g6, either of which moves further disrupts the kingside pawn position.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White wins the piece back and gains another tempo by the double attack on the bishop. Black is kept busy defending and is given no time to consolidate his position. Without having made any moves that were obviously bad, Black has a theoretically lost game.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Abject retreat, but the alternative 15... Be7 lets White take the poorly defended e-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Threatening 17 Qxf7+, and mate in two more moves. Black must be given no respite!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The queen retreats, but no time is lost as mate is threatened at h7.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black has little choice, and this is a better defence than 17... f5, after which 18 Qh4 Bd6 (or 18... Bc5 19 Nxe6 Rxe6 20 Qc4 winning a piece) 19 Qh7+ Kf8 20 Qg6 Nd8 (if the e6-bishop moves, then its colleague on d6 falls) 21 Nh7+ Ke7 22 Qxg7+ leads to a catastrophe.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Again threatening mate on the move. Black is kept on the run and has to place his pieces where White’s mating threats compel them to go.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White cannot be kept from checking at h7, but this prevents the queen’s further inroad at h8. Failure to keep the queen out, for instance by 18... Bd6 instead, would lose after 19 Qh7+ Kf8 20 Nxe6+ Rxe6 (if 20...fxe6, then 21 Bh6#) 21 Qh8+, and White wins a rook.
With the actual move, Black seems to have built a bomb-proof shelter for his king.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: So White brings up the reserves! The dark-squared bishop comes into active play with gain of tempo. The attack on the queen is incidental to the bishop’s real purpose, which is to gain control of c5 for itself or the knight. A knight planted there would dominate the centre and the queenside; a bishop would be useful to prevent Black’s king escaping by way of f8.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black rejects 19... Qc7 as he visualizes the continuation 20 Qh7+ Kf8 21 Bc5+ Ne7 22 Qxg6! fxg6 (or 22... Qxc5 23 Nxe6+ fxe6 24 Qxe8+ Kxe8 25 Nxc5 winning easily) 23 Nxe6+ Kg8 24 Nxc7, when Black’s rooks are impaled on a knight fork.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Once more one of White’s pieces invades the enemy’s half of the board by the timesaving expedient of attacking the queen.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Hoping to get some peace by effecting an exchange of queens.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With the object of smoking the king out and ripping away his pawn protection.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only move left.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: There is often more than one way to win, once a positional superiority has been established. A pretty finish would be 22 Ngxe6+ fxe6 23 Bh6 Re7 (or 23... Bxh6 24 Nd7#) 24 Qh8+ (if only to show that the queen can get to h8) 24... Kf7 25 Qxg7+ Ke8 26 Qg8#.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Threatening 24 Qf7#.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: I was hoping for 23... Re7, when I could have forced the win by the ‘excelsior’ idea, a pawn march up the board, as follows: 24 f4 (threatening 25 fxe5+ Kg8 26 Qh7#) 24... e4 25 f5 (again threatening to deliver discovered check) 25... e5 26 f6 and White wins.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Here I was sorely tempted to go in for the flashy win by 24 f4 e4 25 f5 e5 26 f6 Bh8 27 Nh7#, but common sense prevailed. One must win in the quickest possible way and play the simple, brutal move if thereby it shortens the struggle.
If 24... Kg8, then 25 Nf6+ Kh8 (or 25... Kf8 26 Qxe8#) 26 Qh7#, or if 24... Ke7, then 25 Rad1, and mate follows after 26 Bg5+ or 26 Qxg7+.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Traditional Colle
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Whether for fun, honour or blood, this is one of the best ways to begin the fight. Outlets are created for the queen and a bishop, while the d-pawn itself takes an active part in the struggle for control of the centre. It occupies d4 and stands guard over e5 and c5, making those squares unavailable for the opponent’s pieces.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The simplest way to stop White gaining more ground in the centre. If White is permitted to play 2 e4 freely, the two pawns abreast in the centre will give him the balance of power in that important area.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White offers a pawn in order to eliminate Black’s strong point in the centre. It is necessary to play this move before developing the b1-knight at c3, as the c-file must not be obstructed.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black is set to reply to 3 cxd5 with 3...exd5, maintaining a pawn at d5. If he were to recapture with a piece, White could attack it, drive it off and create a strong pawn-centre by playing e4.
Accepting White’s pawn offer by 2...dxc4 is not recommended policy. Black could not hold on to the extra pawn, so that in the end it would amount to exchanging a centre pawn for a side pawn. It is true that the text-move limits the c8-bishop’s scope, but it is a necessary evil of what is probably Black’s soundest defence. In this lies the great strength of the Queen’s Gambit (for White) and its popularity with the majority of players who feel happy with an opening which lets them exert pressure from the very first move.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight develops aggressively, moving in toward the centre and intensifying the attack on Black’s d-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: An excellent move: it brings the g8-knight to its most suitable square in the opening, exerts pressure on d5 and e4 (to neutralize the influence of White’s knight on those squares), helps defend the central d5-pawn and facilitates early kingside castling.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This powerful move develops a piece, pins one of Black’s and threatens by 5 Bxf6 gxf6 (if 5... Qxf6, then 6 cxd5 exd5 7 Nxd5 and White wins a pawn) to dislocate Black’s pawn position on the kingside.
Strangely enough, although Pillsbury used this move to great effect in a magnificent victory over Tarrasch at Hastings in 1895, the comment on it by Gunsberg, who annotated the game for the tournament book, was, “No good results from this early sortie of the bishop. The attack, or perhaps better speaking, would-be attack differs from similar play in the French Defence, inasmuch as White has not the move e5 at his command. Generally speaking, both the first and the second player in this opening require their queen’s bishop on the queenside.”
This view, it turned out, easily qualified for ‘the clouded crystal ball department’. Pillsbury utilized the attack stemming from 4 Bg5 for some of his most marvellous triumphs, defeating such masters of the game as Steinitz, Maroczy, Janowsky, Burn, Marco and Tarrasch. Others who evaded this line, such as Lasker, Marshall and Chigorin (to name a few) fell victims to other forms of the Queen’s Gambit. Gunsberg, who criticized this form of attack so severely, chose what Lasker called “a peculiar, but not altogether sound, manner of development”, with the result that Pillsbury defeated him in an ending which is one of the most beautiful in the literature of chess. In short, it was Pillsbury’s great success with the Queen’s Gambit that revealed its terrific strength to the other masters and gave it a popularity that has continued to this day.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The simplest: Black develops the bishop where it is best placed for defence – close to home. Incidentally, he neutralizes the pin of the knight.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Pawns should be moved sparingly in the opening, but moves which help pieces come into play are developing moves. In playing 5 e3, White develops because he creates an outlet for his f1-bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king finds safer quarters while the rook prepares to make itself useful.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With the development of this piece, White’s knights now exert pressure on all the four squares in the centre. Moreover, the f3-knight has an eye to utilizing e5 as an outpost. Once firmly stationed there, it will get a death grip on Black’s position.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
It is natural to develop the bishop at b7, especially as it is hemmed in on the other side, and indeed this is one of Black’s soundest plans – however, it would have been more accurate to precede it by 6... h6, so as to remove the h-pawn from the vulnerable h7-square with gain of tempo.
An alternative continuation was 6... Nbd7 to support a thrust at White’s centre by ...c5 or ...e5. The knight move would also curb White’s ambition to anchor his f3-knight at e5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: An ideal spot for the bishop: it commands an important diagonal and aims at Black’s h-pawn. This pawn is in no immediate danger, but it does stand in the line of fire.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black expects to control the long diagonal with his bishop by means of this fianchetto. However, Pillsbury’s next move puts Black in a dilemma.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White removes a pawn and lets Black recapture in any of four ways – none of them satisfactory!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black wants to maintain a pawn in the centre, but this pawn blocks the path of his b7-bishop and prevents it from accomplishing anything useful on the diagonal.
Black could have captured with a piece instead, but that amounts to an eventual surrender of the centre. White would evict the piece by e4 and remain in control of all the strategically important central squares.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is the key move in the famous ‘Pillsbury Attack’. The knight anchors itself on a square from which its striking power is terrific! Its attack extends in all directions, affecting the queenside as well as the kingside.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This knight does what it can: it develops, it threatens to do battle with White’s knight, and it stands ready to support a break by 10... c5, disputing control of the centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This pawn not only strengthens the position of the knight by providing it with a firm base, but it discourages Black from exchanging pieces. On 10... Nxe5, the recapture by 11 fxe5 opens wide the f-file for an attack by the heavy pieces. The capturing pawn itself will then stab at Black’s f6-knight and drive it away from its strong defensive post.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This demonstration on the queenside is either too soon or too late. Black wants to attack on the queenside where, after playing 11... c4, he will have a three to two pawn majority. What he underestimates is the speed and vigour with which White can get an attack rolling on the kingside. It will strike faster and with more force than any action of Black’s on the queenside. Black must deprive White’s attack of some of its strength by effecting some exchanges and then counterattacking in the centre. One possibility was 10... Ne8 11 Bxe7 Qxe7 12 0-0 Nxe5 13 fxe5 f6. This would comply with two important principles in defence:
An exchange relieves a crowded position.
An attack on a wing is best met by play in the centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A defensive measure (the king should be sheltered) but primarily to put the rook immediately to work on the partly open f-file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
With the idea of securing a queenside pawn majority. This is commendable strategy for the ending, but Black has not yet survived the middlegame!
The move 11... c4 is a strategic error. It removes the pressure on White’s d-pawn and relieves the tension. As long as Black has the option of capturing the d-pawn and disturbing White’s centre, it is difficult for White to stabilize the centre. And until the centre is stabilized, the success of a kingside attack for White is doubtful.
The moral is clear: keep the pawn position in the centre fluid; reserve the option of capturing the central pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop retreats but does not relax its grip on the diagonal leading to Black’s kingside.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Preparing a sweeping advance of queenside pawns, beginning with 13... b5 and 14... b4.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White brings up the heavy artillery. White’s object with the queen move is to start a direct attack on the king, and he gains time because he forces Black to deal with the threat to win a pawn by 14 Nxc4 dxc4 15 Qxb7. To defend himself against White’s threats, Black will be forced to move some pawn near his king. This change in the pawn formation will loosen the structure and create an irreparable weakness in the king’s defences.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Marco protects the c-pawn and proceeds with his counterattack on the queenside. Note how Black’s last three moves, filling up light squares with pawns, further reduce what little mobility his light-squared bishop has.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Threatening 15 Nxd7 Qxd7 (certainly not 15... Nxd7 16 Qxh7#), after which White has a choice of three winning continuations:
1) 16 Qxd7 Nxd7 17 Bxe7, and White gains a piece.
2) 16 Bxh7+ Kh8 (if 16... Nxh7, then 17 Qxd7 wins) 17 Bf5+, and White wins the queen.
3) 16 Bf5 Qd8 17 Bxf6 Bxf6 18 Qxh7#.
“All this is very interesting,” you might say, “but how does White plan this series of moves? What makes him look at even so much as the first move in the combination?”
Very well! Let’s try to follow his line of reasoning:
White attacks the critical point, Black’s h7-pawn, with queen and bishop.
If this pawn were protected only by the king, White could capture it and announce mate.
But the pawn has another protector, a knight.
How about removing the knight?
That would not do. It would only be replaced by another knight.
How about getting rid of the other knight? With that knight disposed of, wouldn’t the whole structure collapse?
Once White thinks in this direction and sees the first move in the combination, the rest of it plays itself. In fact, once he finds the key – removing the knight which protects the knight which protects against mate – he can win any way he pleases.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black avoids being mated by making a simple pawn move. What then has White accomplished, if his mating combination can so easily be frustrated?
It is true that White has not inflicted mate, but the threat of doing so has enabled him to achieve his real objective – a disturbance in the line-up of pawns near Black’s king. This change in the pawn configuration weakens the entire defensive structure. After Black’s actual move, his f6-knight, deprived of its pawn support, is a vulnerable object of attack, notwithstanding the fact that it is protected by three pieces.
What other defence did Black have? If 14... h6, then 15 Bxh6 gxh6 16 Qxh6 Ne4 17 Rf3 (threatening 18 Rg3+ Nxg3 19 Qh7#) 17... Ndf6 18 Rh3, is winning for White. Or if 14... Nxe5 (to avoid moving the kingside pawns), then 15 dxe5 Ne4 16 Bxe4 dxe4 17 Rad1 Qe8 18 Bxe7 Qxe7 19 Rd7 and the b7-bishop perishes.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A pawn is a wonderful weapon of attack! This one threatens to break up Black’s pawn cordon by 16 fxg6. The capture will also uncover an attack on Black’s f6-knight by the rook, an attack which could be augmented by doubling rooks.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Clearly 15...gxf5 is out of the question. White could recapture with the bishop with a tremendous game.
Black hopes, with his threat on the c3-knight, to divert White’s attention from the course of events on the kingside. If he can persuade White to delay the attack for even a moment, he might put up a fight. If, for example, White prudently retreats the knight to e2, then 16... Ne4 complicates White’s task.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Ripping right into Black’s position! The rook’s attacking range is lengthened – he has the whole f-file to work on – while the bishop’s attack leads straight to the enemy king!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Let’s dispose of the alternatives:
1) 16...bxc3 17 Bxf6 Nxf6 18 Rxf6 fxg6 (or 18... Bxf6 19 Qxh7#) 19 Bxg6 hxg6 20 Rxg6#.
2) 16...fxg6 17 Qe6+ Kh8 18 Nxd7 Nxd7 (or 18... Qxd7 19 Bxf6+ followed by 20 Qxd7) 19 Rxf8+ Nxf8 20 Qe5+ Kg8 21 Bxe7, and White wins.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Concentrating his fire on the f6-knight, whose position has been weakened by the loss of his pawn support.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black might as well take the knight. The alternative 17... Nxe5 loses to 18 dxe5 bxc3 19 exf6 Bd6 20 Qh6.
Before White makes his next move, let us look at the object of his attack, the knight at f6. Although it has lost the protection of the g7-pawn, which has had to move to g6, it is still immune from capture, since it has a defender for every piece that attacks it. In fact, if White tries something like 18 Bxf6 Bxf6 19 Rxf6 Qxf6 20 Qxf6 Nxf6, he finds himself a rook down. So direct assault doesn’t do it! The answer must then lie in indirect means. We have lured away one of the knight’s defenders, the pawn. Can we get rid of its other protectors? Indeed we can!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This removes one of the props supporting the knight.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
And this recapture draws another one away! Notice the technique of besieging a heavily guarded objective by doing away with the pieces that protect it. In this case, two of the knight’s defenders have disappeared – one removed bodily, and the other lured away by the compulsion to recapture.
Black had no better defence in 18... Nxd7 as 19 Bxe7 Qa5 20 b4 (faster than 20 Bxf8) 20...cxb3 21 axb3 Qb6 22 Rf3, followed by 23 Rh3, forces a quick mate.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Stronger than 19 Bxf6 as Black dare not take the rook.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
If 19... Bxf6, then 20 Bxf6 threatening 21 Qh8# is conclusive.
Black’s actual move prepares 20... Ra6, to help defend the vulnerable g-pawn and perhaps to beat off White’s rook.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Doubling the rooks institutes two new winning threats: 21 Bxg6 fxg6 22 Rxg6# and 21 R1f3, followed by 22 Rh3 and 23 Qh8#.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Logic and poetic justice dictate that this pawn be destroyed!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White was threatening mate on the move.
Pillsbury now showed a forced mate in seven moves by 22 Rxf8+ Bxf8 23 Rxf8+ Kxf8 24 Qh8+ Kf7 25 Qh7+ Kf8 (25... Ke8 26 Qg8# or 25... Ke6 26 Qxg6#) 26 Qxd7 followed by 27 Bh6+ Kg8 28 Qg7#.
More than any other, this game made the chess world aware of the terrific potential of the Queen’s Gambit, a positional opening, as an instrument of attack. The assault on the kingside is carried out with speed and power, and unlike attacks stemming from speculative king’s pawn gambits, it is founded on a position sound to the core.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White announced a forced mate.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: 1-0 White wins by checkmate.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Pillsbury Attack
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The queen’s pawn opening, to paraphrase George Bernard Shaw, “offers the maximum of security with the maximum of opportunity.”
With the first move, White occupies the centre with a pawn and frees two of the queenside pieces.
His general plan of development runs somewhat as follows:
He will establish and maintain at least one pawn in the centre.
This pawn will act as a support to a knight outpost at e5 or c5.
The bishops are to take charge of key diagonals or pin enemy pieces.
The rooks are to control the open or partly open files.
The queen should stand at c2 or e2, close to home but off the back rank.
The king should find safety in castling, preferably on the kingside.
Basically, White’s aim is to gain space and crowd Black to the wall. With less room to move around in, and with the consequent difficulty of manoeuvring his pieces effectively, Black will be forced to weaken his position. He will have to make some poor moves, because good moves are not easily available in a cramped position. The weaknesses will come to light, and the opportunity to exploit them will come in the form of a combination, resolving the issue at one stroke.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is a more forthright move than 1... Nf6. Either of these moves prevents White from playing 2 e4 and establishing two pawns in the centre. The text-move offsets White’s pressure in the centre and creates a state of equilibrium there.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A strangely passive move in an opening where every single moment counts.
Usually, White strikes at Black’s d-pawn by 2 c4 to weaken his grip on the centre. Or, if White does not want to show his hand too soon, he simply develops a piece by 2 Nf3.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: So Black takes the initiative and plays this all-important freeing move. It opens the c-file for the use of the rooks and gives the b8-knight more scope by letting it come out at c6. The c-pawn itself puts up a fight for possession of the centre by its attack on White’s d-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Indicating that he intends to reply to 3...cxd4 with 4 cxd4. This would keep his pawn position in the centre intact and open the c-file for his major pieces.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must protect the c-pawn. Otherwise White might play 4 dxc5, and then hang on to the extra pawn by supporting it with 5 b4.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop develops to a useful diagonal, where it exerts pressure on the centre and is ready to participate in a kingside attack.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A rare opportunity for this knight, who seldom gets good breaks in queen’s pawn openings. From its post at c6 the knight brings considerable influence to bear on e5 and d4 and, as it later turns out, on another important sector.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White has made four out of five moves with pawns in order to secure a particular arrangement known as the Stonewall Attack. Aside from the fact that making so many pawn moves in the opening is a flagrant violation of principle, the adoption of a system which calls for the launching of an attack by a preconceived formation of pieces, without regard to the advisability of an attack and without reference to the requirements of the particular position, is contrary to the concept of proper strategy and to the spirit of chess itself. What such an expedition amounts to is undertaking the risk of assuming the offensive against an enemy whose force is equal, whose line-up of power is unknown and who has betrayed no vulnerable points. Under these conditions, an attack is premature and is sure to be repulsed and turned into a disorderly retreat. If any such system worked, it would be fine for White, who would always win, but then who would want to play Black?

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: An excellent development while awaiting developments! Both Black’s knights are poised beautifully, with one watching over e5 and d4, while the other keeps the two remaining central squares under observation.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This knight has the unhappy choice of making its entrance at this square or at a3. At d2, it blocks the bishop and itself has no bright prospects in view. At a3 it is only half a knight, since it reaches at most in four directions instead of eight.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Very good, since the heavy pieces (the queen and the rooks) fulfil their functions best when placed on open files, or files likely to be opened.
The queen develops with gain of tempo since a positional threat is involved – which White either overlooks, or disregards.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Routine and in this case thoughtless development. White is so intent on carrying out the basic theme of the Stonewall attack (posting of a knight at e5, stoutly supported by pawns) that he fails to stop at every move to ask himself, “What does my opponent threaten with his last move? Has he any checks or captures that cut down my choice of reply?”

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black wrenches the c-file open at one blow!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The point of Black’s move is revealed in this forced recapture. White could not take by 8 exd4 (hoping to maintain strong pawn support for the prospective stationing of a knight at e5) as that permits the brutal reply 8... Qxf4 winning a pawn for Black. The alternative, 8 Nxd4, conflicts with the system White had determined to follow before lines of battle were drawn up. In that scheme of things, the knight belongs at e5, not d4, while the d4-square should be occupied by a pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A disturbing attack on the bishop! Without the services of this piece. White can never hope to work up an effective kingside attack.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
An unusual square of retreat, but the only one available if the bishop wants to stay on the diagonal leading to Black’s kingside.
White is not too troubled by this setback. He expects to drive the enemy knight off with 10 a3 and then reorganize his troops.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A quiet move, but a subtle one. The bishop will make its presence felt, even from this modest start.
Black is now prepared to shift his rook over to c8 to strengthen his grip on the c-file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Before going about his business, White must dislodge the annoying knight, which disconcerts his entire queenside.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This counterattack must have come as a surprise to White.
What shall he do against the threat of 11... Qxc1? If he plays 11 axb4, there comes 11... Qxc1 12 Rxa7 (certainly not 12 Qxc1 Rxc1+, and Black wins a rook) 12... Qxb2 (threatening 13... Rc1, pinning the queen) 13 0-0 Qxb4, and Black is a pawn ahead – and a passed pawn at that.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Now the bishop is guarded by queen and rook, and so safe from capture. The king meanwhile goes into hiding.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop seizesa fine diagonal with gain of time, as White must move his rook out of range.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Clearly forced, since 12 Rf2 loses on the spot to 12... Qxc1, while 12 axb4 Bxf1 (threatening to continue with 13... Qxc1) costs the exchange.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: An attack on both rooks which leaves White no choice of reply. He must remove this terrible knight.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: After the alternative capture 13 Qxc2 , Black plays 13... Qxc2 14 Bxc2 Rxc2 and has a rook on the seventh rank, as in the actual game.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black penetrates into the vitals of the enemy’s position – the seventh rank.
White is almost paralysed:
His e1-rook and queen are prevented from moving by Black’s b5-bishop.
His bishop cannot move at all.
One knight must stay at d2 to prevent 14... Ne4.
The a1-rook can move – but to no avail.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: So he exchanges his helpless queen for Black’s active one.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The upshot of Black’s positional combination is that it has given him full control of the open file and a grip on the seventh rank with his rook. The position of the rook at c2 has a terribly constricting effect on White’s game. It is especially troublesome as the rook is not easily driven off, while White’s pieces are still in each other’s way.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop develops to a useful diagonal.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s idea is to rearrange his forces so as to get some freedom of movement. He plans the continuation 17 Nc3 Ba6 18 Rd1, followed by 19 Rd2, to get rid of Black’s annoying rook. By this means, his bishop might eventually see some action.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight immediately pounces on this excellent outpost! Not only does this throttle any freeing advance of the e3-pawn, but it also sweeps aside White’s plan of reorganization. If White tries 17 Nc3, then 17... Nxc3 18 bxc3 Rxc3 wins a pawn for Black.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White therefore tries to exchange or otherwise dispose of Black’s powerfully placed knight. After that, he might arrive at some reasonable development.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black falls in with this offer, with the stipulation that if knights are to be exchanged, he wants another piece occupying the outpost e4.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White has no option but to clear the board of as many pieces as he can, otherwise he will never be able to extricate his forces from their tangled position. The move 18 Nc3, which earlier would have lost a pawn, is even worse now because after 18... Nxd2 19 Bxd2 Rxd2 Black wins a piece.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black recaptures with the threat of 19... Rxg2+, so White has no time to play 19 Nc3.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White saves the g-pawn by blocking the rook, but he cuts off his own bishop as well – and White’s back to the previous entanglement.
Unfortunately, nothing else is promising. If 19 Bd2, then 19... Rxb2 20 Rc1 (getting an open file for the pawn and threatening 21 Rc8+) 20... Kd7, and White will be driven off the file by the threat of 21... Bxb1 winning more material, or 21... Rc8 opposing rooks on the file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Much more energetic than castling. Mating threats are not likely with so few pieces on the board, hence the king comes out into the open. The king’s power increases with every reduction of force, and, as befits a fighting piece, the king heads for the centre to assist in the attack. Meanwhile, a new avenue has been opened for the benefit of the h8-rook.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s only hope is to keep clearing the board.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
After this recapture, a survey shows the inferiority of White’s position:
The bishop is undeveloped, preventing communication between the rooks.
The pawn cluster in the centre is completely immobilized.
All the pieces are still on the first rank.
Aside from the features of this particular position, it is important to appreciate the peculiar strength with which a rook is imbued when it dominates (as Black’s does) the seventh rank:
It attacks the pawns still remaining on the rank, striking all along the line, so that defending them is difficult.
The rook can get behind pawns that have moved off the rank and maintain constant pressure, since the pawns are always under attack by the rook, no matter how far up the file they move.
The rook restrains the enemy king from coming out to take a hand in the ending, by guarding the line of exit.
The moral is:
In the opening, shift the rooks toward the centre, on files likely to be opened.
In the middlegame, seize the open files and command them with your rooks.
In the ending, post your rooks on the seventh rank. Doubled rooks on the seventh rank are almost irresistible in mating attacks. If there is little material left on the board, the seventh rank is a convenient means of manoeuvring a rook behind enemy pawns.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Preparing to play 22 b4 followed by 23 Bb2, to let the bishop finally see daylight.
It is useless to attempt to dislodge Black’s rook, for example after 21 Kf1 Rhc8 22 Re2 Rxc1+ Black wins a piece.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The doubling of rooks on an open file more than doubles their strength on that file.
Their power is manifest here, where they reduce White’s resistance to the feeble hope of developing his bishop. White’s rooks may not leave the first rank unless the bishop does so first.

Passed pawns must be pushed! This clinches the win, as White cannot stop the pawn without letting Black’s king come in among his deserted pawns.
The continuation might be 37 g4 b4 38 h4 b3+ 39 Kd2 b2 40 Kc2 b1 Q + 41 Kxb1 Kd3 42 Kc1 Kxe3 43 Kd1 Kf2, and the new passed pawn moves up the board to become a queen.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The popular impression of king’s pawn openings is that they offer all sorts of opportunities for whipping up a quick attack. A variety of gambits can be played, pieces may be sacrificed to open lines, combinations ventured on, and speculation indulged in – anything for the sake of mate. Sometimes these tactics succeed, but very often the gambit player finds himself at the wrong end of the attack, as wide-open positions are as dangerous for one side as for the other.
In queen’s pawn openings, the ideal to strive for is development for its own sake. The attack is not the ‘be-all and end-all’. It is not deliberately played for, but, strangely enough, the very fact that all the pieces are developed economically, that they are put to work as quickly as possible on the squares where they function best, seems to imbue them with marvellous powers of attack. Combinations come into life out of nothing! Can it be that the simple posting of pieces where they have the greatest freedom of movement and the greatest command of the board generates in them so much dynamic energy that it must be released somehow? And can it be that knowledge of this fact is what makes the virtuosi of positional play repress their instinct to attack until the time is ripe for an attack to be unleashed?
White’s move of the d-pawn begins the process of getting all the pieces into play as quickly as possible. Two of them are now free to make their debut, while the pawn that released them occupies the centre of the stage.

annotation: White’s motive is evident: he develops the b1-knight first, to support an advance of the e-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: To this, Black counters by clamping a pin on the knight. If White were to play 4 e4, then 4... Nxe4 would leave him helpless to recapture.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
With a twofold purpose: to meet 4... Bxc3+ with 5 Qxc3, keeping White’s pawn structure intact, and to threaten again the advance 5 e4.
There is a prevalent concept that in the opening there is a ‘best move’ at every point. The belief is that the chess master memorizes every one of these best moves and its proper reply. That such reasoning is specious is obvious: the very fact that millions of games have been played without duplication of moves is proof enough in itself.
Let us consider the position on the board. Besides the text-move (4 Qc2), there are at least seven excellent alternatives, each of which has enthusiastic advocates. They are: 4 Qb3; 4 Bd2; 4 a3; 4 Bg5; 4 e3; 4 g3; and 4 Nf3. Which of these is best? No one can say for sure, but the move that leads into positions congenial to your style is the best move, and the one you should play.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black too can conduct the defence (or the counterattack) in the manner that suits his style and temperament. The move he plays immediately disputes White’s control of the centre. It does other things, too: it gives the queen more scope, opens the c-file, protects the bishop, etc.
However, there are other moves, equally effective, at Black’s disposal. He can select from these replies, each of which has something to recommend it: 4... Nc6; 4... d6; 4... d5; 4...0-0; and 4... b6. There is something for every taste.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Strongest for various reasons:
White does not lose time in taking the pawn, as Black in recapturing will return the lost tempo. The open d-file resulting from 5 dxc5 will benefit White, who will occupy d 1 with a rook and exert pressure along the length of it, especially endangering the backward d-pawn.
Other continuations are less energetic. For instance, after 5 e3, Black frees himself by 5... d5, while after 5 Nf3 cxd4 6 Nxd4 Nc6 White has lost the initiative.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black develops another piece before recapturing the pawn.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Somewhere about this stage, the amateur wants things to happen. He begins to look around for surprise moves. “There must be a brilliancy in the position!” The great master, in the same situation, is content to make simple moves. He knows that if he keeps on bringing pieces into play, there will be no need to look for winning combinations. They will evolve naturally out of the position and spring up all over the place!

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Further delay in recovering the pawn might be dangerous.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The aggressive 7 Bg5 is more usual, to pin the knight and keep Black under pressure, but no fault can be found with this method of development. It looks mild, but the bishop surveys an important diagonal and bears down on d6, a tender spot in Black’s position.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Vigorously challenging White’s possession of the centre.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Another quiet move which liberates one bishop and strengthens the position of the other.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black spies a chance to start an attack which will result in saddling White with an isolated c-pawn – a slight positional weakness, so he begins an action against the knight, but “such artificial manoeuvres,” says Tartakower, “can hardly succeed against a Capablanca.”
Black should instead do something to get his c8-bishop into play, for example 8... a6 9 Be2 dxc4 10 Bxc4 b5 11 Be2 Qb6 (not at once 11... Bb7 on account of 12 Nxb5) 12 0-0 Bb7.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
In contrast to White’s classically simple method of development, Black moves the same bishop a third time in the opening, in order to inflict his opponent with an isolated pawn. Such an attempt is premature in view of Black’s incomplete development.
Instead, a plausible continuation is 9...0-0 10 0-0 dxc4 11 Bxc4 Bd7, when Black has a fair game.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king is made secure, while the h 1-rook moves closer to the centre, the theatre of action. The rook, of course, will try to seize an open file, or, if none is available, one which is likely to be opened.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop has moved four times to make this exchange for a knight that has moved only once! So much shifting around of one piece indicates that the strategy behind it must be faulty.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
One of Black’s difficulties is resolved with his king’s escape to safer quarters.
Developing the bishop instead was somewhat risky, since after 11... Bd7 12 Rab1 (attacking the b7-pawn) 12... b6 13 Bd6 White stops kingside castling and threatens 14 Rb5 Qa6 15 cxd5 exd5 16 Rxd5, and the discovered attack on the queen wins a pawn for White.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Another of those subtle moves, whose purpose the average player usually fails to see. “What use is it,” he says, “to waste a rook move in attacking a pawn that is adequately protected?”
True, the pawn is defended, but by a bishop which cannot develop without abandoning the pawn. Sooner or later, Black will be compelled to play ...b6, or have three pieces on his first rank interfering with each other. There are drawbacks to ...b6, though, for example Black’s queen will be cut off and prevented from returning to the kingside and the defence of the king. In addition, his c6-knight’s position will be insecure, once the prop (the b7-pawn) is removed from under it.
White’s move is simple and quiet, but it exerts uncomfortable pressure on Black’s queenside, makes normal development difficult, and creates permanent weaknesses which lend themselves to exploitation.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black wants to develop his bishop, and for that purpose he must play ...b6, but to do so at once might endanger the queen by cutting off her line of retreat. For instance, 12... b6 13 Bd6 Rd8 14 Rb5 Qa6 15 cxd5 Rxd6 (15...exd5 permits 16 Rxd5 discovering an attack on the queen) 16 dxc6 Rxc6 17 Nd4 Rc7 18 Re5 wins material, as 18... Qb7 loses after 19 Bf3 Nd5 20 Bxd5 leading to a surprising back-rank mate following 20...exd5 21 Re8#.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With the posting of this rook on the partly open d-file, White’s development has been completed in an ideal way, every piece taking its best post in no more than one move. White has not so much as hinted at an attacking combination until every piece has been put to work.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
To enable the bishop to come out, but the advance of the pawn takes away the c6-knight’s support and weakens its position.
Guarding the b-pawn by 13... Qe7 instead does not help much, since the bishop cannot develop at d7 next move without cutting off the queen’s protection of the pawn. Nor can Black try to simplify by 13...dxc4 as the reply 14 Bd6 wins the exchange.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The attack begins! The first blow destroys Black’s pawn-centre.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The recapture with the pawn, 14...exd5, is bad in view of 15 c4!. Black could not then escape by 15...dxc4 since 16 Bd6 attacks queen and rook, while protecting the pawn by 15.. Be6 yields to 16 cxd5 Bxd5 17 Rxd5 Nxd5 18 Qxc6, and White has won two pieces for a rook.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A master stroke! The brutal threat of 16 Qxh7# disguises the two real purposes of the move: the strategic concept of forcing Black to move one of his kingside pawns, thereby loosening the defensive structure; and the clearance of the f6-square for the benefit of the dark-squared bishop, who will bear down heavily on the long diagonal.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black had two alternatives:
1) 15... Nf6 avoids moving one of the pawns, but 16 Bd6 wins the exchange.
2) 15... g6 leaves Black’s position riddled with weaknesses on the dark squares.
Therefore, Black moves the f-pawn, staving off the mate, but it weakens his e-pawn and ties the bishop down to its defence.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This arrangement of bishops gives them tremendous raking power along the two parallel diagonals.
White’s chief threat is 17 Rxd5 exd5 18 Bxd5+ Kh8 19 Bxc6 followed by 20 Bxa8, sweeping away a good part of Black’s army.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The queen rushes to the aid of the vulnerable knights. This is what happens on other defences:
1) 16... Nde7 17 Bd6 Qa5 18 Bxe7 Nxe7 19 Bxa8, and White wins a whole rook.
2) 16... Nce7 17 c4 Nb4 18 Rxb4 Qxb4 19 Bxa8, and White wins a piece.
3) 16... Nxf4 17 Bxc6 Rb8 18 exf4, and White has won a piece.
4) 16... Qxc3 17 Qxc3 Nxc3 18 Bxc6 Nxd1 19 Rxd1 Ba6 20 Bxa8 Rxa8, and White is a piece ahead.
After Black’s actual move, he seems to have escaped the worst, but White has an ingenious way to get at the knights:

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This stab at the knight looks harmless, the pawn being pinned and unable to capture, but the point of 17 c4 is to use the pawn to support an attack by 18 Rb5. This will drive the queen off and make the capture 19 cxd5 possible.
The combinations now appear in quick succession.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Counterattack on the queen. All other attempts at defence fail, viz.:
1) 17... Nf6 18 Bd6 Qa5 19 Bxc6 and both Black’s rooks are en prise.
2) 17... Nxf4 18 Rb5! (a pretty ‘in-between’ move) 18... Qe7 (alternatively 18... Nb4 19 Qd2 Qxc4 20 Rxb4 and White wins) 19 Bxc6 Qxg5 20 exf4, and the attack on the queen leaves Black no time to save his a8-rook.
3) 17... Nde7 18 Bd6 Qa5 19 Bxe7 winning a whole rook.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s queen must move, but the threat of 19 Bd6 hangs over Black like the Sword of Damocles.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Not only because there is no other antidote to 19 Bd6, but with the hope of curbing the terrible bishops by putting obstacles in their paths.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This starts a beautiful combination at one end of the board which culminates in a queen sacrifice followed by a smothered mate over at the other end!

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only other move, 19...exf4, allows White to force the win by 20 axb4 Qe7 21 Bxc6 Rb8 22 exf4, and the extra piece wins easily.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
After the recapture 20... Qxc6, there comes 21 c5+ Kh8 22 Nf7+ Kg8 (or 22... Rxf7 23 Rd8+ and White forces mate) 23 Nh6++ Kh8 24 Qg8+! Rxg8 25 Nf7#!
Black did not wait to be convinced by a demonstration over the board but turned down his king in surrender.
An exquisite game played with elegance and precision. Capablanca’s own comment on it was “I made a few little combinations in this game.”

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Berlin Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White opens by stationing a pawn in the centre. This pawn performs various services:
It releases two pieces.
It occupies an important square.
It controls e5 and c5, hindering the opponent from placing pieces on those squares.
It stands ready to give firm support to a friendly piece making use of e5 or c5 as an outpost.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black follows suit, establishing a pawn in the centre, and prevents White from continuing with his intended 2 e4.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White offers a pawn to induce Black to surrender the centre.
White’s move is also an attack on the d-pawn, by means of which he hopes to uproot it and its hold on the centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The customary device for maintaining a pawn in the centre. In the event of White’s playing 3 cxd5, Black must be ready to replace the d-pawn with another pawn. It would not do to recapture with a piece. The piece could be driven off by White’s e-pawn, leaving White in full possession of the central squares.
For instance, after 2... Nf6 3 cxd5 Nxd5 4 e4 Nf6 5 Nc3 White holds all the trumps.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This is more enterprising than the passive 3 Nf3. Pressure is added to the attack on d5, and the knight also takes a hand in the battle for control of e4.
One of White’s objects in queen’s pawn openings is to effect a subsequent advance of the e-pawn, just as in king’s pawn openings an effort is made to gain more ground with a later d4.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The usual move at this point is 3... Nf6 but Black transposes moves to prevent his knight being pinned.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White is content with simple development and places the king’s knight at its most suitable post.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black postponed this move, excellent though it is, and now makes it reluctantly, but how else can he develop the kingside and prepare to castle?

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is not really a pin, but its effect is somewhat similar. Pressure is exerted on the knight, the bishop behind it and even on the last in line, the queen.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Alapin can’t stand pins or pseudo-pins! He attacks the bishop at once, to force it to a decision.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Whether objectively this is the strongest move is immaterial; the fact that the bishop’s pressure bothers Black is enough reason for Janowsky to maintain the pin!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black opens the position to give his pieces more elbow room, but with this capture he gives up his hold on the centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The simplest way to regain the pawn. The f1-bishop will capture it and make a developing move at the same time.
