metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Ready to counter 8 Bxc4 with 8... b5, attacking White’s bishop and gaining a tempo for the development of his own bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Material is now equal, but White’s prospects are better: he has two more pieces in active play than Black, and his pawn position in the centre is superior.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black’s chief purpose in this pawn attack is to vacate the b7-square for his light-squared bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Nobody has yet decided whether this or d3 is the better retreat for the bishop. At b3 the bishop strikes at Black’s centre, but those who favour d3 reason that from there the bishop helps control the vital e4-square and is aimed at the enemy king after a subsequent ...0-0.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Naturally, the knight does not go to c6 where it would obstruct the c-pawn. The pawn must not be hindered from carrying out its mission in life, which is to attack White’s centre and open a file for Black’s rooks.
The knight’s development looks clumsy, but it does back up the other knight, and it is ready to support a thrust at the centre by ...c5 or ...e5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Notice how an expert player puts all his pieces to work before starting any decisive action! This does not look like much of a move for so powerful a piece as the queen, but the simple act of getting a piece off the back rank advances the cause of development and constitutes progress.
Two more points: in the early stages of the game, the queen is most happily placed close to home, for instance at c2 or e2. In getting off the back rank, the queen permits the rooks (after the king castles) to get in touch with each other. A more aggressive development (generally for the sake of picking up a stray pawn) is only courting danger.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: It is hard to tell exactly what Black had in mind with this move. He may have feared the advance 11 d5 by White, or perhaps he wanted to create an outlet for the queen on the queenside. In any case, the move is definitely inferior to 10... c5, disputing the centre without any more delay.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Castling by White is an aggressive measure, to press the rook into active service.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Castling by Black is defensive in purpose, to get the king out of harm’s way.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The rook comes to the head of the c-file, control of which is one of White’s main objectives in this opening.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With the development of the light-squared bishop, Black seems to have solved one of the problems that besets the defender in queen’s pawn openings, but he isn’t out of the woods yet!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Excellent play! The rooks are now beautifully posted. The pressure on the d-file makes it dangerous for Black to try to free himself by 13... c5, as the reply 14 dxc5 opens a file for the d 1-rook.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black gives the c-pawn more support in an effort to get in 14... c5. This would free his position and let him put up a fight for the c-file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White is now ideally developed, with every one of his pieces taking an active part in the game. Black, on the contrary, is hampered by the restricted mobility of his pieces.
White’s knight move prevents a freeing attempt by 14... c5, since 15 dxc5 Rxc5 (15.... Bxc5 16 Nxd7 leaves Black unable to recapture) 16 Bxf6 Bxf6 17 Nxd7 wins a knight and attacks a couple of rooks.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black tries to relieve the pressure by exchanging whatever pieces he can.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This exchange suits White in that he has opportunities for attack along the newly opened d-file. Another effect arising from the pawn’s recapture is the creation of a strong point at d6, a circumstance which White hopes to exploit by planting a piece on that square.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight must block off the rook’s attack on the queen. If instead 15... Nd7, then 16 Bxe7 (in order to remove the guardian of the d6 square) 16... Qxe7 17 f4 and White will either entrench his rook at d6 and double rooks on the d-file or manoeuvre his knight to d6 by way of e4.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: In order to benefit from the weakness of d6 it is necessary to remove the bishop that defends the dark squares.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black destroys the knight before it does him any damage. The alternative 16... Qxe7 lets White swing his knight over to e4 and then anchor it either at d6 or c5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Certainly not 17 Rxd8 (nor 17 Bxd8) 17... Nxe2+ 18 Kf1 N xcl, and Black wins. The text gains a tempo for White in his plan to double rooks on the d-file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Material is even after this recapture, but White has a slightly superior position. Is this enough of an advantage for a master to squeeze out a win?
White’s specific advantage consists of his possession of the only completely open file, and the pressure he exerts on the strategically important d6-square.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Much stronger than the plausible continuation 18 Rd6. The reply to that would be 18... c5 whereupon doubling the rooks by 19 Rcd3 allows the pawn fork 19... c4 and Black wins a piece.
White’s actual move doubles his rooks without loss of time and also threatens to win a piece by 19 Rd7.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The dilemma which the weaker side always faces in this sort of situation is that if he does not dispute the enemy at every point and fight for control of every important file, diagonal or square, he will slowly be driven back and crushed to the wall; if he does oppose him at every turn, the resulting exchanges will simplify the position without improving his chances.
In this particular position, Black could hardly delay opposing rooks, as he was threatened with invasion on the seventh rank by 19 Rd7, as well as 19 Qd2, tripling the heavy pieces on the file. Such a massing of power on the open file would of course be overwhelming!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White stakes out a claim to the d6-square by settling a piece firmly there.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Otherwise, White plays 20 Qd2 next, with intolerable pressure on Black’s position.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This gives White a passed pawn, which exerts a terrific influence on the opponent’s way of life. Nimzowitsch calls particular attention to “the lust to expand in a passed pawn” and says that it must be regarded as “a criminal who should be kept under lock and key”.
To prevent any further advance of the passed pawn, Black must blockade it by placing a piece in its path. In effect, to keep the pawn under surveillance, he must lose the services of one of his four remaining pieces! If constant vigilance is necessary to keep the pawn quiescent, it is obvious that Black will be too busy defending to think of counter-attack. On the other hand, White is free to switch the attack from one point to another!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This is practically forced, as the pawn must be blockaded, and at once! Another forward step by the pawn might be fatal! Witness this possibility: 20... Qd8 21 d7 Rc7 22 Qd2 (threatening to win by 23 Qd6 followed by 24 Qxc7 and queening the pawn) 22... c5 23 Qa5 Rxd7 24 Qxd8+ and White wins.
After Black’s actual move, the pawn is stopped, but in blockading it, Black is tying up the queen, his strongest piece!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Indicating that he intends to play 22 e5, supporting the d-pawn and further cramping Black’s game. White’s pieces, relieved of the necessity of watching over the d-pawn, could then move freely about the board.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black opens a diagonal for his bishop and gives his rook more air.
An effort to prevent 22 e5 by 21.. f6 would have been met by 22 Qg4 and now either 22... Kf7 23 e5 fxe5 24 Qf5+ Ke8 25 Bxe6 Qd8 26 Qf7# or 22... Re8 23 Bxe6+ Rxe6 24 Qxe6+! Qxe6 25 d7, and White wins.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Assisting the d-pawn on to the next stage in its career: first, a pawn undistinguished from its fellows, then a passed pawn, now a protected passed pawn, and finally (if it fulfils its brilliant promise) a queen.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Back to sober reality! Black fights every step of the way to institute countermeasures which will keep his opponent busy on the queenside.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop, though forced back, now overlooks a new diagonal with interesting prospects.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black does not like to have his strongest piece tied down to the job of watching a passed pawn, so he diverts White’s attention by threatening mate. While White is occupied with stopping the mate, Black will have time to switch blockaders.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This puts an end to attacks on the long diagonal, as it leaves Black’s queen and bishop biting on granite.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The chief purpose of the check is to prevent White from playing 25 Qe3 seizing control of the dark-squared diagonals.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White keeps the queens on the board. Apparently he wants to win the game by direct attack, in preference to offering an exchange of queens by 25 Qf2 .
Such decisions are a matter of style more than anything else. A player who has choice of more than one way of winning should select a method that is congenial to his temperament and aptitudes. In the present position, I imagine that a Rubinstein or a Capablanca would unhesitatingly offer the exchange of queens and simplify, confident in his ability to turn a small but safe advantage into a win; they would be happy to leave the brilliancies to other masters. It is to these varying techniques that we must be grateful for the creation of a wealth of masterpieces in so many colours and moods.
After 25 Qf2, if Black avoids the exchange of queens and continues 25... Qxe5, White wins elegantly by 26 Qb6 Bc6 27 Qxc6! Rxc6 28 d7, regaining the queen by promotion and ending up a piece ahead.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The rook takes over the job of keeping the pawn covered.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A very fine move! The queen threatens to invade Black’s kingside by way of 27 Qh4 or his queenside by 27 Qa5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Nailing down the passed pawn for the time being.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: An outlet for the king in case of need. If White’s queen and rook leave for the attack, his king must not be caught by surprise and mated on the first rank.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Another regrouping so that the rook may leave its post, and the bishop (a lesser piece) stand guard.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Preparing a breakthrough by 29 f5 – pawns make excellent instruments of attack. They can break into almost any stronghold and make gaps wide enough for an invasion by the pieces.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The rook vacates d7 for occupation by the bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: To this vigorous thrust Black may not reply 29...exf5 as 30 e6 fxe6 (otherwise White obtains two connected passed pawns on the sixth rank) 31 Qxe6+ Kh8 (31... Rf7 32 d7 wins) 32 Qc8+ Kh7 33 Bxf5+ wins for White.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black completes the changing of the guard. Since one of his pieces must act as blockader, he assigns the task to the least important, the bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This battering ram of a pawn will force a breach in Black’s defensive structure. White’s threat is 31 Qg3 (intending 32 Qxg7#) 31... g6 32 Bxg6 fxg6 33 Qxg6+, and mate in two.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
On 30...gxf6 White wins by 31 Qg3+ Kh8 (31... Kf8 32 Bh7 mates) 32 Qf4 f5 (or 32... Qxe5 33 Qxh6+ Kg8 34 Qh7+ Kf8 35 Qh8#) 33 Qxh6+ Kg8 34 Qg5+ Kf8 35 Qf6 Kg8 36 Rf1 Bc6 (or else Rf3 and Rg3+) 37 Bxf5 exf5 38 Rxf5 Be4 39 Rh5 with a quick mate.
After the actual move, the change in the pawn configuration provides White with fresh objects of attack. One thing he must watch out for, though, is the preservation of his invaluable e-pawn, which so stoutly supports the two advanced pawns. Note that the position of these pawns gives them a powerful grip on the dark squares c7, e7 and g7. These squares are in the enemy’s camp and close to his king, but he (Black) cannot place pieces on those squares. With fewer facilities at his disposal, it will be difficult for Black to beat back the invaders.
The play for the win from this point comes under the heading of instruction and entertainment.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Threatening to win at once by 32 Bxg6 fxg6 33 Qxg6+, followed shortly by mate.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only way to protect the pawn. Advancing it instead by 31... g5 allows White a winning reply in 32 h4.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The g6-pawn is pinned and White prepares to hit it again by 33 h5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Hastening to bring the queen over to the danger zone. If Black tries to stop the pawn’s advance by 32... h5 then the queen works her way in by 33 Qg5 (threatening 34 Qxh5+) 33... Kg8 34 Qh6 and 35 Qg7#.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Concentrating his fire on a vulnerable spot.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Not 33... Be8, which protects the pawn but blocks the queen. The queen is the only piece agile enough to defend against White’s attack as it shifts from one point to another.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White makes use of all his resources. The rook will take part by switching over either to the h-file or the g-file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop helps defend the g-pawn so that the queen is free to protect the h-pawn, White’s next target of attack.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Revealing the plan: mate in three by 36 hxg6+ fxg6 37 Rxh6+ Kxh6 38 Qh4#.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only possible defence.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A pretty manoeuvre! White’s last move lured the queen away from the g-pawn. Now that this pawn has one piece less defending it, White attacks it with a fourth piece, the rook.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The queen rushes back to defend.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The threat on the rook gains time for White’s real purpose, an attack on the h-pawn at the other side of the board.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The rook flees but cannot get over to help defend the king.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Renews (and shortens) the earlier threat: 39 hxg6+ fxg6 40 Qxh6#.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Once again, the queen shifts over to protect the h-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Bringing up the infantry! White throws everything into the attack and now threatens 40 g5 followed by 41 hxg6+ fxg6 42 Rxh6+ Kg8 43 Qh3, with an easy win. If after 40 g5, Black tries 40...hxg5 then 41 hxg6++ Kg8 42 Rh8+ Kxh8 43 Qh3+ forces mate.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black unpins the g-pawn and prepares 40... g5 41 Qe4 Qg8, when White will have trouble breaking through the defence.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Tearing apart the cordon of pawns guarding the king.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This capture is the lesser evil, as otherwise White’s next move, 41 g7+, is fatal.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Killing off another bodyguard.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: If 41... Kg8, then 42 Qh3, doubling pieces on the open file, is conclusive.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Certainly not 42 g5 Rxh6+ 43 gxh6, when the h-file is closed and useless to White.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White is only one pawn up, but his attack has lost none of its virulence.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Now White plans to penetrate by 44 Qh5+ (exploiting the plight of the pinned g-pawn) 44... Kg8 45 Bxg6, and the last barrier is destroyed.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black avoids a queen exchange, as 43... Qh6+ 44 Qxh6+ Kxh6 45 f7 Bxf7 46 d7 results in White getting a new queen.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Beginning of the final movement!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king is driven back and the g-pawn loses a protector.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White sacrifices a piece to bring about a position where the passed pawns will decide the issue.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
An attempt to counterattack by 45... Qb7+ is futile. White simply replies 46 Kh2 and the king, seemingly exposed, is not in the slightest danger.
White wins as 46... Bxg6 fails to 47 d7.
The whole game is a marvellous blend of clear-cut positional play and ingenuity in attack. The opening is sound and simple, the middlegame is a lesson in attacking technique, and the ending is artistic.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: and White won.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Regarded objectively, 1 e4 is one of the strongest possible opening moves. It establishes a pawn in the centre and permits two pieces to come into play. More could hardly be asked of one move.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This opening, the Sicilian Defence, is currently one of the most popular openings. Black’s first move has the defect that only one piece is released, but in one respect it has a similar aim to 1... e5: it covers d4 and so makes it more awkward for White to form a ‘two-abreast’ pawn-centre by playing d4. If White insists on d4, then Black can reply ...cxd4, thereby exchanging White’s central pawn for a less central one.
The Sicilian Defence is perfectly sound and leads to a fighting game in which Black has many counterattacking chances, especially against an over-ambitious opponent, too intent on a kingside attack.
Black aims at queenside counterattack, and for this, control of the cfile is essential to offset White’s superiority in the centre and on the kingside.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A normal developing move. White brings a piece to a square where it exerts influence on the centre – but what a placid move this is!
More to the point is the energetic 2 Nf3. This develops a piece on the kingside (facilitating early castling) and prepares 3 d4 – action in the centre and release of the queenside pieces.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black’s move is quiet but effective! Diagonals are opened for the f8-bishop and the queen, and preparation is made to occupy the centre, if appropriate, with 3... d5.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This excellent move places the knight at once on its most suitable square, increases the pressure on the centre, and makes early kingside castling feasible.
Playing 3 d4 instead leads to 3...cxd4 4 Qxd4 Nc6, when Black gains a tempo by the attack on the queen.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: If Black plays 3... d5, then the reply 4 exd5 exd5 5 d4 opens lines to the advantage of the better developed player – in this case White, who has two pieces out to Black’s none.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The characteristic break in the Sicilian, by means of which the mobility of White’s pieces is increased. A diagonal is opened up for the c1-bishop, while the queen gets some more air.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black exchanges to kill off one of the two centre pawns in return for his c-pawn. Meanwhile, he opens the all-important c-file for the use of his queen and a8-rook.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The recapture centralizes White’s knight and increases the attacking range of White’s pieces.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
By a devious route, the players have arrived at the Four Knights Sicilian, a tricky variation in spite of its classical appearance.
What should White play now? The choice is more a matter of style, mood and temperament than anything else – and this is what makes chess so fascinating.
White can decide to be methodical and stick to straightforward development by 6 Be3 or 6 Be2. He can be bold and combinative with 6 Ndb5, or cautious with 6 a3, preventing a powerful pin. He can be patient and devote his efforts to trying to build up a positional advantage after 6 g3 or 6 Nxc6.
Whatever he does, the play will reflect something of his own personality. The way he directs the activities of his small army will mirror the thoughts, moods, and instincts of the individual.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White is content with the slight positional advantage that results from the exchange of knights. Let us take a quick look at some of the alternatives:
1) 6 Be3 Bb4 (pinning the knight and threatening 7... Nxe4) 7 Bd3 d5! and Black has overcome all his difficulties.
2) The quiet 6 Be2 (certainly not 6 Bd3, leaving the knight en prise ) is also met by 6... Bb4 with good counterplay.
3) Preventing the pin by 6 a3 is not attractive. It is answered by 6... d5, and White must fight to retain the initiative. Time is too valuable in the opening to waste on pawn moves.
4) The double-edged 6 Ndb5 is not to everybody’s taste, leading as it does to wild complications after 6... Bb4 7 Bf4 Nxe4 8 Nc7+ Kf8 9 Qf3 d5 10 0-0-0 or the sharp Pelikan variation after 6... d6 7 Bf4 e5 8 Bg5.
One merit of the text-move is that Black, in recapturing with a pawn, closes the c-file, his chief avenue of attack in the Sicilian.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This is superior to 6...dxc6; for one thing, it is usually better strategy to capture toward the centre. In this case, it keeps a cluster of pawns in the centre and opens the b-file for the benefit of the a8-rook.
The continuation after 6...dxc6 might be 7 Qxd8+ Kxd8 8 Bg5 Be7 9 0-0-0+ and Black is kept on the move.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Not only does this evict the f6-knight from its fine post, but it also strengthens White’s grip on the d6-square.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Little thought would have been required to make this centralizing move. The only other spot available to the knight was g8, home base.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Exchanging knights would forfeit any advantage White enjoys. The move actually made intensifies the pressure on d6.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
No loitering on the premises! Either the knight leaves or it declares its intentions!
Black had another defence in 8... Qc7 9 f4 Qb6, aiming to prevent White from castling kingside.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight must stay where it is for White to carry out his purpose, which is to take possession of the critical d6-square.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black does not take with the pawn, as that is answered by 10 Qh5+. This would force his king to move and thereby deprive him of the privilege of castling.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Compelling an exchange of pieces which leaves Black with a ‘bad’ bishop, one which is ineffective because of the pawns standing on squares of the same colour as the bishop. A bishop can accomplish little if its pathway is cluttered up by pawns.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only other move, 10... Ke7, is not inviting.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The recapture gives White a stranglehold on his opponent’s position. Not only does White blockade the d-pawn, preventing the freeing ...d5 advance, but he also enables his king to flee to safety by castling. In addition, White exerts a great deal of pressure on the dark squares, a pressure that is accentuated by the fact that Black’s king’s bishop, operating on those squares, is off the board.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The queen must be driven off quickly, or Black will choke for lack of air.
There is no relief in 11... Qe7 12 Bf4 Qxd6 13 Bxd6 Ne4 14 Ba3!, when White still bears down with a heavy hand.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: In retreating, the queen manages to attack in two directions, threatening both the knight and the enemy g-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only move to parry both the threats.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White tries again, as he hates to relinquish this dominating position. Meanwhile, he hints that he can always draw if he wants to, by a repetition of moves.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black cannot let the queen stay at d6, and delay in evicting her might prove to be fatal.
That Black’s difficulties are not insuperable was demonstrated by Alekhine, who suggested this continuation: 13... Qb6 (Black threatens 14... Qxf2+ 15 Kxf2 Ne4+) 14 Bd3 c5 15 Bf4 Bb7 16 0-0 Rc8.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Very strong! If the queen cannot establish permanent residence at d6, this square is the next best thing. At b4 (odd place though it is) the queen attacks the knight, controls a diagonal which makes castling for Black impossible, and in a third direction prevents Black’s a8-rook from seizing the open b-file.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black protects his knight and prepares to challenge White’s queen by 15... Qd6. Black’s pawn-centre provides some compensation for his troubles.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: An ideal move, as a piece develops with a threat – 16 Bxe4 dxe4 17 Qxe4 winning a pawn.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black offers to exchange, which will either rid the board of White’s attacking queen or induce her to retreat from a dominating position.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White is willing to simplify. He will still have advantages in his two powerful bishops and an enduring grip on the dark squares.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black is content with his part of the bargain: both his rooks have open files on which to operate, and he has a group of pawns in the centre with which he expects to limit the scope of the bishops.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
“An eye for the microscopic betokens the master,” says the great Marco.
The e5-square is now controlled by White, while Black’s e-pawn is restrained from advancing. One effect of this pawn’s inability to move is that it fearfully circumscribes the mobility of Black’s bishop.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must do something about getting the bishop into play. With this move he plans to develop it at a6 and exchange it for White’s more powerful bishop.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Excellent! This holds back Black’s c-pawn, while two more dark squares, d4 and c5, come under White’s domination.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With this move Black hopes to clear the board of one of White’s menacing bishops.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The king is a strong piece and should be used aggressively in the ending. As the number of pieces on the board decreases, so is the danger of the king being exposed to a mating attack reduced, and its own power as a fighting piece magnified. In the ending, the king is unexcelled as a means of causing damage by getting in among the enemy’s pawns.
That is why, in the present position, the king comes closer to the centre, where he is most useful, instead of castling and then working his way there.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Practically forced, as Black was attacking both e3 and b2.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Let us size up the situation: the white bishop enjoys far more freedom than does Black’s. The latter is greatly hampered in its movements by the many pawns standing on light squares, the colour of the squares on which the bishop operates.
White’s king, being nearer the centre and the critical squares d4 and e5, is much better situated for the endgame than Black’s.
Black’s centre, the heart of his game, is held fast. The three pawns he has in that area are fixed and unable to move.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Blockade! The a5-pawn is stopped dead in its tracks; it is now a fixed target, always in danger of being attacked by Bb6. In order to make sure it is not captured (for its removal gives White a passed a-pawn) Black must watch over it constantly with his a8-rook. Because of the need to guard this one pawn, Black is thereby deprived of the services of a rook.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black brings his king toward the centre for the endgame.
The rooks are now united, while the king himself heads for d6, where he hopes to support an advance by the e-pawn or the c-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White attacks the bishop to force it to the side of the board. You will note that the bishop’s scope is cut down as pawns on both sides are placed on light squares, the colour of the diagonals on which the bishop must travel.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only flight square open to the unhappy bishop!

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Continuing the trek to d4, e5, and, as we shall see, all points north! 24 Bc5 was a bit more cruel, to prevent any demonstration by 24... Rf8 .

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White dominates every important square on the board! The bishop stops the h8-rook from getting to f8, the a6-rook from moving to b6, the king from d6, the d-pawn from advancing and the c-pawn from moving at all! Compare its control of eight squares with that of Black’s bishop, whose influence is confined to one square! This difference in their potential accounts in great measure for the extent of White’s attacking opportunities, and for the consequent difficulty Black will have in defending. Every gain or control of territory by White will result in more and more cramping of Black’s position.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Stepping aside, the king makes the d7-square accessible to the black bishop.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Tightening the noose! This king also makes way – for the benefit of the h1-rook, who will turn the e-file to account.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black will try to manoeuvre the bishop over to the kingside, for instance to g6.
His h8-rook seems to have a great deal of scope, but what does it avail him? If it moves to b8 (as good a file as there is) at what point can it penetrate? It cannot get to any useful square on that file.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Much stronger than the immediate occupation of e5 by the king. White intends to use this key square as a transfer point for his rook on its way to the g-file. After it gets there, White will settle his king at e5 and tighten his grip on the dark squares.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black prepares a pawn barricade against the rook’s threatened attack on the kingside.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Second stop on the trip to g5.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Battening down the hatches, Black gets ready for a hard winter.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White attacks the g-pawn and simultaneously makes room for his king.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The pawn must be protected, and this of course is more elastic than 29... Rh6, when the rook has no mobility to speak of.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Further penetration along the convenient dark squares. The threat is 31 Kf6 Be8 32 Re1 (even stronger than 32 Kxe6), followed by 33 Rxe6.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black abandons the e-pawn, as he cannot hope to save all his pawns. There is a slight chance, if White captures the pawn at once, 31 Kxe6, of putting up some resistance by 31... Bd7+ 32 Kf6 Bf5.
Black’s pitiable bishop is sadly hemmed in by the five pawns firmly fixed on squares of the same colour.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Before committing himself to decisive action, White applies more pressure. Notice how a master player puts every piece to work before he strikes a blow.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
To get back into the game, this rook has to return home!
There was no satisfactory defence in 31 ... Kd7 as the reply 32 Kf6 uncovers the rook’s attack on the e-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White completes the plan of encirclement. Notice the effects of the arrangement of Black’s pawns at e6, d5 and c6 – Black’s own pieces are kept under restraint, while White’s can utilize the weakened dark squares c5, d4, e5 and f6 to penetrate into the vitals of the enemy position. Notice also that these dark squares are ‘holes’, squares from which pieces cannot be dislodged by the opponent’s pawns.
White does not resort to brutal attack or to intricate combination to accomplish his purpose but puts his trust in the dynamic power inherent in an overwhelming positional superiority.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black reveals another reason for his previous move. In the continuation 33 Rxg6 Rxg6+ 34 Kxg6 Rg8+ 35 Kxh5 Rxg2, Black suddenly turns on his foe.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: To guard against this possibility, and to lessen any chance of a breakthrough by one of Black’s rooks, White fashions a chain of pawns on the kingside.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black can do nothing to improve his position, so this amounts to no more than a waiting move.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White could play 34 Rxg6 and have little trouble winning, but he makes doubly sure. He blockades the e-pawn first, to quell even a shadow of resistance!

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: “While there’s life...”

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The first tangible gain. The rest is an interesting display of the art of winning a won game.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Fearing threats against his isolated h-pawn, Black prepares to double rooks on the h-file in an attempt to save it.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White keeps on gaining ground. Now he invades the seventh rank.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black holds on grimly.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Simplest, hence the scientific way to force the win. In endings where one side has a material advantage, the prescribed strategy is to exchange pieces, not pawns, and to bring it down to a pawn ending. Endings with only pawns on the board are the easiest to win.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The recapture leaves Black only a pawn down – for the time being!

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With every exchange, the king’s power increases! Now the king threatens the rook and helps attack the h-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Strangely enough, the rook has only one move on the board!
Does White now settle the issue by removing the h-pawn?

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
No, no, a thousand times no! If 39 Rxh5? then 39 ... Be8+, when Black wins a whole rook and the game. How easy it is to go wrong even in a simple ending!
White’s actual move first banishes the rook from the premises.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The rook must leave the file, abandoning the pawn.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Now the capture is safe.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Hoping to bring the bishop over to the kingside and then attack White’s queenside pawns.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The rook hastens to the seventh rank, a rook’s proper post in the ending.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Otherwise, White’s procedure is 42 Kf6+ Bd7 43 g4, and the pawn cannot be stopped.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king must stay within range of his rook.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The exchange of rooks cannot be avoided, so Black captures first to draw White’s king away from h5. If the bishop can get there, it might still stir up some trouble.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This meets with White’s approval. His kingside pawns are mobile, while Black’s pawns either cannot or dare not make a move.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Now to get behind the queenside pawns!

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The queenside pawns cannot be rescued, so White starts his kingside pawns rolling.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: After so much inactivity, this bishop not only threatens the lives of all the pawns on light squares but restrains (for the time being) all the pawns on the kingside.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: To save itself, this pawn flees to a dark square.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black takes a pawn, more to distract White than anything else, since he has no real threats.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Ready to refute 46... Bxa4 with 47 f5 Kd7 (after 47 ... Bc2 48 Kg6 the h-pawn walks up, or 47... e5 48 f6 Kd7 49 f7, and White wins) 48 f6 Ke8, and 49 Kg7 escorts the pawn through.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king rushes over to hold back the pawns.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: “The passed pawn’s lust to expand”, as Nimzowitsch puts it.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Desperation, but there is no promising defence. If 47... Ke8, then 48 g6 Bc2 49 h5 Bf5 50 Kg7 wins for White.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The simplest. White’s three connected passed pawns should be convincing enough.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: After 48 ... Bc2, 49 Kg6 is the clincher, protecting the f-pawn and making way for the h-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Indicating that it’s time to concede. The pawn cannot be stopped by 49 ... Ke8 as 50 Kg7 sees it through.
A beautiful illustration of the technique of exploiting weaknesses on the dark squares.

metadata.Opening: Sicilian Defense: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This move, more than any other, offers chances of an opening advantage without taking risks.
Two pieces are released at once, and a pawn occupies a central square, as with 1 e4, but extra benefits accrue from 1 d4:
The d-pawn is protected and safe from immediate attack.
White is not exposed to the threats to his f2-pawn, which often arise in king’s pawn openings. His control of c5 makes it impossible for Black to develop his dark-squared bishop at c5 to attack the vulnerable f2-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The simplest way to prevent White from dominating the centre with 2 e4 next move.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The characteristic move of the Queen’s Gambit. The versatile c-pawn does many things. Three of these things are concerned with doing away with Black’s centre:
It offers itself in exchange, so that Black may be lured into accepting a side pawn in return for his centre pawn.
It threatens, when the right moment comes, to destroy Black’s centre by capturing the d-pawn.
It exerts constant pressure on the d-pawn, so that Black is kept occupied with its protection.
Besides all this, the move of the c-pawn assures that the c-file is kept free and clear for the convenience of White’s major pieces, while a pathway is opened for the queen, leading to the queenside.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black strengthens the position of his centre pawn. In the event that White plays 3 cxd5, he is ready to recapture with a pawn and thus maintain a pawn in the centre of the board. This is Black’s safest defence, even though it does limit the scope of his c8-bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This is an excellent move, though not so sharp as 3 Nc3, which adds pressure to the attack on Black’s d-pawn. Either move complies with an injunction particularly applicable in queen’s pawn openings:
Develop all the pieces as quickly as possible!
“The main principle in the openings,” says Capablanca, “is rapid and efficient development .” (The italics are his.)

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black’s knight moves in toward the centre, attacks the e4-square and adds its weight to the protection of d5.
It is good policy to mobilize the kingside pieces first, since only two of them need be developed to make castling possible.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A powerful move! The bishop is developed and a restraining hand is put on the enemy knight. There is no immediate threat in the move – White just ‘threatens to threaten’.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The proper way to unpin a knight. The inexperienced player often grows impatient and drives the bishop off by 4... h6 5 Bh4 g5 6 Bg3 only to find that he has ruined the pawn position on the kingside as a result of his violent action.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White strengthens his pawn-centre and frees the light-squared bishop for action.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black gets his king into safety before revealing his plans for the development of the queenside pieces. His b8-knight may go to d7, or following an attack on White’s centre, perhaps to c6.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White has no such problems. His queen’s knight can move to c3, since it does not obstruct the c-pawn and the opening of the c-file. At c3 the knight takes an active part in the struggle for control of the centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This knight must never be developed at c6 before the c-pawn is moved. The pawn must be free, either to advance to c5 and fight for equal rights in the centre or to move one square to c6 where it bolsters Black’s own centre. But the pawn must not be obstructed by ... Nc6!
The development by 6... Nbd7 is stronger than appears at first glance. Black’s position is cramped for the moment, but the knight is ready to support a liberating movement and an attack on White’s centre by ...c5 or ...e5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A magnificent square for White’s queen! From c2, the queen exerts her powerful influence in several directions: on the partly open c-file and on the centre, preventing Black from freeing himself by 7... Ne4. This attempt to force some exchanges and shake off the pressure is refuted by (after 7... Ne4) 8 Bxe7 Qxe7 9 cxd5 Nxc3 (if 9...exd5, then 10 Nxd5 wins on the spot) 10 Qxc3 exd5 11 Qxc7 Qb4+ 12 Qc3, and White has won a pawn.
Another feature of 7 Qc2 is that it vacates d1 for the queen’s rook, whose presence on the same file as Black’s queen will discourage the opponent from making a break in the centre. Exchanges of pawns in the centre would clear away some of the obstructions and intensify the rook’s pressure on the file – a pressure which reaches all the way up the file to the queen.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This move provides solid support to the centre pawn and gives the queen access to the queenside. It looks substantial enough, but the more aggressive 7... c5, disputing control of the centre by establishing a state of tension there, might be more to the point. The danger in delaying ...c5 is that Black may never again have a favourable opportunity to get in this thrust.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White develops a fifth piece, pointing it at Black’s kingside, and is ready to castle instantly on either wing.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black waited for White to move his f1-bishop before making this capture. Otherwise, the bishop recaptures and develops at the same time. Black’s intention, in clearing d5, is to swing his knight over to that square, force some exchanges, and free his cramped position.
Nevertheless, Black has surrendered the pawn-centre, which he so carefully built up.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White is content with the result of the pawn exchange. Lines are opened which increase the mobility of his pieces.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Obviously to compel White to exchange bishops.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is safer than 10 Bf4 Nxf4 11 exf4, when White is left with an isolated d-pawn. The pawn itself is in no great danger, but the d5-square, directly in front of it, is! It is in danger of being occupied indefinitely by one of Black’s pieces. A piece stationed on a square in front of an isolated pawn can never be driven off by enemy pawns.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The proper recapture, letting the queen come into play; taking with the knight would be developing backwards.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The king finds a safer shelter while the rooks get in touch with each other.
White’s position is excellent, the result of simple straightforward development.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The usual manoeuvre of protecting the b-pawn, so that the c-pawn is free to attack White’s centre. If Black can get in 13... c5 he will still have a respectable game.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Uncovering an attack! The queen threatens the c-pawn, while the knight restrains it from advancing to c5. White’s idea is to prevent the indispensable freeing move ...c5 forever and then barricade Black completely by planting a piece at c5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black protects the pawn by developing another piece.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Very fine strategy! Before settling a piece on c5, White plays to get rid of one of the guardians of that square, Black’s knight at d7. If he plays 14 Nc5 at once, then 14 ... Nxc5 15 Qxc5 Qxc5 16 dxc5 leaves him with a pawn occupying c5. This does not have the same effect as a piece standing on that square. A pawn is immobile and does little to restrain the opponent, but a piece radiates power in all directions and has a terribly cramping effect on the enemy’s movements in the whole surrounding area.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Developing another piece and defending the pawn which was attacked by two pieces.
Black did not care for the exchange 14... Nxe5 15 dxe5. White could then anchor his remaining knight at d6, follow up by planting his queen at c5, and throttle Black thoroughly.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Removing one of the pieces guarding the vital c5-square...

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: ...and luring the other one away!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With the domination of this square, White’s advantage is decisive in the strategic sense. What remains is to exploit his superior position, to translate it into actual victory, and this process of consummating the win is one of the most fascinating parts of chess.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Both queen and bishop were attacked, so the queen stays near the bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The practice of the masters has shown that rooks are most efficient when they control open files.
Suppose there are no open files? Then the rooks should be placed on partly open files, or on files likely to be opened.
Suppose none of those seem to exist? Then the rooks should be brought to the centre, to exert pressure on the centre files.
But the rooks must be developed!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
There are various reasons for this move:
The rook has no future on the c-file while the pawn at c6 impedes its movements (and there is little prospect of the pawn coming to life).
The rook vacates c8 for the bishop. The bishop cannot stay indefinitely at b7, where it is hampered by the c-pawn, and where the queen is tied down to its defence.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s incidental threat of winning a pawn by 19 Nxb7 Qxb7 20 Qxc6 is subordinate to the strategic concept of intensifying the pressure on the c-file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black parries the threat of 19 Nxb7 and frees his queen from the job of watching over the bishop. Now he can speculate on getting some counterplay by the break 19... e5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Magnificent centralization by the queen, who prevents 19... e5 (when that pawn would be simply snapped up) and prepares to switch over for a kingside attack.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The knight, best defender of the castled position, returns to f6, incidentally with an attack on the queen.
Against other moves White could play 20 Bd3, threatening 21 Qxh7#. This would compel either a retreat by the knight or a weakening advance of one of Black’s kingside pawns.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The queen evades the knight’s threat and swings over to the kingside to get an attack rolling against the king.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black tries counterattack on the queenside – mostly to distract his opponent’s attention. There is little he can do to strengthen the defence of his kingside. Any move of a pawn only loosens the position and reduces his chances of resistance. The break in the centre by 20... e5, which he contemplated making, is risky, to say the least, as 21 Qg3 in reply, pinning the pawn, is troublesome.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The simplest way to save the a-pawn and to keep the queen from moving to b4.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Hoping to disrupt White’s queenside by continuing with 22...bxa3.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White avoids any exchanges that might let the queen set foot in his territory.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Trying to shake off the grip of the knight, which is strangling his queenside to death. metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The bishop guards both lightsquared pawns, but its mobility is almost nil.
The subject of mobility is interesting. While it is not always true that the player whose pieces have more room in which to manoeuvre enjoys an advantage, it applies often enough in practice for us to disregard the exceptional cases. It stands to reason that pieces that are free and untrammelled not only have more striking power in the portion of the board they occupy, but they also control and limit the activities of the enemy. Add to this the ease with which they can reach other parts of the board, and you can see the advantages to be derived from the ability to move freely about.
Let us compare all the moves the pieces on each side can make. We are not evaluating their worth, whether good, bad or indifferent. What we want to see is the range of their action.
White Black
King 2 King 1
Queen 12 Queen 5
c1-Rook 8 f8-Rook 1
c5-Rook 11 d8-Rook 8
Bishop 9 Bishop 2
Total 42 Total 17
White’s pieces are 250% as efficient as Black’s! With so great a disparity in mobility (and consequently in attacking force) how long can Black continue the struggle?

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
If 27... h6, then 28 Qe4 forces 28... g6, when two pawns have been uprooted. White could then continue by 29 Rh5 Kg7 (if 29...gxh5, then 30 Qh7#, or if 29... Kh7, then 30 Qf4 wins) 30 Qe5+ f6 (or 30... Kh7, when the neat double pin 31 Qg5 wins) 31 Qg3 g5 (if 31... f5, then 32 Qe5+ Kh7 33 Qc7+ Kg8 34 Rxh6 wins) 32 Rxh6! Kxh6 33 Qh3+ Kg7 34 Qh7#.
A simpler way, if White doesn’t want to bother analysing combinations, is to maintain the pressure and then apply more! For instance, after 27... h6 28 Qe4 g6, instead of playing 29 Rh5 White could advance 29 h4, threatening to break up the pawns by 30 h5. If Black replies 29... h5 to stop the advance, White can either snap the h-pawn off with his rook or keep hammering away by 30 g4 hxg4 31 h5.
After the actual move, Black has weaknesses on the dark squares and holes in his position.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The queen plants herself securely in one of the holes created by Black’s ...g6 advance. A hole is an unguarded square such as f6 or h6 brought into being by the advance of a nearby pawn. It is a weak square, because it is no longer under the surveillance of a pawn and is vulnerable to invasion by an enemy piece. Such a piece can settle itself comfortably in one of these holes, secure in the knowledge that no enemy pawn can disturb it.
White’s plan, now that the queen has worked her way into a dominating position on the kingside, is classical in its simplicity: he will just advance the h-pawn to h4, h5 and h6, and then play Qg7#. If, after the pawn reaches h5, it is captured en route, then mate by the rook is the instant punishment.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Rubinstein Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Attacking the queen with his unprotected rook. A pretty enough conclusion, but pedants may point out that White missed a brilliancy in 38 Qg7+ Ke7 39 Rxe6+! Kxe6 40 Qe5#. Many a player has had quicker wins or more artistic ones than actually occurred pointed out to him by lesser lights, who revel in the fact that they found something the master overlooked. The reason the master didn’t see the shorter line is that he was not looking for it in the first place! The move with which he wins is the one whose effects he foresaw earlier and analysed thoroughly before starting his final combination. Once the series of forcing moves clicks, there is no reason at all for him to waste time finding other moves that might win. It takes time to analyse combinations, and the shorter way, ventured on hurriedly, might turn out to have a hole in it. The moral is: play the move that forces the win in the simplest way and leave the brilliancies to Alekhine and Keres.

Winning the queen and the game.
Magnificent play by White, who never once relaxed his iron control of the game. A remarkable feature is the circumstance that none of Black’s pieces or pawns, with the exception of the one brave little pawn at b4, ever crossed the fourth rank into White’s side of the board!

annotation: In his delightful book Chess for Winter Evenings, written more than 140 years ago, H.R. Agnel proposed an interesting argument for the superiority of 1 e4 to 1 d4: “Moving the d-pawn two squares,” he said, “gives the queen a range of two squares and the c1-bishop a range of five squares. But moving 1 e4 gives a range of four squares to the queen and five squares to the f1-bishop. You see therefore that e-pawn two squares is the most desirable move with which to open the game. There is another reason why this move is desirable – the pawn occupies a portion of the centre of the board. Two pawns abreast at your e4- and d4-squares, supported by pawns and pieces, must be considered as your best military position, and maintained with all the skill in your power.”

One of the drawbacks of Black’s system of defence is that it subjects his queen to harassment by the minor pieces without her being able to bother them in return. The queen, for example, cannot threaten to capture a knight that is protected as that amounts to giving up the queen for a knight. The knight, though, can attack and threaten to capture the queen, whether the queen is protected or not.
