Rxb4+ wins a couple of pawns, while after 26 b5 Na5+ 27 Kc5 (not 27 Kb4 Nd5+, and White’s in the mating trap) 27... Nb7+ 28 Kc4 (moving to b4 or d4 allows a check by the other knight winning the exchange) 28... Na5+ the king is making no progress – he must either retreat or submit to a perpetual check.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Simple and strong! White guards the b-pawn and prepares to advance the a-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: There is no way to stop 27 a5 so Black tries to get counterplay on the open file.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Brutal but necessary. White must oppose rooks on the file. Black will either have to exchange rooks or move his rook away, leaving White in full possession of the file.
One of the points a beginner learns painfully is that he must fight for control of every bit of territory, whether it is a file, a diagonal or a square. It is often necessary to offer an exchange of pieces to secure possession of an important point or area. Such offers must not be avoided for fear of their leading to a dull game, or that such strategy is unsportsmanlike. The player with a material advantage who temporizes because he wants to win brilliantly, and avoids exchanges because they are dull and unsportsmanlike, is only torturing his opponent. A win must be completed in the quickest, most efficient way possible.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Relinquishing the file offers the black rook no future on any other file – so he exchanges.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White is left with one piece to two, but his lone rook with its enormous mobility is more than a match for Black’s knights, who must keep in constant touch with each other to assure their mutual safety.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king rushes to the queenside to head off the passed pawn.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Every move of this pawn increases Black’s danger. Keeping it under restraint will tie up his pieces so that he will have no time to think of counterattack.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black moves closer to the a-pawn, meanwhile unpinning his knight.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Putting a stop to the king’s little trip, as 30 ... Kc8 is punished by 31 b5, when Black must give up one of his knights. Note again that having the two knights lean on each other for support is not an ideal arrangement.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight is on its way to the queenside. Meanwhile it attacks the loose f-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: One way to dispose of a threat is to disregard it and counter with a more urgent one! White’s threat is 32 a7, which would force Black to sacrifice his knight for the pawn.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The pawn must be blockaded! On 31... Nxf4+ 32 Ke4 Nxg2 33 a7 Nxa7 34 Rxa7 the win is elementary.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White stabilizes the kingside pawn position before proceeding with affairs on the queenside.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With the double object of making it more difficult for White’s b-pawn to advance, and to vacate c7 for his king.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
“Every one of White’s moves in this ending deserves an exclamation mark!” enthusiastically cries Mieses, who played the black pieces in this game.
White’s idea is to protect the bpawn so that he can then oust the black knight from its strong post in the centre by 34 c4.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight does not wait but turns on the rook.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only way to save the pawn. Black can try interposing the knight at d5 instead, but after 35 Kc4 and 36 Kb3 (to protect the b-pawn) White evicts the knight by 37 c4 and wins the unguarded h-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Keeping the knight away from d5 forever!

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black is running out of good moves: he cannot play 35... Kd6 on account of 36 c5+ nor can he solidify the kingside position by 35... f5 without letting White’s king break in later by way of e5.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Rather surprising! White delays any further manoeuvres with the queenside pawns and proposes to bring his king and rook to more aggressive positions. The king will move to d4 and then c5 and the rook to the open e-file, eventually to penetrate to the sixth or seventh rank. Black will then have to fight off the rook’s threats against the kingside pawns as well as to hold back the dangerous pawns advancing on the queenside.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black can do nothing but defend patiently.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Meanwhile White proceeds to bring his king to c5.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: If Black plays 37... Kc7, ready to reply to... Kc5 with 38... Ne4+, White forces an entrance by... Re1 (threatening a deadly check at e7) 38... Kd7... Kc5 Ndc8 40 b5.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king is now ideally placed, and White is set for a quick finish by 39 b5 and 40 b6.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Certainly not 38... Nd6, when... Rd1 pins the knight. A pretty continuation could then be 39... Nc8... Rxd6+! Nxd6 41 a7, when the pawn cannot be stopped.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Poised for invasion at e6 or e8 and a raid on the kingside pawns.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: If 39... Kd7 (to keep the rook from moving to e6 or e8), then 40 b5 cxb5 41 cxb5 Kc7 42 Re6 and White wins as he pleases.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The rook finally breaks into the enemy camp!

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Not, of course, 40... Kb8, when White’s reply... Rb7+ wins a knight or two.
Black’s interposition with check looks as though it might still give White some trouble. For instance, after 41 Kd4 c5+ 42 bxc5 Nc6+ Black wins a whole rook.
A brilliant finish! After 41... Kxd7, 42 b5 cxb5 43 cxb5 Nc8 (or 43... Kc7 44 b6+) 44 b6 followed by 45 a7 resolves any lingering doubts.
An impressive display in the art of utilizing the advantages accruing from gain of time in the opening.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black resigns.

metadata.Opening: Scandinavian Defense: Anderssen Counterattack, Goteborg System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Although queen’s pawn openings are played with the idea of obtaining an early positional advantage, Marshall considered the best way to start an attack was to begin the game with 1 d4. One reason for his view might have been that the e-pawn openings no longer could be depended on to lead to wide-open games with opportunities for combinative play. In the old days when White began with 1 e4, the reply almost automatically was 1... e5. White could then offer a pawn by 2 f4, rely on its being accepted, and joyfully swing into the excitement of a King’s Gambit. In taking the pawn and grimly holding on to it, Black gained material, but the loss of time involved threw him on the defensive. Gradually, after sustaining many defeats, the players of Black tired of being the victims of brilliancies. They took a more rational attitude, and grew cautious. They resorted to 1... e6, 1... c5 or 1... c6, steering the game into channels of their own choosing. The result was that an aggressive player, starting the game with 1 e4, found himself facing ‘irregular’ defences, which forced the game into unfamiliar channels. He found himself involved in tightly knit positions requiring systematic planning, when he was itching to get an attack rolling. He was supposed to have the initiative, but here it was wrested away from him! How could he play a gambit (even at best a risky matter) if his opponent did not oblige him with a forthright 1... e5 in answer to his own enterprising 1 e4?
In beginning the game with 1 d4, White gets an advantage, slight though it may be, against any system of defence – and with it he retains excellent attacking chances as well!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Undoubtedly one of the strongest replies. Black stabilizes the pressure in the centre, prevents White from strengthening his hold there by 2 e4, and himself opens lines for two of his pieces to get into the game.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: An offer of a pawn (with strings attached) to induce Black to surrender the centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Taking the pawn is perfectly sound, but why give up the centre to win a pawn which it turns out you cannot keep? Playing 2...dxc4 is equivalent to exchanging a centre pawn for a side pawn, in itself an unprofitable transaction. However, many leading players are happy to play this opening, so there must be some counterbalancing plus points. The main advantage is that Black no longer has the responsibility of supporting the d5-pawn, and this makes it easier for him to organize the crucial thrust ...c5, exchanging his own c-pawn for White’s d-pawn. Thus, although White has a temporary superiority in the centre, it is often not long before Black can restore a symmetrical central situation.
After Black’s actual move, his d-pawn is firmly supported. If now 3 cxd5, Black recaptures with a pawn , maintaining a pawn in the centre.
It is true that Black’s c8-bishop is shut in by the e-pawn, making its development difficult, and this is a drawback to the defence. But if Black’s first two moves are good, and they probably form the best reply to the Queen’s Gambit, then one can appreciate the terrific strength of this opening, and why so many players adopt 1 d4 unhesitatingly whenever they have White.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is somewhat sharper than developing the other knight first, as additional pressure is immediately put on the central point d5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Tarrasch did not approve of this knight move, which most of us would make instinctively. It is true that f6 is the most useful square for the king’s knight 99.44% of the time, since from there it influences affairs in the centre strongly, enjoys great freedom of movement, and is magnificently placed for attack and defence. However, Tarrasch feared the strength of the pin that White can clamp on the knight next move. Instead of 3... Nf6, he therefore recommended that Black challenge White’s centre at once by 3... c5 (the advance ...c5 is almost a must at some stage in queen’s pawn games), meanwhile opening up the c-file for the use of his own heavy pieces.
Why then, you may ask, did Tarrasch play a move that he himself disparaged? His explanation is that this was the first game of a match against one of the world’s leading masters (Marshall had recently won the Cambridge Springs tournament without losing a game, ahead of Lasker, Schlechter, Pillsbury and Janowsky) and he did not wish to stray so soon from orthodox paths.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Naturally! Not only because the bishop exerts uncomfortable pressure on the knight, but also because it is good policy to play moves that the opponent finds disturbing. If Tarrasch thinks that pinning the knight is troublesome - pin the knight and make him uneasy!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This looks clumsy, with the knight blocking what little view the c8-bishop had, but pieces can easily step out of each other’s way. The knight belongs on d7 and not on c6, where it obstructs the c-pawn. This pawn must not be hindered from advancing sooner or later to c5. Little as the pawn is, it represents a major force in disputing possession of the centre!
With 4... Nbd7 Black sets a little trap for the unwary, invented by Tarrasch. If White, relying on the impotent state of Black’s pinned knight, tries to pick up a pawn by 5 cxd5 exd5 6 Nxd5, Black gives up his queen with 6... Nxd5 (breaking the pin by force) 7 Bxd8, only to regain it with another piece thrown in by 7... Bb4+ 8 Qd2 Bxd2+ 9 Kxd2 Kxd8.
The moral is: don’t go pawnhunting in the opening!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This sort of pawn move is not a waste of time. Without a liberating pawn move the bishops can never get off the ground, so this is part of the process of bringing the pieces into play.
With the text-move, White opens two diagonals at once, one for his f1-bishop and another one for the queen. The e-pawn contributes an additional service in bracing up the pawn-centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black too reinforces his pawn-centre and gives his queen an outlet on the queenside.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
It is customary to develop the minor pieces first, roughly in this order:
First the knights, generally to c3 and f3, but toward the centre in any event; then the bishops (after the necessary pawn moves), either to control vital diagonals or to pin enemy knights; following this, it is time for the queen to make her entrance. If the queen comes into the game too early, she incurs the danger of being harassed – perhaps even surrounded and captured – by enemy minor pieces.
Last come the rooks, which after castling are brought to e1, d1 or c1, to head files in the centre which are partly open. These files are likely to become completely open after pawn exchanges in the centre.
This method of development is not by any means to be considered a fixed course to pursue. Nothing in chess – no convention, principle or recommended procedure – is to be practised rigidly. The value of any single move or combination of moves can only be measured with respect to the particular position on the board. It must fit in with the scheme of the game you are playing and be tempered by the demands of the opponent. A great deal depends on what he does, or lets you do. This is why you may find it expedient to develop the queen at the sixth move or to castle at the sixtieth move.
In this position Black has indicated that he might counterattack by 6... Qa5 and 7... Bb4, pinning the c3-knight and then increasing the pressure on it. It might have been more to the point for White instead to mobilize another minor piece by 6 Nf3 (like putting money in the bank), with an eye to speedy castling or perhaps to neutralizing the anticipated pressure on the c3-knight by swinging the f3-knight over to d2.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A many-sided move: the queen not only unpins the f6-knight but starts a counteraction by pinning the white knight; Black threatens to intensify the pressure by bringing the f8-bishop to b4. As an extra, added attraction, Black sets a little trap to catch the careless – and this might even include expert players who at times treat the opening in a perfunctory way. The trap might snap shut on a player who innocently develops his bishop at d3 only to find that 7...dxc4 threatens both his bishops at one blow. White cannot escape from the trap by 8 Bxf6 as 8...cxd3 attacks his queen and wins a bishop.
It might be as well to state at this point that Tarrasch did not expect to catch Marshall with such a primitive trap. Master players do not set traps if it involves injuring their own position. A trap which arises in the natural course of development is one thing, but to play for them deliberately at the risk of wasting valuable time is unforgivable.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White neutralizes the queen’s indirect attack on his bishop and clears away the c-file for the benefit of his major pieces.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Tarrasch had planned to recapture by 7...exd5 in order to maintain a pawn in the centre. Now he realizes that danger may be involved in delaying the development of the queenside pieces any longer.
His c8-bishop is locked in on one side by the d7-knight, and this knight must stay where it is, as it supports the other knight on f6. If he tries to develop the bishop on the queenside, then after ...b6 he cuts off the queen’s retreat. But the strategy of a master player must be flexible: it must be consistent with the requirements of the particular position at hand. Tarrasch would very much like to have a strong pawn-centre but dares not neglect the exigencies of development. So he heeds Nimzowitsch, who once said, “Giving up the centre must not here be regarded as illogical; was happiness no happiness because it endured for but a short time? One cannot always be happy.”
Meanwhile the knight does add to the pressure on White’s pinned knight and renews the threat of winning the exposed bishop by 8... Nxc3 9 bxc3 Qxg5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
“In his anxiety,” says Tarrasch, “to guard the threatened bishop, White makes a decisive mistake.”
This is an interesting example of the value of accurate timing in chess. The fact that a normal developing move has intrinsic strength is secondary to the question of its usefulness in the one position in front of you, not in vaguely similar positions.
Despite the fact that the knight occupies a most useful post at f3, and at the same time protects the bishop, its development is either too soon or too late. White is doing nothing about the problem of his pinned knight. This is where pressure is exerted; this is where danger is threatened.
More to the point is 8 e4 instead, evicting Black’s knight and forcing it to declare its intentions. If then 8... Nxc3 9 Bd2 Qa4 10 Qxc3, White has resolved an uncomfortable situation.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Tripling the attack on the knight. Black threatens to win at once by 9... Nxc3 10 bxc3 Bxc3+ followed by 11... Bxa1.
How shall White meet the threat? If he plays the natural 9 Rc1, the knight is adequately guarded since it is attacked three times and defended three times. However, Black then capitalizes on a curious fact about the power of a pinned piece: not only is it helpless to make a move but it has also lost its ability to defend! Translated into chess language, this means that 9 Rc1 can be met by 9... Qxa2, a capture startling at first glance but an obvious one if we realize that the knight’s defensive power is illusory! I stress this circumstance because it is important. Knowing it, recognizing it and applying it has caused (chess) kingdoms to topple.
All this fuss about winning a miserable a-pawn? Let’s see what would happen thereafter:
After 9 Rc1 Qxa2, Black’s method is classical in its simplicity. He follows up by... Bxc3+ and after the recapture by the pawn exchanges queens. He has an extra pawn, but this is not enough advantage to bring about checkmate. He must increase his material superiority sufficiently to justify him in going after the king, and this can only be done by turning one of his pawns into a queen. So he selects the most likely candidate, in this case the passed a-pawn, and pushes it step by step up the board. The pawn’s advance faces the opponent with a problem that becomes more acute with every step taken by the pawn. He must head off the pawn or blockade it completely, in either case tying up one or more of his pieces to do so. The defence is under the strain of keeping the pawn under constant surveillance, while at the same time having to guard against a sudden switching of the attack toward his king. What often happens is that he either has to give up a piece for the pawn or allow further exchanges of pieces, a procedure which leads to inevitable loss.
Such long-range plans are not based on exact calculation; they represent a general idea of the method for winning in positions of this nature.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Not an appetizing move, as the king loses the privilege of castling, but it’s the only way to guard against losing some material.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: “Hits the nail on the head,” says Tarrasch. With the subsequent exchange of pawns, the c-file will be prised open, further endangering the unfortunate knight.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White is anxious to bring matters to a head. The alternative 10 e4 yields to 10...cxd4 11 exd5 (or 11 Nxd4 Nxc3 12 bxc3 Qxg5+ and Black wins a piece - the exposed bishop that seemed doomed from the start) 11...dxc3+ 12 bxc3 Qxd5+ and Black is a pawn up with a winning position.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Tarrasch simplifies and avoids the difficulties attendant on winning the exchange, such as: 10...cxd4 11 axb4 dxc3+12 Qxc3 Qxa1... Qxg7 Rf8 14... Nxb4... Bb5 Qxh1... Qf6 and White forces mate. It is true that Black could win the game at his fifteenth move by playing 15... Qa5, but why risk all these complications when the advantage can be maintained by less hazardous means?

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only way White may recapture.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Continuing the good work of opening up the c-file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Again, White has no choice of recapture: the c-pawn is pinned, and 12 Nxd4 is refuted by 12... Nxc3 13 Qxc3 Qxg5, when Black has won a pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s pinned knight is gone, but it has been replaced by a pawn – and this pawn is also pinned! It makes a fine target, so Black directs his fire on it. He threatens to strike at it again by 13... Na4 or by 13... Bd7 followed by 14... Rc8.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Finally, another kingside piece sees daylight!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black can pounce on the pawn with 13... Na4, but he prefers to complete his development first and then bring all his pieces to bear on it. “Besides,” as he says, anticipating Nimzowitsch, “the pawn does not run away.”

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White must develop and defend at the same time. If he gets a moment’s respite, he will free the pinned pawn by... Ke2, 16 Bd2 and 17 c4.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: But Black doesn’t let up even for a moment! The rook seizes control of the beautiful open file and immediately adds its weight to the pressure on the immobilized c-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: “First,” thinks Tarrasch, “let’s get the king away from the fighting and bring the other rook closer.”

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Clearly the c-pawn must be lost, as Black can attack it with more pieces than White can summon up for defence, so White saves time by abandoning the pawn and fleeing with his king.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Much better than taking with the knight. Black’s idea is to occupy a strategically strong outpost on the only open file or force an exchange of queens. The removal of the queens would simplify matters to his advantage, as he is a pawn ahead.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Forced into retreat, White manages to incorporate the threat of... Bxh7+, regaining his pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The simplest way of saving the pawn, this also provides the king with a useful escape square against a surprise check on the last rank.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Modern Variation, Knight Defense
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The queen reluctantly leaves the beautiful outpost at c3 but stays on the all-important c-file. Note the reason the queen selects the c7-square: at c6 the action of the bishop is interfered with, at c8 that of the rook.

annotation:
In this game, the art of chess is reduced to a simple formula: get a passed pawn, move it up the board, and win!
White begins by getting a foothold in the centre, while releasing two of his pieces.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black applies the same formula, developing his g8-knight to its most effective post. Aside from its admirable potential for attack, the knight also serves while it stands and waits. In the service of the king, especially after castling, the knight defends as no other piece can.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Not the most energetic procedure, but White need not be aggressive from the start. The opening itself is so strong that White can build up a promising position merely by developing his pieces so that they occupy the most suitable squares immediately. The method is simplicity itself:
Put every single piece to work, and move no piece twice until development is complete.
The fact that 3 e3 releases one bishop but shuts in another is of little moment, as the c1-bishop can get into the game by way of b2. White does not indicate his specific intentions: he might play the Colle Attack or perhaps simply develop the bishop at d3 with a view to early kingside castling.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black supports his d-pawn, anticipating an attack on it by 4 c4. He prefers this to the alternative pawn support by 3... e6, which confines his queen’s bishop.
However, if Black wants to free his bishop, why not move it at once to f5? There it would stand ready to oppose White’s bishop when it moves to d3. The almost inevitable bishop exchange then removes White’s attacking bishop from the board and takes the sting out of the Colle system of attack.
Another possibility was pushing on to c5 at once with his pawn, striking at White’s centre, and opening the c-file for the use of his own heavy pieces. But why play 3... c6, moving a pawn unnecessarily in the opening? Why waste time defending when nothing is threatened?

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Quiet, forceful development: the bishop surveys two fine diagonals and is ready for action in either direction. Meanwhile the kingside is cleared for castling.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White defends the f3-knight with a minor piece, relieving the queen of a duty. This method of developing the knight is preferable to placing it at c3, where it might interfere with the future operations of the queen or the rook on the c-file.
The sortie 6 Qb3 yields no immediate advantage, since Black’s reply 6 ... Qb6 leads either to an exchange of queens or a retreat by White’s queen.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System

So White puts a stop to any such ideas! An advance by 8... e5 now costs a pawn, as White’s knight, no longer pinned, is free to pick off the pawn.
The queen’s development at c2 is modest, but in the early stages of the game, the queen should rarely venture beyond the third or fourth rank. What is important, though, is to move the queen off the back rank and into active play.

Nxe5 10 dxe5 Nd7 11 Bxh7+ wins a pawn for White) 10 f4 gives White a powerfully centralized knight and excellent attacking prospects.

Opening up lines of attack, which, says theory, will favour the player whose development is superior.

It is subordinate to the overall strategy of the game, which is being conducted on positional lines and will be won that way. Any combinations that arise will be incidental to the general plan, which is to create a passed pawn, move it up at every opportunity and promote it to a queen.

annotation:
Now we can appreciate the significance of White’s offer of the queen. It was not an attempt to win the game by surprise tactics; it was the employment of a combination as a device to gain ground positionally!
White’s doubling of the rooks on the d-file gives him full control of that file, and his pawn majority of three to two on the queenside offers the possibility of creating a passed pawn on the c-file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System

annotation: Black’s object is to drive the queen off and command the d-file himself with his rook.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A shrewd move: the queen keeps in touch with the rook, prevents Black’s rook from coming in at d1, and keeps a weather eye on the strategically important c5-square, the c-pawn’s next stop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king approaches the field of action. In the event of a general exchange of pieces, he is prepared to head off the c-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s pawn advances at every available opportunity.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Expecting White to recapture by 28 bxc5, whereupon he blockades the pawn effectively by 28... Qc6 .

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Very clever! White need not recapture immediately, as Black’s pawn is pinned and cannot escape capture. Meanwhile, the queen move stops the intended blockade by 28... Qc6 and prepares 29 bxc5 followed by 30 c6.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The rook rushes to help the c-pawn.
There is a temptation for White to go pawn-hunting now by 29 Qxh7 followed by 30 Qh8+ and 31 Qxg7, picking up a couple of pawns and creating for himself a passed h-pawn. But this sort of random play would not be consistent with White’s orderly, economical conduct of the game, and entirely out of character for a Capablanca!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A passed pawn at last!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: It would not do to recapture by 29... Rxc5 as White punishes the offending rook by 30 Qb4 pinning and then winning it.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Passed pawns must be pushed! With each step forward, the scope of White’s rook increases, while the freedom of Black’s pieces becomes more limited.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black realizes that bringing the king to the centre might be suicidal, viz.: 30... Ke7 31 Qh4+ Kd6 32 Qb4+ Ke5 33 Qf4#!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A beautiful preparatory move! If White were to play 31 Qb4 at once, aiming for 32 Qb7 (in order to dislodge the blockader) Black could exchange queens and then stop the pawn by 33... Rb5, coming behind it. However, with White’s a-pawn at a4, Black could not bring his rook to b5!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: In spite of the heavy guard surrounding the pawn, White with one stroke will lift the blockade!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: No matter how Black gets out of check, he cannot stop the coming combination.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Destroying one of the guards!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
And the recapture lures the other one away!
The pawn becomes a queen next move, leaving White a whole rook ahead.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: and White wins.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
One way of getting a good share of the centre is to take it!
White does so here by planting one of his pawns right in the middle of the board. It occupies d4, one square, and secures a grip on two others, e5 and c5.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: More elastic than 1... d5. Black develops a piece and bears down on the centre instead of occupying it with a pawn. His knight attacks d5 and e4, and prevents White gaining more ground with 2 e4.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This advance is a valuable freeing move in queen’s pawn openings. It attacks the central square d5, makes the c-file a favourable one for the rook (because of the likelihood of the file being later opened up) and offers the queen access to the queenside.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Not at once 2... d5 as 3 cxd5 Qxd5 (or 3... Nxd5 4 e4 Nf6 5 Nc3, when White has more of the centre than he is entitled to) 4 Nc3 gains time for White by the attack on the queen.
With 2... e6, Black prepares a pawn support for a later occupation of the centre by ...d5. Meanwhile, he releases his f8-bishop.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is sharper than developing the g1-knight. It backs up a threat of 4 e4, presenting a formidable array of pawns in the centre.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop clamps down on the knight and, by its pin, deprives it of the power to attack or defend. Thus, if White carelessly played 4 e4, Black could snap up the pawn at once.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Wresting control of e4 from White and restraining his ambitious e-pawn from taking too long a first step.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Quiet, perhaps too quiet. It gets the king’s knight off the ground, but the lull gives Black an opportunity to seize the initiative.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
“Black equalizes in any queen’s pawn opening,” says Reuben Fine, “where he can play both ...d5 and ...c5 with impunity.”
With 5... c5 Black aims to destroy White’s pawn-centre, or at the very least to maintain a state of tension in that important area. As a fringe benefit, his queenside pieces have a bit more elbow-room.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s idea is to clarify the position in the centre. The disappearance of his c4-pawn also helps to increase the pressure of the queen on the c-file.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Preferable to 6...exd5 which allows 7 Bg5, an annoying pin of the knight. The queen is strongly centralized at d5, and in no danger of being annoyed by White’s minor pieces.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White has had enough of this tiresome bishop!

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must exchange. If instead 7... Ba5, then 8 b4 (threatening 9 Nxd5) 8...cxb4 9 Nxd5 b3+ 10 Bd2 bxc2 11 Nxf6+ gxf6 12 Bxa5 and White has won a piece.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Capturing with the queen instead lets Black gain a tempo by 8... Ne4 attacking the queen, whereupon the prospect of White’s playing e4 seems further away than ever.
In compensation for White’s theoretical advantage of the two bishops against knight and bishop, Black’s pawn position on the queenside is distinctly superior.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight develops with a threat. There is now a triple attack on White’s d-pawn, and this limits his choice of reply.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The least of the evils, though it does shut in the c1-bishop. The alternative 9 dxc5 Qxc5 saddles White with two weak, isolated pawns, while after 9 c4 Nxd4 10 Qa4+ (or 10 cxd5 Nxc2+ and Black wins a rook) 10... Qd7 Black is a pawn up.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king finds a safer shelter, while the h8-rook makes its appearance.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop develops gingerly. A more energetic procedure was 10 c4 to dislodge the queen from the centre, followed by 11 Bb2, with fair chances.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This clever pawn exchange keeps the position fluid and gives Black a slight advantage after any recapture.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Understandably, White rejects 11 Nxd4 as 11... Qxg2 12 Bf3 Nxd4 in reply is ruinous. With his actual move, White adheres to the principle of capturing toward the centre and increases the queen’s sphere of action by opening the c-file. Nevertheless, it might have been better policy to play 11 exd4, activating his dark-squared bishop.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Preparing to develop the bishop at b7, where it will command one of the longest diagonals on the board.
Black’s advantage consists mainly in his two pawns to one on the queenside, and this, after an exchange of pawns, can turn into one pawn against none. As for the c-file, it can be seized by the a8-rook. The rook will drive White’s queen off and remain in control of the file.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White wants the long diagonal for himself, so he vacates f3 for the bishop. He hardly hopes to lure Capablanca into a cheap trap by 12... Qxg2, when 13 Bf3 wins apiece. This sort of thing does not happen in real life.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop stands beautifully here, despite the fact that two pieces obstruct its path. Meanwhile, the c8-square is ready for occupancy by another tenant, the a8-rook.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop is well posted here, but at what a cost in time!The knight has had to retreat, and the development of White’s queenside pieces has been neglected.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The queen keeps in touch with the knight, which is under attack by two pieces.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Trying to get in the advance of the e-pawn is premature as 14 e4 Nxd4 costs a pawn, while 14 Bxc6 Bxc6 15 e4 Qxd4 16 Qxc6 Qxa1 loses the exchange.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black threatens 15... Nxd4, and thereby suggests that White’s queen leave the c-file.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The aggressive 15 Qa4 is risky as 15.. Ne5 16 Qxd7 (16 Qxa7 Nxf3+ 17 Nxf3 Qc6 followed by 18... Ra8 puts the queen in trouble) 16... Nxf3+ 17 Nxf3 Nxd7 is strong for Black.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Offering an exchange of bishops. Refusing it leaves Black in full possession of the long diagonal.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: It might have been safer to concede the diagonal by 16 Be2 and keep more pieces on the board. Exchanging simplifies the position and accentuates Black’s superiority.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black is now ready to exploit the circumstance that his opponent’s light squares are vulnerable to invasion. These squares have been weakened by the disappearance of the light-squared bishop. This advantage, together with that of Black’s pawn majority on the queenside (a circumstance which generally results in the creation of a passed pawn) should be enough to forecast a win for him.
From this point on, we will see a demonstration of the technique of winning a won game.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Finally, White gets his queenside rolling. Laudable as this object is, it was essential to anticipate Black’s next move and play 17 Qd3. This would strengthen White’s weak squares and hold off for a time the threatened invasion.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A very fine manoeuvre! The queen takes leave of the long diagonal to exert great pressure on a more important one.
The queen threatens to come in strongly at e2 and make coordination by White’s pieces difficult.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Parrying the threat. On 18 Rc1 instead (to put up a fight for the c-file), Black plays 18... Qe2 19 Nf3 (or 19 Ra2 Ng4 20 Rxc8 Qxf2+ and Black wins) 19... Nb3 20 Rxc8 Rxc8 21 Ra2 Rc1+!, and White must give up his queen or be mated.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Admirable centralization – but it’s only temporary. The knight is on its way to the queenside, the theatre of action.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Intending either to oppose rooks by 20 Ba1 followed by 21 Rc2 or to continue with 20 Qa1 preventing 20... Nc3.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Clearly in order to double rooks on the c-file. Black is in no hurry to move his knight to c3; first he wants to induce White to dislodge the knight from the centre.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A deceptive move. It looks strong, but the central pawns are exposed and can easily become targets of an attack.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: It may seem strange that Black gives up a healthy knight for a sickly bishop, but this precaution is necessary before the rooks venture into enemy territory. With less material on the board, the rooks will be less exposed to the stings of the minor pieces.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight had to be removed, as it was attacking queen and rook.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The recapture enables the rook to penetrate deeper into White’s position.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White makes an effort to regroup his pieces. If he tries to dispute the c-file by 22 Rc1 then 22... Rxc1+ 23 Qxc1 Qd3 24 Qb2 Rd8 wins a central pawn.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The doubled rooks now dominate the open file.
Theoretically, Black has a won game. His positional superiority is undeniable, and winning, in a favourite phrase of the masters, ‘is simply a matter of technique’. A pleasant state of affairs, but one which involves a psychological danger. There is a tendency to relax and let up on the attack. It is easy to be lulled into a false sense of security, a circumstance which prompted Marshall’s observation, “The hardest thing is to win a won game”.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White gives his king an escape square – in lieu of anything better to do.
Black’s rooks cannot be driven off (if 23 Re3, then 23... Rc1+ wins the queen) so White temporizes and awaits the turn of events.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The first in a series of skilfully blended moves which speed up the tempo. To begin with, there is a triple attack on the a-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: No other move saves the pawn.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Very neat! The knight attacks the queen and simultaneously cuts off the a-pawn’s protection by the rook.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Voluntarily giving up a pawn which he cannot keep. If he tries to hold on to the pawn by 25 Qd1, then 25... Qc4 26 Rb2 (the rook was attacked) 26... Nc2 (now the other one is threatened) 27 Re2 Qxa4 28 Ne1 (striking at the pinned black knight) 28... Qxd4! wins for Black.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The first tangible gain. Now watch the greatest genius the game of chess ever produced demonstrate the art of transforming a passed pawn into a queen. Notice how any combinations that do not relate to that objective, no matter how attractive, are carefully avoided. Such intensity of purpose is frightening (especially to one who has to face it!).

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Passed pawns must be pushed! Everything else – combinations to win pieces, gathering up stray pawns, even attacks on the king – must be relegated to the background as incidental to the main theme of queening the advanced pawn.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White opens lines for some sort of counterattack, trying to create a diversion.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: In return for this, White’s e2-rook looks out on a completely open file. In fact, White threatens 29 Qxc3 Rxc3 30 Re8#.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Complying with the Manhattan Chess Club epigram, “Black passed pawns travel faster than White”.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This holds out longer than 30 R al Rc2 31 Qe3 b2, when Black wins more quickly.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black’s play is crystal clear: the passed pawn must be pushed and its path is blocked by a rook. Therefore the blockader must be removed!

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The proper rook to capture, this begins a series of pretty moves that decides the game.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White must recapture.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: An attack on queen and rook which threatens to win the exchange.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White rescues the rook by pinning the knight. It would not do to play 33 Qxb3 instead as Black simply takes the rook, and his knight now protects the queen.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The pin of the knight is met by a counter-pin of the rook, which Black now threatens to take with his queen.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: But the rook wriggles out of the pin. Has Black let the win slip?

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Not at all! This compels capitulation since after 35 Rxc1 b2 (the pawn must move on) 36 Rb1 Rb8 37 Kf1 Na3 (driving off the last blockader) 38 Rd1 Qb1 the passed pawn wins the game for Black.

metadata.Opening: Nimzo-Indian Defense: Classical Variation, Noa Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A favourite of modern players, this is one of the best possible ways to begin the struggle for mastery of the centre – by occupying it with a pawn and permitting two pieces to come quickly into play.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Unlike 1... d5 this does not meet the opponent head-on, but it does prevent him from continuing with 2 e4 and has the added merit of developing a piece at once to its proper square in the opening.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
There are many good points about this move:
1) It restrains Black from an immediate 2... d5, as the reply 3 cxd5 forces a recapture with a piece and destroys his short-lived pawn-centre.
2) It opens the c-file for the use of White’s major pieces.
3) It makes a diagonal available to the queen.
4) It enables the two pawns standing side by side to get a grip on four squares on the fifth rank.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black’s f8-bishop is to be developed aggressively, to influence affairs in the centre. If White replies 3 Nc3, for example, in order to follow up with 4 e4, Black pins the knight and makes 4 e4 impossible.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White cannot enforce the advance of the e-pawn, so he makes a normal developing move and awaits events.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Further restraint on the project! Black intends to place his bishop at b7, where it attacks from a distance. The bishop will add its strength to that of the knight in the control of the critical e4-square.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s best course is to oppose bishops on the long diagonal as one does with rooks on an open file. In setting up an equal opposing force, he takes the sting out of the enemy bishop’s attack.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Strictly a modern concept! In olden times they filled up the centre with pawns and then fianchettoed the bishop, with the result that the bishop was deprived of any usefulness. Nowadays the bishop is free to strike all along the diagonal, unhampered by fixed pawns cluttering up his path.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With the completion of the fianchetto, White’s kingside is cleared, and he is ready to castle.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Before attempting to undermine the centre by ...c5, Black develops a piece. Not only does the bishop’s move expedite castling, but it also brings about a favourable exchange of bishops.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is preferable to 6 Nbd2, a passive interposition which gives Black time to castle and then attack the centre by 7... d5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black proceeds with the exchange as the best means of freeing his somewhat cramped position. Instead, withdrawing the bishop to e7 throws him on the defensive and lets White retain the initiative.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Theorists and critics of master chess recommend that White capture with the queen instead. Despite their shrieks that the knight belongs at c3 in order to help attack the d5-square, the players themselves persist in recapturing with the knight. They advance as argument that in doing so another minor piece is developed, but the real reason might be sheer stubbornness – rebellion against authority. In any case, if it is less effective than 7 Qxd2, it is not to be so roundly condemned.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Before taking any decisive action in the centre, Black sees to the welfare of his king and removes him to a safer part of the board.
A strong alternative is 7... c5 challenging White’s pawn-centre. To this, White cannot reply 8 d5 as it loses a pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White makes his king’s position more secure and presses the h1-rook into service.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A strong move, whose object is to undermine White’s centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White has little choice. Moving the pawn to d5 loses a pawn, supporting it with 9 e3 (in order to recapture with a pawn and maintain a pawn in the centre), ties down the e-pawn to the job of defence. The chances then of the e-pawn’s ever reaching e4 are rather dubious.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black has gained three advantages by a simple exchange of pawns:
1) He has exchanged a centre pawn for a less central pawn.
2) His c-pawn controls d4, making it impossible for White to settle a piece on that square.
3) His queen and a1-rook will be able to operate with good effect on the newly opened b-file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
In most cases the function of the queen in the opening is not so much to be moving around as it is to get off the back rank and out of the way, so that the rooks can get together and work on the centre files.
With the departure of the queen, the f1-rook can occupy d1, exert pressure on the d-file, and make life uncomfortable for Black’s forces on that file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight develops toward the centre and intensifies the pawn’s grip on d4.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The tempting 11 e4 meets its refutation in 11... e5 (strengthening the pressure on d4) followed by 12... Qe7 and 13... Nd4. White would then face a problem: the pressure of the knight at d4 is almost intolerable, but removing it lets Black recapture by 14...cxd4, leaving him with a passed pawn on the d-file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Now there are three pieces bearing down on d4, while the queen herself gets a purchase on the open b-file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White has no wild dream of starting a counterattack with 13 b4; mainly he wants to rule out... Nb4 at some later stage.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Fine positional play! One is apt to forget that a rook’s first duty is to seize upon any file that is open, not only since the rook’s attack extends the whole length of the file but because the rook has a convenient avenue for its progress to other points.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s rook also goes to b1, but what a world of difference there is in the two moves! White’s rook has no open file; it has little prospect of increasing its mobility, and its function is purely defensive. In protecting the b-pawn, though, it relieves the queen of a responsibility.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The rook was doing nothing at f8, so it is transferred to a file where it is likely to become useful.
There was no hurry about playing 13... a5 since White is in no position to try for the break by 14 b4.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s move has a superficial appearance of strength. In reality, the pawn occupies a square that should be kept clear. White’s pieces lose a great deal of mobility in not being able to make use of e4 as a jumpingoff point to their various destinations.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Stifling 15 e5, White’s e-pawn’s lust to expand.
Notice how Black has reinforced his hold on d4. This point now has the power of the queen, a knight and a couple of pawns trained on it.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White hopes for some counterplay along the d-file, either by 16 Qd6 or in manoeuvring his knight by way of f1 and e3 to d5. In the meantime, he prevents Black from playing 15... Nd4, the response to which is 16 Nxe5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A witty, almost impudent, reply. Black guards the e-pawn (so that he can play 16... Nd4) with a pawn which itself is unprotected!
White, of course, must not take the d-pawn, the penalty for 16 Qxd6 being 16... Rd8, winning the queen.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Indicating that he wants to deploy the knight to e3 and then d5. Excellent strategy, if White can carry it out.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: However, Black gets there first! Not only does he establish an outpost at d4, but he also hinders White from continuing his manoeuvre. If White tries 17 Ne3, then 17... Bxe4 18 Nd5 Bxd3 19 Nxb6 Nxf3+ 20 Bxf3 Rxb6 21 Rxd3 e4 wins a piece neatly.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The advanced knight cramps his style, so White gets rid of it.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black is happy to exchange: he has a passed pawn on the d-file, which in the course of time might become a queen. More than that, the pawn guards the exits. It hinders White’s knight from coming out at e3 and puts an end to its ambition to reach d5.
The passed pawn at d4 is apparently the logical candidate for promotion to queen, but there are surprises to come – many of them!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Suddenly White bursts forth! His chief threat is 19 bxc5 Qxc5 (Black must recapture with the queen, as she is doubly attacked) 20 Rxb7 Rxb7 21 e5, and the discovered attack will net White two pieces for a rook.
How does Black meet this threat? Obviously not with 18...cxb4, as 19 Rxb4 gives White the better of it. Also not by 18... Qc7, when after 19 bxc5 dxc5 (to protect the passed pawn) 20 f4 threatening 21 e5 follows, and White’s pieces spring to life.
Capablanca’s actual reply initiates a remarkable combination. He lets White obtain an advantage in material in return for a position which looks far from promising – except to a Capablanca!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White plays to win! He takes a pawn off, opens a file for his rook, and threatens to remove the passed d-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must recapture with the pawn to preserve the precious passed pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This tempting combination wins two pieces for a rook.
Has Capablanca been caught off-guard, or does he see much further into the resources of the position than his opponent?

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black captures with the queen to maintain control of the valuable open file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Discovered attack on the queen, and direct attack on the knight.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A remarkable offer to exchange queens! Usually, the side that is ahead in material tries to clear the board and simplify to an ending.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White rejects 22 Qxb3 as it leads to 22... Rxb3 23 exf6 Rxa3, when Black is left with two passed pawns.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The idea of this is to force the white rook off the last rank. The rank then becomes available to Black’s rook as a point of entry, enabling it to get behind White’s pawns.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White has no choice.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The knight is pinned as a start, and White has to scramble frantically to break the pin.
Against passive play, Black continues with 24... Re8 followed by 25... Ree1 and 26... Rec1. This wins the c-pawn since White cannot protect it by 27 Bd5 without abandoning the knight. After capturing the pawn, Black would have two dangerous connected pawns rushing to become queens.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s plan is clear: he protects the precious c-pawn and vacates a square for his king. Following 25 Kg2, the knight, no longer pinned, can come into the game.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The doubled rooks give Black undisputed possession of the all-important b-file.
White is now faced with two threats:
1) 25... Rc1 intending 26... Rbb1. The attack on the knight would compel the bishop to return to g2, whereupon Black picks up the c-pawn.
2) 25... R8b3, forcing an exchange of rooks, after which one of White’s queenside pawns must fall.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White unpins the knight, which has been a spectator for the last ten moves.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A daring concept! Black offers to exchange rooks and let White remain with two pieces to his one!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White is happy to oblige!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Now the a-pawn is in peril.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White could not save the a-pawn (if 27 a4, then 27... Rb4 28 a5 Ra4), so the knight counterattacks by going after a pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Winning a pawn and simultaneously creating a passed pawn on the a-file. Will this be the one to become a queen?

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Now White’s pieces spring into action! The threat is 29 Nxc5, knocking the support out from under the d-pawn and giving himself a passed c-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Much better than 28... Ra5 which ties the rook down to defending a pawn and makes his role in the ending a subordinate one.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: After this capture, White’s own passed pawn begins to look menacing.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Not so much to gain a pawn as to give the king more freedom. If at once 29... Kf8, then 30 Nd7+ drives the king back to g8, as 30... Ke8 allows 31 fxg7 winning for White.
29... d3 allows 30 Kf3 followed by 31 Ke3, when White wins the d-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king turns back to head off the passed pawns.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black does not fear a double attack on this pawn by 31 Bc6. He would refute this by 31... Ra1+ followed by 32... a3, and the pawn has moved another step forward.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The king comes closer, definitely putting an end to any danger from the d-pawn.
How does Black proceed?

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: By scaring White with the threat of queening the a-pawn! Black intends 32... a3, followed by 33... a2, 34... Re1+ (to make way for the pawn without loss of time) and 35... a1 Q .

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Back at the seventeenth move it seemed that the d-pawn would reach the eighth rank and become a queen. The d-pawn is blockaded, and it now appears that the a-pawn is the one that will be promoted.
But will it be the a-pawn?

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White’s pawn can cause trouble, too!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Threatening to win on the spot by 34... Re1+ 35 Nxe1 a1 Q .

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king steps aside to evade the check.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This move, which attacks the knight as well as threatening to queen the pawn, adds to White’s difficulties.
