metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White must destroy this dangerous creature at all costs!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With this capture Black nets a piece for his a-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White does not fall into the trap 36 Ke2 losing his passed pawn after 36... Rc3.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The text-move attacks the bishop and the f-pawn. Moreover, it revives the d-pawn’s prospects.
Is this pawn to be the candidate after all?

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
An admirable spot for the bishop.
Black can now easily go wrong by 37... Rxf2 38 c6 Rb2 (if 38... Rc2, then 39 Kd5 wins for White) 39 c7, and White’s pawn crashes through!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king takes over the job of restraining the dangerous pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Advancing the c-pawn is useless: 38 c6 Ke7 and the pawn can go no further. With the text-move, White offers his h-pawn in return for Black’s d-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black falls in with the suggestion. Instead of grimly holding on to the passed pawn, he is willing to simplify, confident that his superiority is enough to secure the win. This requires a belief in justice on the chessboard, and confidence in one’s ability to mete it out properly.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With this capture, White’s prospects look brighter. His king and bishop are in close attendance on the passed pawn and will bend all their efforts to escort it to the far side of the board.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Ready to blockade the pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Apparently with the idea of switching the bishop to e4. From there it guards his f-pawn, prevents Black’s doubled pawns from advancing, and is prepared to protect his c-pawn when it reaches c6.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Threatening 41... Rg2 42 g4 h4, when Black wins.
Is the h-pawn to be the passed pawn that becomes a queen?

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The king comes closer to rescue the g-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: In forcing the king to defend the g-pawn, Black draws him farther away from his own passed pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only move. Against 42 g4 the win is easy: 42... h4 43 Bf1 Rc2 44 Kd4 Rf2 45 Bh3 Rxf3 46 Bg2 Rg3 47 Bf1 h3, etc.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Now to get behind the passed pawn! In the ending, the rook does its best work behind the enemy’s pawns. Its power to strike extends all along the line, so that no matter how far the pawn advances on the file, it can never escape from the rook’s attack.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Preparing to protect the pawn when it reaches c6. If at once 43 c6, then 43... Rc1 44 Be4 (but not 44 Bb5 Rc5 45 Ba4 Rc4+ winning the bishop), and we have the position reached a little later in the game by a transposition of moves.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
To the uninitiated, this appears strange! Why help the pawn move farther up the board?
Black’s idea is to compel the pawn to move to a light square. This will tie the bishop down to its defence and considerably limit the bishop’s sphere of activity.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The pawn moves up to come under the bishop’s protection.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: A tremendously effective move! It reduces White to a state of zugzwang – compulsion to move. What this means is that White might hold the game, except that he must make a move, and any move he makes is fatal because it disturbs the position unfavourably!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Voluntarily giving up the pawn he cannot save! The alternatives are extremely interesting:
1) 45 Kf5 Rc5+ (to drive the king back) 46 Kf4 Ke6 47 Ke3 (a bishop move loses the pawn at once, while 47 g4 allows 47... h4 giving Black a passed pawn) 47... f5 48 Bd3 Rxc6 and Black wins.
2) 45 Bd5 Rc5 46 Ke4 (46 Be4 Ke6 leads to play as in line ‘1’) 46... f5+ 47 Kd4 Rxd5+! 48 Kxd5 f4! 49 Kc5 (or 49 gxf4 h4 50 Kc5 Kd8 51 Kb6 Kc8 wins) 49...fxg3 50 Kb6 g2 51 c7 g1 Q + 52 Kb7 Qb1+ 53 Kc8 Qb6 54 f4 Qa7 55 f5 Qa8#.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Removing a potential danger. The ending still requires winning, and the manner of achieving the win is an illustration of smooth, flawless technique. The demonstration is as lucid and accurate as though it were the solution of a composed endgame study.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: To keep Black from moving his king to the fine square e6.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The rook intends to pursue the bishop until it leaves the diagonal overlooking the e6-square.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Understandably, the bishop tries to stay on the diagonal as long as possible. If instead 47 Bb3, then 47... Rb5 forces 48 Ba2 (48 Bc4 Rb4 pins the bishop, while 48 Ba4 Rb4+ also wins the bishop) 48... Rb2 49 Bd5 Rb4+! 50 Kf5 (50 Be4 Ke6 51 Ke3 f5 wins, or if 50 Ke3 then 50... f5 followed by 51... Kf6 and Black wins) 50... Rb5 51 Ke4 f5+ 52 Kd4 Rxd5+! 53 Kxd5 f4 54 gxf4 h4, when the pawn cannot be stopped!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Complete domination! The bishop has no moves!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Or 48 Ke4 f5+ 49 Kf4 Kf6 50 Ke3 (the bishop cannot move, and 50 g4 loses to 50...hxg4 51 fxg4 Rb4+ 52 Kf3 fxg4+) 50... Rb4 51 Bd5 f4+ 52 gxf4 h4 53 Kf2 Rb2+ 54 Kg1 Kf5 55 Bxf7 Kxf4 56 Bd5 Kg3 57 Be4 Ra2 58 Kf1 h3 and Black wins.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Allowing the bishop one square on the a2-g8 diagonal.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop could not go to b3 on account of the ensuing pin, and 49 Bb1 is answered by 49... Ke6 50 Kf4 Ra4+ 51 Ke3 (51 Be4 f5 wins the bishop) 51... f5 52 Bc2 f4+ 53 gxf4 (or 53 Kd2 fxg3) 53... Ra3+ 54 Kd2 Ra2 55 Kc1 Rxc2+ and Black wins.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Dislodging the bishop from the diagonal leading to e6.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: 50 Kd4 Rg5 wins a pawn at once, while 50 Ba2 is refuted by 50... f5, clearing f6 for Black’s king.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Another step nearer the centre and White’s remaining pawns.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White puts up a hard fight! He is ready to pounce on 51... f5 with 52 Kg5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Again restricting White to a move by the bishop. Playing 52 Ke4 succumbs to 52.. f5+ 53 Kf4 Kf6, etc.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White must keep watch over c4, otherwise (if he plays 52 Bb7, for example) 52... Rc4+ forces his king to retreat while Black’s can advance.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Finally! This pawn moves up a square and vacates f6 for the king.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The number of moves White has left is dwindling! 53 g4 fxg4 54 fxg4 h4 55 g5 h3 56 Kg4 h2 57 Bg2 Rc1 wins for Black, while after 53 Kg5 Rxf3 54 Bc4+ Ke5 55 Kh4 f4 Black again wins easily.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Stalemating White’s king. What remains now is to force him back to the third rank while Black’s king moves up to the fourth.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: If the bishop stays on the longer diagonal, for instance by 54 Be2, Black plays 54... Rb3 and then drives the king back by 55... Rb4+.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Compelling the king to retreat.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The only move.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: With the pretty threat 56... f4+ 57 Kd3 (57 gxf4+ Rxf4 gives Black a passed pawn, while 57 Kf2 Rc2+ 58 Kg1 fxg3 gives him two) 57...fxg3 58 Kxc4 Kf4!, and Black wins neatly.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A thrust at the rook by 56 Bd5 allows this finish: 56... f4+ 57 Ke2 Rc2+ 58 Kd3 Rc7 (simple but brutal), and Black wins.
With the text-move, White retreats in order to head off the potential passed pawn, whichever one that may be!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is the key move in all cases! Black threatens to win at once by 57... Rc2+ 58 Kg1 fxg3.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Ready to reply to the check with 58 Kh3 saving the pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Passed pawns must be pushed. This pawn, which stood patiently at f7 for 56 moves, is, believe it or not, the one that was destined to become the passed pawn that wins the game!
White does not wait for the proof: After 58 Kh3 fxg3 59 Kxg3 h4+ (a likely-looking candidate, but not the final choice) 60 Kh3 Rc3 61 Bd5 Kf4 62 Kxh4 Rxf3 63 Bxf3 Kxf3 64 Kh3 f4 65 Kh2 Khe2 the pawn marches straight through to be queened.
The whole game is beautiful, and the ending so fascinating that I could not resist a detailed analysis of its many fine points. A study of it is far more rewarding in entertainment and instruction than the playing over of a host of ‘brilliancies’ that feature a flinging about of pieces in wanton display.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Indian Defense: Capablanca Variation
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This opening move, seizing the centre with a pawn and making room for two pieces to come out, is efficient. White intends to develop all his pieces as quickly as possible, posting each of them in one move on its most suitable square. He will make only those pawn moves that speed his development (by releasing pieces or attacking the centre) or hinder that of his opponent.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Model development in every respect: the knight leaps in toward the centre where it has the greatest potential for attack, exerts immediate pressure on the important squares d5 and e4, and prevents White from establishing a strong pawn formation by 2 e4.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White develops the kingside pieces first, to enable early castling on that side. At f3, the knight stands on its most useful square in the opening. It is beautifully placed for attack – notice how it supplements the pawn’s grip on e5 – and is a peerless defender of the kingside after White castles.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black cannot wrest the initiative by brute force. He may get it if White plays carelessly (wasting time in the opening or chasing after pawns) but against normal development Black must content himself with achieving equality.
Black’s second move neutralizes White’s central pressure and opens lines for two of his own pieces.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: One of the rare occasions when a pawn move which does not aid development is opportune. This one attacks and threatens to eliminate, by 4 cxd5, Black’s centre. It does additional service in increasing the mobility (actual and potential) of White’s pieces. It clears a diagonal for the queen and assures the opening of the c-file for the later use of the queen or a1-rook.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black supports the d-pawn with another pawn. If White tries breaking up the centre by 4 cxd5, Black is prepared to recapture with a pawn, to keep the centre intact by maintaining a pawn at d5.
Although 3... e6 has the drawback of shutting in the c8-bishop, it is still Black’s best move. The difficulty in developing the bishop effectively may not seem alarming, but if it is not overcome, it will amount to Black playing a piece short. For the present, in partial compensation, the f8-bishop has lots of elbow-room.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This move has a terribly cramping effect on Black’s game. It clamps a pin on the knight and thereby exerts pressure on any pieces behind it. Black cannot move freely about while his kingside is gripped by the bishop.
In the 19th century, White would more often have developed the dark-squared bishop at f4, where it commands a useful diagonal. Nowadays we look for sharper, more vigorous moves. If we can mobilize our forces and at the same time restrain the enemy’s development, we accomplish more than with routine, often innocuous, measures. The pin of the knight paralyses Black’s only developed piece.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Why all the fuss when the pin is so easily lifted? For one thing, in unpinning the knight, the bishop is restricted to a defensive, passive role. Its development has been dictated by the fact that White put pressure on the knight.
Black’s play, incidentally, is in no way to be deprecated. The bishop’s move, modest as it is, is a step forward in the process of development. The bishop has left the last rank, taken up a strong defensive post, and cleared the kingside, enabling Black to castle.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Pawns should be moved sparingly in the opening, but since some pawns must be moved to get the bishops into play, this must be regarded as a developing move.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
In the Queen’s Gambit Declined, the ideal square for the development of the b8-knight is not c6 but d7. From d7, the knight supports an eventual thrust at White’s centre by the e-pawn or the c-pawn.
The knight must not develop at c6, where it blocks the c-pawn. This pawn must not be prevented from advancing to c5, where it can dispute control of the centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The white queen’s knight, contrariwise, is posted excellently at c3. It does not block the c-pawn and bears down on d5 and e4, two of the four important squares in the centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black transfers his king to a more secure location and brings his h8-rook closer to the centre files.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The rook develops where it has the most attractive prospects for attack. At c1 it controls and will exert pressure all along the open c-file. The file is obstructed now by White’s own knight and pawn, but the pawn can be disposed of by an exchange and the knight can move and clear the file. Strictly speaking, the file is only partly open, but open or not, the rook goes to c1 because:
Control of the c-file is absolutely vital in the Queen’s Gambit.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black’s rook moves to a centre file, where it may play a useful part in any action that takes place in the centre. The rook’s presence on the file is of little consequence now, but with every clearance on the file, its influence grows stronger and stronger.
Black’s game is cramped, but alternatives aimed at freeing it immediately are not convincing:
1) 7...dxc4 8 Bxc4 and White gains a tempo with this bishop, since it recaptures and develops at the same time.
2) 7... a6 (in order to continue with 8...dxc4 9 Bxc4 b5 10 Bd3 Bb7) 8 c5 can be very constraining.
3) 7... c5 8 dxc5 Nxc5 9 cxd5 exd5 (not9... Nxd5 10 Nxd5 exd5 11 Rxc5! Bxg5 12 Rxd5, when White wins the bishop) and Black’s d5-pawn is weak, while White has the fine d4-square as a central point for manoeuvring his pieces to any part of the board.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The best place on the board for the queen! From c2 the queen increases the pressure on the c-file and seizes control of the centre, making the problem of freeing himself troublesome for Black.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black gets impatient and tries to break loose. It would have been better to delay this capture, though, and wait for White to move his f1-bishop. Then the recapture costs the bishop an extra move. Black might have played instead 8... c6, strengthening the position of the d5-pawn and offering the queen an outlet to the queenside.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Obviously a gain of time for White, whose light-squared bishop recaptures a pawn and develops to a good square simultaneously.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must counterattack or be crushed to death. This offers the most practical chances in that he establishes tension in the centre and disputes control in that area. Furthermore, he prepares to oppose rooks on the c-file and fight for equal rights on the file.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The simplest way to keep up the pressure is to continue developing. At one stroke White removes his king to a safer part of the board and brings the h1-rook out of the corner and toward the centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black’s intention is to force White to a decision regarding the centre. If White recaptures with a pawn, it saddles him with an isolated pawn in the middle of the board; if with a piece, then his pawn-centre is no better than Black’s.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Rubinstein prefers this to 11 exd4, which maintains a pawn, but one that is isolated, in the centre.
The weakness of a pawn separated from its fellows lies not so much in the fact that the pawn can only be defended by pieces, but in the peculiar circumstance that enemy pieces can settle themselves on the square directly in front of the pawn (in this case d5) and stay there indefinitely, secure in the knowledge that no enemy pawns can drive them away.
The strength of an isolated pawn in the centre (for instance at d4, if White recaptured by 11 exd4) consists of its control of the strategically important e5- and c5-squares, its ability to spearhead an attack to break up a position, and its value as a support for an outpost – in this case a knight at e5.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Mainly to secure the b5-square from invasion by one of White’s minor pieces. The objection to this move is that pawn moves that do not contribute to development are a waste of valuable time in the opening. More to the point is 11... Ne5 12 Bb3 Bd7 13 Rfd1 Qb6, with a view to getting some action out of his pieces.
Notice that White has made only those pawn moves which were necessary to release pieces, or which added to the mobility of pieces already developed. Every single move, of piece or pawn, furthered the development of White’s position and increased its potential energy.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Now the rook swings over to the centre, placing itself at the head of a file facing the queen. The queen is sure to feel uncomfortable, no matter how many pieces separate the two, as threats are constantly in the air. For instance, if Black should play the plausible 12... Nb6, attacking the bishop, the reply 13 Nxe6 wins the queen by a discovered (and double) attack.
Yates and Winter comment admiringly at this point, “A classical example of correct development. White has brought his queen, rooks, bishops and one knight to almost ideal squares in one move each.”

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The queen flees the line of fire, gaining a little time by attacking a bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop retreats but maintains pressure on the knight.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Now the other bishop is threatened, apparently with more gain of time for Black.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Both bishops have been driven back, but, despite this, their latent power is enormous. The potential of two bishops working in harmony is not be to given up lightly, so White does not consider a move such as 14 Bd3 which lets Black play 14... Nxd3 and exchange a short-stepping knight for a long-range bishop. Condensed, it comes down to this:
It is an advantage to keep both bishops.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Swinging over to the kingside, the knight attacks the dark-squared bishop and forces it still further back. Meanwhile, more and more barriers are being put up about Black’s king, who now seems firmly entrenched in a bomb-proof shelter.
Despite all the time Black seems to have gained in his attacks on the white bishops, he should have done something to get his queenside pieces off the ground, for instance by 14... Bd7 instead. Then the continuation 15 Nb3 Qc7 16 Qb1 Bc6 gives him reasonable fighting chances.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The bishop must step back a square and relax its pressure on the knight, but now it commands a magnificent diagonal.
Black cannot continue chasing the bishops in an effort to get rid of one of them since after 15... Nh5 16 Nb3 Qg5 (the queen must protect the knight) 17 Ne4 Qh6 18 Bc7 White dominates the board.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
An extremely attractive move! These are all the things the pawn does:
1) It occupies a square in the centre.
2) It opens a path for the c8-bishop.
3) It cuts down the scope of White’s g3-bishop.
4) It will drive off White’s knight from its centralized position.
Against this, Black’s move offers one objection, seemingly a slight one. The d5-square, no longer under the pawn’s control, has been weakened. It offers White the prospect of utilizing this central point for the easy manoeuvring of his pieces to any part of the board.
Will this one liability outweigh all the assets? It is this judgement of imponderables, where exact calculation is not possible, that makes chess a fascinating blend of art and science.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight must leave but retaliates by getting in a thrust at the queen.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The queen evades the attack, and Black prepares to regroup his pieces, perhaps by 17... Bd7, 18... Bc6 and 19... Rad8.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
This is White’s fifth retreating move in succession, but with every step backward his position improves! Though driven back to the first three ranks, his pieces will gain in dynamic energy. Gradually they will take up stronger positions, dominate the board, and put the enemy to flight.
Black has no time now to develop his c8-bishop as after 17.... Bd7 18 Nd5 Qd8 (if 18... Nxd5, then 19 Rxc7 Nxc7 20 Rxd7 wins) 19 Nc7 White wins the exchange.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black’s queen was forced to retreat (by the threat of a discovered attack) while White’s queen moved to b1 voluntarily.
The difference in the positions is apparent:
1) White’s queen does not obstruct the rooks, which together control the two open files; Black’s queen and bishop separate his rooks, one of which is completely shut in, while the other’s action is severely limited.
2) White has two agile, longrange bishops; Black has one, with the other undeveloped and still at home.
3) White’s queen can leap into the fray quickly; Black’s must skulk on the fringes of the board.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop seizes the long diagonal and prevents Black from playing 18... b5 (the punishment being 19 Bxa8) and then fianchettoing his bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black’s manoeuvring is tortuous, but evidently he wants to bring his rook to b8, then play ...b5, and finally develop his queen’s bishop at b7 .

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A fine preventive move! It stops 19... Rb8 followed by 20... b5 as then 21 Nc6 wins the exchange, while the direct 19... Bd7 or 19... Be6 costs Black his b-pawn.
Notice how White not only sees to the development of his own pieces but hinders that of his opponent.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black tries to chase off the knight, which is hampering the free movement of his queenside pieces.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The knight must leave, but in compensation it enjoys the advantage of being nearer the centre.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The bishop moves to the only square available for its development! If Black tries instead 20... Be6, then 21 Nxe5 wins a pawn, while on 20... Bg4 21 Bxg4 Nxg4 22 Nd5 the threats of 23 Nxb4 (winning a piece) and 23 Nc7 (winning the exchange) cannot both be met.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Obviously, such a dangerous beast must be removed!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: White recaptures with the threat of 23 Bxf7+ Kxf7 24 Rxd7+, winning a pawn. He gains a tempo with this, as Black must drop whatever he is doing to parry the threat.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black must rid the board of the terrible bishop which attacks his kingside and restrains his queenside. It would not do to play 22... Bc6 as 23 Bxc6 bxc6 24 Qe4 wins the c-pawn or the e-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A master move in every respect, and a one-move lesson in positional play! Where most of us think of an exchange in terms of what happens after 23 Bxe6, the great master visualizes an exchange as an opportunity to substitute another piece for one that must come off the board. White is willing to exchange, but only if he can be assured of keeping control of d5 by replacing the bishop with another piece.
Let me reword this, so that the message is unmistakable:
Supporting a piece under attack (here the bishop at d5) puts more pressure on Black, where a direct exchange or a retreat might relieve it.
Note incidentally the full effect of the queen’s magnificent centralization, and her radiation of power in so many directions:
1) The queen supports the bishop at d5.
2) The queen adds to the bishop’s attack on the b-pawn.
3) The queen helps in the attack on the e-pawn.
4) The queen threatens (indirectly) Black’s b4-bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Practically forced in view of the many threats. An attempt to drive the queen off by 23... f5 is brusquely refuted by 24 Qxf5 and Black (whose bishop is pinned) is unable to take the queen.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black rids himself of one troublesome piece only to have another one take its place! For the third time, White anchors a piece at d5, each time intensifying his grip on the position. Now there is a fourfold attack on the e-pawn, by rook, knight, bishop and queen. While this pawn is being rescued, White will gain the time needed to double his rooks on the d-file, guaranteeing him permanent possession of this vital highway. The effect on Black will be to cut communication between his forces, making an organized resistance difficult.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Protecting the pawn indirectly by pinning one of its attackers.
White cannot take the pawn with the knight on pain of mate, nor with the rook or the queen, as that results in loss of material to White. This leaves 25 Bxe5, and Black is ready to punish that with 25... f6 26 Bd4 Rxe4 27 Bxa7 Rexc4, when he has gained a piece.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Doubling the rooks on an open file, an act that more than doubles the strength of the rooks. White’s knight is now unpinned, and the attack on the e-pawn renewed, with incidentally a threat of discovered attack on the bishop.
White has a won game theoretically, and Rubinstein wins it in a way that is both efficient and artistic.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Black transfers the exposed bishop to the defence.
Against the immediate counterattack by 25... f5, White has a winning continuation in 26 Qxf5 Rxc4 27 Rd8! Rxd8 28 Rxd8+ Nf8 29 Qe6+ Kh8 30 Qxc4, when he is the exchange ahead.
After Black’s actual move, he can answer 26 Nxe5 with 26... f6, winning the unfortunate knight. In addition, he contemplates the thrust 26... f5, which after 27 Qd3 (to protect the knight) 27... f4 occasions some trouble for the bishop.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Frees the queen from the duty of guarding the knight and stops any such move as 26... f5, when the pawn would simply be snapped up.
Against passive play, White will continue by 27 Rd7, invading the seventh rank.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: The object of this is not so much to dislodge the knight as it is to open a line for the queen, enabling her to return to the kingside and the defence of the king.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A knight fork which will force an exchange – a simplification to White’s advantage. He will maintain the pressure inherent in a superior position without running the risk of being involved in unnecessary complications.
A premature attack, in fact, might even result in a loss for White! Consider this pretty possibility (instead of the actual move): 27 Nxe5 f6 28 Rd7 (apparently a saving move, as White attacks the queen and threatens to follow with 29 Qd5+ unpinning his knight) 28... Qxd7! and Black wins! The recapture by the rook allows Black to mate, while 29 Nxd7 Rxe4 leaves Black a rook ahead.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Black had no choice, as the knight attacked both his rooks.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The recapture vacates the d5square for occupation by the queen; the tripling of heavy pieces on the d-file would increase the advantage that White already has. However, an even more potent threat is the possibility of establishing a beachhead on the seventh rank by 29 Rd7.
The posting of a rook on the seventh rank, in the middlegame or the ending, is a tremendous positional advantage.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: This is the key to the decisive attack! The obvious threat is 30 h5, dislodging the knight, and then capturing the e-pawn. The ulterior purpose is to compel Black to protect the endangered pawn by 29... f6, weakening the cordon of pawns near his king. Further weaknesses may then be induced by h5 and h6, attacking the g-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Clearly, to give the e-pawn the solid support only another pawn affords.
The alternative 29... Rce7 succumbs to 30 Qc6 followed by 31 Rd8, with an easy win, while 29... h5 (to prevent 30 h5) allows 30 Qf5, winning the h-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
Against the only other possibility, 31... Ne7, White wins easily by 32 Qf7 with a million threats. Let’s take a look at some interesting possibilities then:
1) 32... Rg8 33 h6 (threatening 34 Rd8 followed by mate at g7) 33... Nf5 34 hxg7+ Nxg7 35 Qxf6 and Black both loses a pawn and falls into a deadly pin.
2) 32... Qb8 33 h6 gxh6 34 Qxf6+ Kg8 35 Bxe5 Ng6 36 Rd7 with a quick mate.
3) 32... Rcc8 33 h6 gxh6 34 Bh4, threatening 35 Bxf6#. Black cannot guard against that mate by a knight move as it leaves his queen en prise.
How many of these variations did White foresee? And how many did Black know he was avoiding when he moved his knight to f8 instead of to e7?
The answer is – probably none! A good player can, almost at a glance, sense the effect of a move that is obviously decisive. He saves himself a great deal of valuable time when he does not even bother about analysing the resources of such a defence as 31... Ne7. The fact that it permits such a paralysing entrance into the vitals as 32 Qf7 practically rules it out from more than fleeting consideration.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
White drives the wedge in still further. White’s object is to break up the pawn position around Black’s king. If Black’s g-pawn can be uprooted, it will make the f-pawn, the keystone of his game, vulnerable to attack. And if that falls. Black’s whole position falls with it.
White’s immediate threat is 33 hxg7+ Kxg7 34 Bh4 Rf7 35 Qc6, with an attack on the e8-rook and a triple attack on the f-pawn.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
A spectacular move! White is not playing to the gallery in offering a queen sacrifice. All that he wants is to penetrate still deeper into the heart of Black’s position, and this is the simplest way to do so. The move is brilliant nevertheless, and making a move of this sort (even vicariously) gives one a thrill.
I must warn the player who likes the excitement of springing a surprise move on his opponent that it is a waste of time to look for brilliant moves in the course of a game unless the position warrants it. You must first get an advantage, however slight. Work on increasing the advantage until you have built up a position that is definitely superior. Once you have established your right to look for combinations, the brilliant moves will come of themselves.
White of course does not expect Black to take his queen and allow 34 Rd8+ and a quick mate. What he has in mind primarily is to secure complete control of d7, an important square for his rooks to exploit.
One of the most interesting things to me in the position is that White threatens his opponent with disaster on three ranks:
1) On the eighth rank by 34 Qxe8+ followed by mate.
2) On the seventh rank by 34 Rd7 followed by 35 hxg7#.
3) On the sixth rank by 34 hxg7+ Kxg7 35 Qxf6+, winning easily.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: There isn’t too much choice, in view of all the threats. Black’s move gives the f-pawn added protection.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: Threatening 35 hxg7# – mate on the move!

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation: 34... Rxd7 is no better since the recapture 35 Rxd7 threatens mate on one side, and the queen on the other. White also forces mate after 34... Rg8 35 hxg7+ Rxg7 36 Rd8+.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev

annotation:
The bishop, which has stood in one spot for twenty-five moves, applies the finishing touch! The threat is 36 Bxf6+ x Rf6 37 Qxf6+ Kg8 38 Qg7#.
If 35... Nxh4, then 36 Qe7 threatens 37 Qxf8#, 37 Qg7# or 37 Qxh7#, and no one can survive such a display of feminine power!
An impressive, deeply satisfying game, one of the finest in the literature of chess.

metadata.Opening: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Main Line
metadata.StudyName: Logical Chess Move by Move: Chernev
